title: Node.js Runtime and Express
description:
Backend foundations: the Node.js runtime, Express, API design, background jobs, real-time systems and backend practices.

---

This part is the floor the whole backend phase stands on. Part 2 (5.3-5.5) assumes you can already read a framework; here you learn what the framework is actually running on: the event loop, the thread pool, streams, the file system, process management, and the HTTP layer as Express builds it.

**The through-line of this part:** Node is *not* a faster browser. It is a single-threaded event loop with a pool of OS threads behind it, plus V8's compiler and garbage collector. Almost every Node performance and reliability question reduces to one question: **is this work on the main thread, and is the event loop free when it matters?** An interviewer who hears you answer that question unprompted, three times, is already impressed.

**How to use this part**
- 5.1.1-5.1.4 and 5.1.10-5.1.11 are the ones that get asked in *every* backend interview. Learn the orderings by hand, not by recognising them.
- 5.1.6 (streams) and 5.1.7 (`fs`) are the two where most candidates have a mental model but cannot write working code. Do the exercises in the MUST-IMPLEMENT block.
- 5.1.12, 5.1.13, 5.1.16 are what separate a mid-level from a senior. You need the *vocabulary* and the *commands*, not mastery.
- 5.2.1-5.2.7 is Express's daily vocabulary. 5.2.8-5.2.14 is where production quality lives. 5.2.15 is the "pick the right tool" answer.

**Cross-references you should not look up twice**
- NestJS, REST, and GraphQL: **PHASE 5, PART 2**. When 5.2.11 says "use a controller/service/repository split", 5.3.1 is the same split expressed as a DI graph.
- Token bucket / sliding window and shared rate-limit state: **PHASE 6 Caching Layers** (canonical rate limiting entry).
- WebSocket protocol, sticky sessions, Redis adapters: **PHASE 5, Real-Time Systems**. Hono appears there as an edge-transport option.
- AuthN/authZ primitives, JWT, OAuth, session storage: **PHASE 7**. Here we only place the check in the pipeline.
- Deployment, containers, autoscaling, load balancers: **PHASE 8**. 5.1.8 and 5.1.11 stop at the process boundary.
- Worker queues and message brokers: **PHASE 5, Background Processing and Messaging**. 5.1.8 covers in-process parallelism, not durable jobs.

This part finishes the backend phase. Part 1 covered the raw runtime and the HTTP layer itself (Node, Express, middleware, request parsing, error handling, security headers, logging, project structure). This part is about what you build **on top** of that: a framework that gives you structure (5.3), the design of the HTTP contract you expose (5.4), and the alternative that lets clients shape their own queries (5.5).

**Difficulty markers:** ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· âš« Expert / staff-level.

**How to use this part**
- 5.3 is the one you will be interviewed on if you write NestJS at work. If you have never used it, read 5.3.1, 5.3.3, 5.3.6 and 5.3.7 properly; the rest is vocabulary.
- 5.4 is the one that separates "I built a CRUD app" from "I designed an API". Interviewers reward precise status codes, cursor pagination and idempotency answers far more than framework trivia.
- 5.5 is partly a GraphQL part, partly a "pick the right tool" part. The last third of 5.5 (REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC vs tRPC, when GraphQL is wrong) is the highest-value part.

objectives: Explain the Node.js event loop phases and where blocking happens
Design a REST API with predictable errors, pagination and versioning
Add background jobs without losing work

practice.title: Drill 1 â€” The canonical ordering puzzle
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: synchronous code completes; then the *entire* nextTick queue drains (D); then the *entire* microtask queue drains (E); then the loop reaches its timers phase. B (0 ms) and C (check phase) are genuinely unordered at the top level of a module because we are already inside a tick that passed its timers phase. F at 1 ms is a later timers phase.
probe: re-run it 100 times; you will see both B C and C B. Then move the two calls inside an fs.readFile callback and note that C always comes first. Explain the difference: the loop has already passed timers, so a new 0 ms timer cannot fire until the next tick, while an immediate scheduled right there runs in this tick's check phase.

practice.title: Drill 2 â€” nextTick drains to exhaustion
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: the nextTick queue is drained completely, and anything added *during* the drain is also drained, so the recursion is effectively synchronous â€” it is a hang, not a stack overflow. The microtask runs *after* the whole tick queue, not interleaved. The fix for deep work: setImmediate to yield, or a loop.

practice.title: Drill 3 â€” Microtasks starve I/O
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: microtasks are un-preemptible. A million of them run before the loop turns over at all, so the 0 ms timer and even the check phase wait. This is why "async" code with no real suspension (await Promise.resolve() in a loop) is still blocking.

practice.title: Drill 4 â€” Thread pool step function
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: fs.promises is not "off the main thread with no limit"; it is the thread pool, and latency is a step function of concurrency / poolSize. The same is true of zlib, crypto.scrypt/pbkdf2, and dns.lookup.

practice.title: Drill 5 â€” Stream pipeline: which side blocks, and when
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: write() returning false is a request to pause, not a failure; the producer is Readable.from an async generator and the async iteration suspends it; that is why peak memory is HWM + one chunk, not the whole 640 KB.

practice.title: Drill 6 â€” flush(cb) and the dropped tail
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
items: With buggy, the promise never settles
practice.sayOutLoud: a Transform that buffers must implement _flush; the last record is silently lost otherwise, and the stream never ends, which also keeps the process alive.

practice.title: Drill 7 â€” StringDecoder and split multi-byte characters
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: a UTF-8 sequence can straddle a chunk boundary; StringDecoder holds the partial sequence. Every text-processing Transform needs it, and its absence is a bug that shows up roughly 1 in 4,096 chunks â€” never in a small test.

practice.title: Drill 8 â€” Express onion order
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: code after next() is on the *response* path. To time a request you must use res.on('finish'), because next() returns as soon as the *next layer's synchronous part* finishes, not when the response is sent.

practice.title: Drill 9 â€” next(err) skips the rest
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: Express keeps one ordered list; on error it walks it looking for length === 4. Every non-error layer is skipped. This is also why the error handler must be registered *after* the layer that throws.

practice.title: Drill 10 â€” The 3-arity trap
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: Express identifies error middleware by declared arity (fn.length === 4). next may be unused, but it must be *declared*. Underscore-prefixing a parameter does not reduce arity.
practice.reference:
```js
app.use((err, req, res) => { console.error(err); res.status(500).end(); });   // NOT an error handler
// and this one:
app.use(function (err, req, res, next) { console.error(err); res.status(500).end(); });  // IS
```

```js
app.use((err, req, res) => { console.error(err); res.status(500).end(); });   // NOT an error handler
// and this one:
app.use(function (err, req, res, next) { console.error(err); res.status(500).end(); });  // IS
```

**Behaviour:** the first is registered as ordinary middleware, runs on *every* request with `err === undefined`, and every real error reaches Node's default HTML page.
**Say out loud:** Express identifies error middleware by declared arity (`fn.length === 4`). `next` may be unused, but it must be *declared*. Underscore-prefixing a parameter does not reduce arity.

---

practice.title: Drill 11 â€” The parameter-route shadowing trace
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
fix: literals first. And note app.use('/users', r) would match /users/anything/extra as a *prefix*, unlike app.get('/users', r).

practice.title: Drill 12 â€” app.use('/api') also matches /api-key
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: app.use is prefix matching with no path-segment boundary. This is the exact reason /api and /api-key cannot coexist in that order. Put the specific one first, or validate the remaining path.
practice.reference:
```js
app.use('/api', apiRouter);        // registered FIRST
app.use('/api-key', apiKeyAuth);
```

```js
app.use('/api', apiRouter);        // registered FIRST
app.use('/api-key', apiKeyAuth);
```
**Request `GET /api-key/secret`:** it matches `app.use('/api')` (prefix) and enters `apiRouter`, which 404s it â€” so `apiKeyAuth` never runs.
**Say out loud:** `app.use` is prefix matching with no path-segment boundary. This is the exact reason `/api` and `/api-key` cannot coexist in that order. Put the specific one first, or validate the remaining path.

practice.title: Drill 13 â€” Express 4 vs 5: what each does with a rejected promise
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: the Express 4 fixes are the ah() wrapper, express-async-errors, or an upgrade. A process.on('unhandledRejection') handler makes the log louder and leaves the request hanging.
practice.reference:
```js
app.get('/boom', async (req, res) => { throw new Error('kaboom'); });
```

```js
app.get('/boom', async (req, res) => { throw new Error('kaboom'); });
```

**Express 4:** nothing catches it. No response is sent; the client hangs until the proxy times out; Node logs an `UnhandledPromiseRejection`. **Express 5:** the rejection is forwarded to `next(err)` and your error handler runs.
**Say out loud:** the Express 4 fixes are the `ah()` wrapper, `express-async-errors`, or an upgrade. A `process.on('unhandledRejection')` handler makes the log louder and leaves the request hanging.

---

practice.title: Drill 14 â€” req.body is undefined without a parser
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: the parser only activates for a matching Content-Type, and req.body is undefined (not {}) otherwise. A missing header is the single most common cause of "my POST body is empty". This is also the whole reason for the order rule: parsers before anything that reads the body.

practice.title: Drill 15 â€” Express 5 query parser change
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: Express 5 defaults to the standard URLSearchParams parser; set app.set('query parser', 'extended') (or install qs and write a custom parser so you own depth, arrayLimit, allowPrototypes) if you relied on nesting. This is the most common silent Express 4 â†’ 5 break.

practice.title: Drill 16 â€” The two-send bug
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
fix: if (res.headersSent) return next(err); as the first line of every error handler.

practice.title: Drill 17 â€” Compression and Vary
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: Vary must be present on both, or a shared cache will serve compressed bytes to a client that did not ask for them (or vice versa) â€” a cache-correctness bug, not a performance one. And the header must be set by whatever compresses; if a proxy also compresses, you get gzip(gzip(x)), which is *larger* than the original.
practice.reference:
```bash
curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' localhost:3000/api/data | grep -iE 'content-encoding|vary'
# content-encoding: gzip
# vary: Accept-Encoding
curl -sI localhost:3000/api/data | grep -iE 'content-encoding|vary'
# vary: Accept-Encoding          â† still there, and NO content-encoding
```

```bash
curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' localhost:3000/api/data | grep -iE 'content-encoding|vary'
# content-encoding: gzip
# vary: Accept-Encoding
curl -sI localhost:3000/api/data | grep -iE 'content-encoding|vary'
# vary: Accept-Encoding          â† still there, and NO content-encoding
```

**Say out loud:** `Vary` must be present on both, or a shared cache will serve compressed bytes to a client that did not ask for them (or vice versa) â€” a cache-correctness bug, not a performance one. And the header must be set by whatever compresses; if a proxy also compresses, you get `gzip(gzip(x))`, which is *larger* than the original.

practice.title: Drill 18 â€” req.query vs req.params vs req.body vs req.url inside a mounted router
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
practice.sayOutLoud: req.url is rewritten by each app.use mount, so it is the single most common cause of "my 404 handler prints the wrong path". req.originalUrl is never rewritten.
practice.reference:
```js
app.use('/api/orders', ordersRouter);            // ordersRouter has: router.get('/:id', h)
```

```js
app.use('/api/orders', ordersRouter);            // ordersRouter has: router.get('/:id', h)
```
**Request `GET /api/orders/42?expand=items`:**
| expression | value |
|---|---|
| `req.baseUrl` | `/api/orders` |
| `req.url` | `/42?expand=items` (rewritten â€” relative!) |
| `req.path` | `/42` (no query string) |
| `req.params.id` | `42` |
| `req.query.expand` | `items` |
| `req.originalUrl` | `/api/orders/42?expand=items` â† **log this one** |

**Say out loud:** `req.url` is rewritten by each `app.use` mount, so it is the single most common cause of "my 404 handler prints the wrong path". `req.originalUrl` is never rewritten.

practice.title: Scenario 1 â€” p99 is 40Ã— p50 and CPU sits at 100% of one core
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: average latency 4 ms, p99 380 ms, one core pegged, GC normal-looking. It only appears above ~200 rps. Lowering concurrency makes it disappear.

(a) a CPU-bound handler (hashing, JSON of a large graph, a synchronous library); (b) excessive allocation causing scavenge storms; (c) a synchronous API in the request path (readFileSync, bcrypt); (d) a megamorphic hot property access (5.1.16); (e) deoptimisation introduced by a recent deploy.
investigation: event-loop delay histogram (monitorEventLoopDelay) â€” if the p99 loop delay is ~300 ms, the loop is blocked and it is *not* a dependency problem. Then a CPU profile under load (not at boot): node --cpu-prof, load in speedscope, sort by self time. Read the [GC] section first. Then --trace-deopt for functions that "used to be fast".
fix: by finding the frame: move it to a worker (5.1.8), memoise it, reduce the allocation rate, or replace the sync API. If it is a deopt, normalise the object shape at the boundary (construct the object with all fields, in one order).
prevention: per-route event-loop delay as a metric; a p99 SLO with an alert; allocation-rate budgets; a load test that runs *concurrently* rather than serially, because a serial benchmark cannot see concurrency effects.
tools: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, eventLoopUtilization(), --cpu-prof, --trace-deopt, --trace-gc, clinic.js.
practice.reference:
**Symptoms:** average latency 4 ms, p99 380 ms, one core pegged, GC normal-looking. It only appears above ~200 rps. Lowering concurrency makes it disappear.

**Likely causes:** (a) a CPU-bound handler (hashing, JSON of a large graph, a synchronous library); (b) excessive allocation causing scavenge storms; (c) a synchronous API in the request path (`readFileSync`, `bcrypt`); (d) a megamorphic hot property access (5.1.16); (e) deoptimisation introduced by a recent deploy.

**Investigation:** event-loop delay histogram (`monitorEventLoopDelay`) â€” if the p99 loop delay is ~300 ms, the loop is blocked and it is *not* a dependency problem. Then a CPU profile **under load** (not at boot): `node --cpu-prof`, load in speedscope, sort by self time. Read the `[GC]` section first. Then `--trace-deopt` for functions that "used to be fast".

**Tools:** `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`, `eventLoopUtilization()`, `--cpu-prof`, `--trace-deopt`, `--trace-gc`, `clinic.js`.

**Fix:** by finding the frame: move it to a worker (5.1.8), memoise it, reduce the allocation rate, or replace the sync API. If it is a deopt, normalise the object shape at the boundary (construct the object with all fields, in one order).

**Prevention:** per-route event-loop delay as a metric; a p99 SLO with an alert; allocation-rate budgets; a load test that runs *concurrently* rather than serially, because a serial benchmark cannot see concurrency effects.

practice.title: Scenario 2 â€” Latency cliffs every few hundred milliseconds on an otherwise idle service
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: p50 3 ms, but every ~1 s a batch of requests takes 300-800 ms. No CPU spike. Raising the error rate is unrelated. Only affects endpoints that do file or crypto work.

libuv thread pool saturation (default 4). Something in the process is doing fs, zlib (gzip from compression!), crypto.scrypt/pbkdf2, or dns.lookup â€” and the pool is shared, so an unrelated route queues behind it.

practice.title: Scenario 3 â€” RSS grows 60 MB/hour, heap is flat
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: container OOM-killed on a 512 MB limit after ~8 hours. heapUsed is stable at 90 MB. external climbs steadily. Heap snapshots show almost nothing retained.
a Buffer/ArrayBuffer leak â€” Buffer.allocUnsafe with a partial write, a cached subarray pinning an 8 KB slab, an unconsumed stream, a native addon, or V8 fragmentation.
investigation: process.memoryUsage() over time, separating external/arrayBuffers from heapUsed â€” flat heap plus rising external is the signature. rss minus heapTotal gives the native total. Take two --heapsnapshot-signal snapshots; if the heap delta is near zero, confirm the leak is off-heap and go to native tooling.
fix: at the retainer â€” for Buffers, that means finding the owner. Common real causes: a Map cache of Buffers with no bound (make it LRU); a subarray held in a long-lived object (Buffer.from(view) to copy); a readable stream never resumed or never destroyed; a base64 string kept alongside its decoded bytes.
prevention: cap every cache; assert external stability in a CI test with a create/destroy loop; lint for allocUnsafe; alert on the rss slope, not the level.
tools: process.memoryUsage() gauges, --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit, clinic heap, valgrind --leak-check (slow, definitive), a Buffer-usage lint rule banning allocUnsafe without a following fill/write of the full length.

practice.title: Scenario 4 â€” Listeners grow with connection count; memory climbs after disconnects
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: memory grows with concurrent connections and does not come back after they close. CPU on an event fan-out rises quadratically. MaxListenersExceededWarning appears on a bus.

investigation: emitter.listenerCount(ev) and emitter.rawListeners(ev) (which unwraps once); emitter.eventNames(); a setInterval(â€¦ , 30_000) sweep asserting counts; activeHandles() to spot stray timers. tools: events.getEventListeners, the MaxListenersExceededWarning trace, --heap-prof, process._getActiveHandles().

practice.title: Scenario 5 â€” Every deploy produces ~200 502s over 20 seconds
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: during rolling deploys, a spike of 502/504 for roughly the grace period. Requests that arrived *before* SIGTERM are the ones failing. Health checks pass.

(a) no SIGTERM handler â€” default is immediate termination; (b) server.close() with keep-alive sockets never finishing, so the drain exceeds the grace period and SIGKILL lands; (c) readiness not flipped, so the proxy keeps routing to a dying instance; (d) liveness flipped, so the orchestrator killed it mid-drain; (e) CMD ["npm","start"] so the signal never reaches Node.
investigation: correlate the 502 timestamps with the pod's StartedAt/TerminatedAt and its termination message (OOMKilled vs Error); check whether the last log line is from a draining message; look at whether the drain duration exceeded the grace period (kubectl describe pod â†’ Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error); verify the entrypoint with docker inspect.
fix: the full sequence from 5.1.11/problem 9 â€” flip readiness first, keep liveness green, track and end idle sockets, wait on a counter with a deadline under the grace period, flush in order, exit 0. And change the entrypoint to CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"].
prevention: a deploy test that kills under load; an alert on drain duration; a documented deadline arithmetic; a preStop sleep so endpoint removal propagates.
tools: kill -TERM under a load test, kubectl describe, orchestrator termination messages, a shutdown_inflight gauge, drain-duration metric.
practice.reference:

practice.title: Scenario 6 â€” Client reports "blocked by CORS policy" but curl works
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: browser console shows a CORS error; the actual status is invisible. Works on one origin, not another. Sometimes only on preflighted requests (PATCH/DELETE or with Authorization).

cors mounted after the routes so OPTIONS 404s; the preflight hitting authentication or the rate limiter; an origin not on the allowlist (the cors origin *function* throwing a 403); Access-Control-Allow-Headers missing a header the client sends; Vary: Origin missing so a cache serves the wrong response; credentials: true with origin: true reflecting any origin.
investigation: reproduce the preflight by hand â€” curl -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: â€¦' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: PATCH' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization' and read the real status; check the response headers for Access-Control-Allow-Origin/-Headers/-Credentials; check whether the failing origin is in the allowlist; if it works in curl but not the browser, suspect a *simple vs preflighted* difference.
fix: move cors above routes, auth and the limiter; allowlist the origin explicitly; add the headers the client sends; set Vary: Origin; if cookies are used, use an explicit allowlist function instead of reflecting.
prevention: a preflight integration test for a protected, non-simple route; a config-driven allowlist validated at boot; a runbook entry that says "CORS errors: read the real status with curl -X OPTIONS first".
tools: DevTools network panel with "Disable cache", curl -v, the cors package's own debug output, a preflight integration test (the one in problem 8).
practice.reference:

practice.title: Scenario 7 â€” Compression made p99 worse and CPU doubled
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: after adding compression(), throughput up, p50 down, p99 up 5Ã—, and the event-loop delay histogram got fat. Only burst traffic is affected.

practice.title: Scenario 8 â€” Webhook signature verification fails intermittently
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: most webhooks verify; a small fraction fail with a signature mismatch. Failures cluster after a deploy and around larger payloads.

reading the *parsed* body instead of the raw bytes (any re-serialisation changes them); a body parser mounted globally before the webhook route, so the raw buffer is already consumed; a proxy that re-encodes or decompresses the body; using === instead of timingSafeEqual with different-length buffers throwing; two secrets during a rotation with the wrong one checked first.
investigation: capture the raw body (express.raw() or the verify hook) and hash both the captured and the re-serialised body and compare; check the order of the middleware in app.js; check the proxy for Content-Encoding transformation; check whether failures correlate with payload size above some threshold.
fix: mount express.raw() (or verify) on the webhook path before express.json(); hash the captured buffer; support both secrets during rotation; handle unequal lengths without throwing.
prevention: a test with a stored real-world raw body; a route-level integration test through the real middleware order; a runbook note that the raw body is required for signature verification.
tools: express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) on a narrow path, a verify hook, crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers, a stored raw-body fixture in tests.
practice.reference:

symptoms: sparse 500s on a single replica, correlated with one account, correlated with time. No code change in the window. Reproduces only with production data.

practice.title: Scenario 11 â€” The process will not exit after tests or in a CLI
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
symptoms: the script finishes its work and then hangs; tests pass but the process never terminates; Ctrl-C needed.

a setInterval without clearInterval and without unref(); a server socket still listening; a fs.watch handle; a process.stdin read handler (interactive CLIs read stdin, which keeps the loop alive); a pool of workers that was never terminated; an open DB pool; a pending setTimeout longer than the test timeout.
investigation: process._getActiveHandles() and process._getActiveRequests() and read the constructor names: Timeout, Socket, FSWatcher, ReadStream, Worker, ChildProcess, Pipe.
fix: unref() on timers/handles that should not keep the process alive; server.close(); watcher.close(); worker.terminate(); pool.end(); process.stdin.unref() in a non-interactive CLI.
prevention: an after() hook in the test bootstrap that closes every resource the app created; --detect-open-handles on the test run for a week.
tools: process._getActiveHandles(), why-is-node-running (the third-party module built for exactly this), --trace-exit.

items: What are the event loop phases, in order?
Predict: console.log(1); setTimeout(â€¦0); setImmediate(â€¦); nextTick(â€¦); Promise.resolve().then(â€¦)
So when *is* setImmediate guaranteed to beat setTimeout(0)?
What is libuv, and what is the thread pool?

questions.text: What are the event loop phases, in order?
questions.answer: timers â†’ pending callbacks â†’ idle/prepare â†’ poll â†’ check â†’ close, then repeat. setTimeout lives in timers, I/O callbacks in poll, setImmediate in check. The microtask queue and the nextTick queue are drained after every phase *and* after every callback within a phase

questions.text: Predict: console.log(1); setTimeout(â€¦0); setImmediate(â€¦); nextTick(â€¦); Promise.resolve().then(â€¦)
questions.answer: 1, then nextTick, then the promise, then a race between the 0 ms timer and the immediate. The first three are guaranteed; the last two are not â€” the loop is already past its timers phase, so whether a 0 ms timer is "already due" is timing

questions.text: So when *is* setImmediate guaranteed to beat setTimeout(0)?
questions.answer: From inside an I/O callback or a timer callback. The loop has already passed timers for this tick, so a new 0 ms timer cannot run until the next tick, while an immediate scheduled right there runs in this tick's check phase

nextTick queue drains completely before the microtask queue, at every boundary, and anything queued during the drain is also drained â€” so unbounded recursion is a hang, not a stack overflow. Promises are the microtask queue; both starve I/O. nextTick is a Node-specific ordering tool, not a scheduler

After a synchronous operation must be allowed to complete cleanly before you touch state it would surprise the caller â€” e.g. reporting from an uncaughtException handler inside an emit. Never to schedule work, never to "yield". To yield, use setImmediate

questions.text: What is libuv, and what is the thread pool?
questions.answer: libuv is the C cross-platform I/O library under Node's core: the loop, async I/O (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), and a default 4-thread pool used for fs, zlib, dns.lookup, and crypto (randomBytes, pbkdf2, scrypt, randomUUID). Socket I/O does not use the pool

questions.text: Which of these use the thread pool?
questions.answer: fs.* (all), fsp.readFile, zlib.gzip (async form), crypto.randomBytes/pbkdf2/scrypt/randomUUID, dns.lookup. Not sockets, not dns.resolve4 (c-ares), not fs.readFileSync (main thread)

questions.text: How do you know the thread pool is your bottleneck?
questions.answer: Sweep UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 vs 16 at the same load. Latency is a *step function* of concurrency Ã· pool size, so the p99 collapses at 16 and barely moves at 1. If neither changes anything, the pool was never involved

questions.text: Why did raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE make things worse?
questions.answer: It is the wrong lever when the real problem is work in the process. More threads cost memory, add context switching, and increase contention. The right fix is usually to move compression to a proxy, precompress static assets, or move hashing to a worker

Code that *computes* rather than *waits*. The event loop only progresses between callbacks, so a synchronous computation blocks every other request, every timer, and every I/O completion â€” with no preemption. The signature is p99 â‰« p50, correlated with concurrency, one core at 100%

questions.text: Three ways to fix CPU-bound work?
questions.answer: (1) Make it cheaper â€” measure, memoise, use a faster algorithm. (2) worker_threads for a bounded pool. (3) A child process or a separate service for isolation. For anything over ~100 ms or anything retryable, a job queue, not a worker

questions.text: How do you tell a CPU-bound route from a slow dependency?
questions.answer: Event loop delay histogram (monitorEventLoopDelay): fat if the loop is *blocked* (CPU-bound); flat if the loop is idle and you are *waiting* (dependency). Then a CPU profile under load, and eventLoopUtilization() to separate "busy" from "stalled"

questions.text: What is a Buffer and why not a string?
questions.answer: A view over raw bytes, off the V8 heap. Strings are UTF-16 code-unit sequences and cannot hold arbitrary bytes: 'ðŸ˜€'.length === 2 but Buffer.from('ðŸ˜€','utf8').length === 4. Use Buffers for binary, strings for text, convert at the boundary
alloc zero-fills. allocUnsafe reuses pooled memory and can contain data from a *previous request* â€” a real data-leak vector. Use it only if you immediately fill() or completely overwrite
subarray is a view â€” same memory, no copy, and it pins the whole 8 KB pool slab. slice copies. Buffer.from(view) copies. Cache copies, not views
write() returning false: the writable's internal buffer exceeded highWaterMark. It means "stop", not "failed". Ignoring it and continuing is the most common Node memory bug

pipeline propagates errors, destroys every stream on failure (so a truncated output is not left looking valid), handles backpressure correctly through N stages, and waits for 'finish'. .pipe() forwards neither errors nor teardown
A threshold, not a cap. Readable: how much it buffers before pushing back. Writable: the level at which write() returns false. It is the knob that determines your memory ceiling per stream

Readable (in), Writable (out), Duplex (both â€” net.Socket), Transform (a duplex that maps a stream to a stream â€” every zlib transform, every line parser). objectMode switches the unit from bytes to objects

Multi-byte UTF-8 characters can straddle a chunk boundary. chunk.toString('utf8') inserts U+FFFD; StringDecoder holds the partial sequence. Any text Transform needs it, and without it you corrupt data roughly 1 in 4,096 chunks

questions.text: fs.promises â€” is it off the main thread?
questions.answer: It is the thread pool, not the main thread. So it does not block the loop, but it shares four threads with zlib, crypto, and dns.lookup, and a createReadStream holds a pool slot per in-flight chunk

questions.text: How do you serve a 5 GB upload without OOM, and reject >1 GB?
questions.answer: Content-Length as a fast reject, then stream to a temp file through a counting Transform that errors past the cap, via pipeline so it tears down on failure. Clean up in finally. Never readFile a user-controlled path

questions.text: How do you prevent path traversal?
questions.answer: path.basename (kills .. and separators) â†’ fs.realpath (resolves symlinks) â†’ compare the resolved path against the resolved root. startsWith is wrong: /srv/uploads-evil starts with /srv/uploads. Use path.relative and check for ..

No. Write to a temp name with open(..., 'wx') (fails if it exists â€” blocks the symlink attack), write, sync, then rename, which is atomic within a filesystem. Durability of the rename needs an fsync of the *directory*

Workers: N V8 isolates in one process, fast message channel, transferable memory, shared process fate. cluster: N processes, so a native crash takes down one and the master respawns it; the cost is NÃ— memory and no shared state. Workers for CPU work; cluster for crash isolation

questions.text: How do you size a worker pool in a container?
questions.answer: os.availableParallelism(), never os.cpus().length â€” inside a container the latter reports the *host*, so you oversubscribe. In practice, one less than the available parallelism, because the main thread needs a core

questions.text: How do you send a 200 MB buffer to a worker cheaply?
questions.answer: Transfer list: worker.postMessage({ buf }, [buf.buffer]) â€” ownership moves, zero copy, and the sender is detached. Cloning copies. SharedArrayBuffer shares bytes but needs Atomics

questions.text: When would you use child_process over a worker?
questions.answer: Untrusted or crash-prone native code, a tool you cannot instrument, or a hard isolation boundary. Also for anything that is *not* CPU work: a CLI's git, an ffmpeg, a pg_dump. exec with a shell and interpolated input is remote code execution â€” use execFile/spawn with an argument array

questions.text: What does the 'error' event rule say?
questions.answer: Emitting 'error' on an EventEmitter with zero listeners throws, synchronously, from emit. With one or more listeners it is a normal event. Streams and process additionally route an unhandled 'error' to uncaughtException

questions.text: What is a listener leak and how do you find one?
questions.answer: A long-lived emitter accumulating one listener per connection/resource, so memory never drops and each emit costs more. Find it with listenerCount, rawListeners (which unwraps once), a periodic production sweep, or a heap-snapshot retainer path. setMaxListeners(0) hides the only built-in signal and is never the fix

questions.text: Walk me through a graceful shutdown.
questions.answer: SIGTERM (and SIGINT) handler â†’ flip readiness to 503 (keep liveness green) â†’ server.close() â†’ end idle keep-alive sockets explicitly â†’ wait on an in-flight counter with a hard deadline â†’ flush resources in order with allSettled â†’ process.exit(0). A second signal forces exit 1. The in-code timeout must be shorter than the orchestrator grace period

questions.text: How do you know in-flight work is done?
questions.answer: A counter incremented in middleware and decremented on both res.on('finish') and res.on('close') â€” an aborted request emits close without finish, and missing that is how a drain hangs. Plus a hard deadline, because a counter alone can never be trusted

Off-heap: external/arrayBuffers â€” Buffers, ArrayBuffers, native addons, or V8 fragmentation. Confirm by comparing process.memoryUsage() fields; a heap snapshot will look nearly empty, which *is* the confirmation. allocUnsafe partial writes and cached subarrayes are the usual causes

questions.text: How do you actually find a leak?
questions.answer: Two --heapsnapshot-signal snapshots, load both into DevTools, take the Objects allocated between snapshots delta, then read the retainer path upward to the object that should not be holding it. Then add a CI test: 10,000 create/destroy cycles, forced GC, assert the heap returns to baseline. --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit catches it in staging

asyncId, triggerAsyncId (the causal chain = the async stack), executionAsyncId, and the init/before/after/destroy/promiseResolve hooks. It powers async stack traces, APM agents, and AsyncLocalStorage. The cost is a hook per async resource, so never do I/O inside one, and always delete from your map in destroy

questions.text: AsyncLocalStorage vs process.nextTick for request context?
questions.answer: ALS is the right tool: propagate a store (request id, user, trace) across the whole async chain without threading parameters, and read it anywhere. enterWith mutates the current context and can leak into a later request on the same socket, so use als.run at a well-defined boundary. Context does not cross worker or child-process boundaries â€” pass it in the payload

| 5 | `nextTick` vs microtask order? | The entire nextTick queue drains first, at every boundary |
| 6 | Is top-level `setTimeout(0)` vs `setImmediate` deterministic? | No â€” a genuine race; deterministic from inside an I/O callback |
| 7 | What is a 0 ms timer, really? | "Next timers phase, at least 1 ms later" â€” not "immediately" |
| 8 | Can a microtask chain starve I/O? | Yes â€” microtasks are un-preemptible |
| 9 | Does an `await` yield to the event loop? | No, only to other microtasks, unless it suspends on real I/O |
| 10 | What does `queueMicrotask` beat? | Nothing else in the microtask queue; it is FIFO with promises |
| 11 | Is the event loop busy when idle? | No â€” it blocks in `epoll_wait` at ~0% CPU |
| 12 | How do you measure loop blockage? | `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay` â€” a timer cannot observe blockage, because blockage is when it cannot run |
| 13 | What is `eventLoopUtilization`? | The ratio of loop-active to loop-elapsed time â€” "busy" vs "stalled" |
| 14 | Do timers keep the process alive? | Yes, unless `unref()`'d |
| 15 | What ends a request that never responds? | A proxy timeout, plus a leaked socket â€” which is why `server.setTimeout` exists |

## libuv, thread pool, blocking

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | Default thread pool size? | 4, shared by `fs`, `zlib`, `crypto`, and `dns.lookup` |
| 17 | Do sockets use the pool? | No â€” kernel-level async I/O, no pool thread |
| 18 | `dns.lookup` or `dns.resolve4`? | `lookup` is `getaddrinfo`, in the pool; `resolve4` is c-ares, on the loop |
| 19 | Which zlib call is most likely to saturate a pool? | `compression` middleware, on every compressible response |
| 20 | Is `fs.promises` off the main thread? | It is the thread pool; not the main thread, but shared and finite |
| 21 | `readFileSync` in a request handler? | A self-inflicted outage â€” it blocks every other request |
| 22 | Is sync `fs` ever correct? | Yes: boot paths, scripts, and CLIs, where nothing else is waiting |
| 23 | How do you raise the pool size? | `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, set **before** the process starts (env, not code) |
| 24 | How do you know the pool is the bottleneck? | Sweep the pool size at fixed load; latency is a step function of concurrency Ã· pool |
| 25 | What blocks a whole process in a `for` loop? | Everything: no other request, timer, or I/O completion, and no preemption |
| 26 | Three fixes for CPU-bound work? | Cheaper code; a worker thread; another process (or a queue) |
| 27 | What is the signature of a CPU-bound route? | p99 â‰« p50, one core at 100%, correlated with concurrency |
| 28 | Why is raising `--max-old-space-size` not a fix? | It delays the OOM; it does not remove the retention |

## Buffers, streams, fs

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 29 | `'ðŸ˜€'.length` vs `Buffer.from('ðŸ˜€','utf8').length`? | 2 UTF-16 code units vs 4 UTF-8 bytes |
| 30 | `alloc` vs `allocUnsafe`? | `alloc` zero-fills; `allocUnsafe` may contain a previous request's bytes |
| 31 | `subarray` vs `slice`? | `subarray` is a view (no copy, pins the slab); `slice` copies |
| 32 | `Buffer.poolSize`? | 8 KB; `allocUnsafe` allocates from it, so caches of views pin whole slabs |
| 33 | What is backpressure? | The producer being told to pause because the consumer's buffer is full â€” `write()` returning `false` |
| 34 | Is `highWaterMark` a cap? | No, a threshold |
| 35 | Why `pipeline` over `pipe`? | Errors, teardown, and multi-stage backpressure; `.pipe` has none of the three |
| 36 | What must a buffering Transform implement? | `_flush(cb)`, or the stream never ends and the last record is lost |
| 37 | Why `StringDecoder`? | A UTF-8 sequence can straddle a chunk boundary; `toString('utf8')` corrupts it |
| 38 | `objectMode` changes what? | The unit from bytes to objects, and the HWM to 16 objects |
| 39 | Is `rename` atomic? | Yes, within one filesystem; durability needs a directory fsync |
| 40 | How do you block path traversal? | `basename` â†’ `realpath` â†’ compare resolved paths (`startsWith` is wrong) |
| 41 | Why is `app.use('/api')` risky? | Prefix matching, so it also matches `/api-key` |
| 42 | Is `fs.watch` reliable? | No â€” inotify limits, NFS, and event coalescing; use a real mechanism in production |

## Processes, emitter, shutdown, memory

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 43 | Worker thread vs `cluster`? | Isolates in one process (fast IPC, shared fate) vs separate processes (crash isolation, NÃ— memory) |
| 44 | Pool size in a container? | `os.availableParallelism()`; `os.cpus().length` reports the host |
| 45 | How do you avoid copying a big buffer to a worker? | Transfer list â€” and the sender is detached afterwards |
| 46 | `exec` vs `execFile`? | Shell + string (injection risk) vs no shell + argument array |
| 47 | Two things you must set on a buffered exec? | `timeout` and `maxBuffer` â€” otherwise "wait forever" and "grow until OOM" |
| 48 | Emitting `'error'` with no listener? | Throws synchronously from `emit` |
| 49 | Why is `setMaxListeners(0)` wrong? | It disables the only built-in leak signal |
| 50 | `once` and `off`? | `once` registers a wrapper, so `off(ev, originalFn)` does not remove it |
| 51 | What must a signal handler avoid? | Long sleeps and unbounded waits â€” you will be SIGKILLed. Use a deadline |
| 52 | Readiness or liveness first on shutdown? | Readiness; liveness must stay green or you get killed mid-drain |
| 53 | `finish` vs `close`? | `finish` = response handed to the OS; `close` = socket gone, and an aborted request emits only `close` |
| 54 | `heapUsed` flat, RSS rising? | Off-heap â€” `external`/`arrayBuffers`: Buffers, native, fragmentation |
| 55 | How do you find a leak? | Two heap snapshots, the between-snapshots delta, then the **retainer path** |
| 56 | `AsyncLocalStorage` for? | Carrying a request/trace context across the async chain without threading parameters |
| 57 | What does `async_hooks` `triggerAsyncId` give you? | The causal chain â€” which is exactly what an async stack trace is |
| 58 | `heapTotal` >> `heapUsed`, both stable? | Fragmentation or an inflated reservation, not a leak |
| 59 | Two-snapshot test in CI? | 10,000 create/destroy cycles, forced GC, assert the heap returns to baseline |
| 60 | Why not Bun/Deno for a running service? | Startup-time wins do not apply to a long-running process; the ecosystem, native addons, APM, and LTS cost is real |

---

practice.title: -5.2 SECTION READINESS CHECKLIST
practice.afterTopic: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
items: Reading list, by name (no URLs, by design)
practice.reference:
Print this. Every line is something a reviewer should be able to answer "yes" to before the design is approved.

## Runtime mechanics

- [ ] I can name the event loop phases in order, and say which phase `setTimeout`, I/O callbacks, and `setImmediate` live in.
- [ ] I can predict the output of an ordering program, and can say precisely which orderings are guaranteed and which are a race.
- [ ] I know that the *entire* `nextTick` queue drains before the microtask queue at every boundary, and can explain why recursive `nextTick` is a hang rather than a stack overflow.
- [ ] I can explain why top-level `setTimeout(0)` vs `setImmediate` is nondeterministic and why it becomes deterministic from inside an I/O callback.
- [ ] I know the default thread pool size, and can classify ten operations as pool or non-pool (`fs`, `zlib`, `crypto.scrypt`, `dns.lookup` vs sockets, `dns.resolve4`).
- [ ] I know how to test the thread pool as a hypothesis: sweep `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` at fixed load, and the env var must be set before the process starts.
- [ ] I can distinguish a CPU-bound route from a slow dependency using the event loop delay histogram, CPU profile, and `eventLoopUtilization`.
- [ ] I know `Buffer.alloc` vs `allocUnsafe`, `subarray` vs `slice`, and that a cached `subarray` pins a pool slab.
- [ ] I can explain backpressure as `write()` returning `false`, and that `highWaterMark` is a threshold, not a cap.
- [ ] I can name the four stream types and say when `objectMode` is the wrong choice.
- [ ] I know why `pipeline()` exists, what `.pipe()` fails to do, and that a buffering Transform needs `_flush`.
- [ ] I know that `fs.promises` still uses the thread pool, and that a `createReadStream` holds a pool slot per in-flight chunk.

## Process management and lifecycle

- [ ] I can walk a graceful shutdown end to end: signals, readiness before liveness, socket tracking, in-flight counter with a deadline, flush order, exit code.
- [ ] The in-code shutdown timeout is **less** than the orchestrator grace period, and the arithmetic is written down.
- [ ] In-flight work is tracked on both `res.on('finish')` **and** `res.on('close')`, because an aborted request emits only `close`.
- [ ] The entrypoint is `CMD ["node", â€¦]`, not `npm start`, so signals actually reach the process.
- [ ] Liveness and readiness are separate endpoints with separate meanings, and a drain keeps liveness green.
- [ ] Every timer, socket, watcher, worker, and pool has a teardown path, and a test asserts the process can exit.
- [ ] `SIGTERM` twice is handled (idempotent, second one forces exit), and `SIGINT` is treated the same way.

## Memory and diagnostics

- [ ] I can explain `heapUsed` vs `heapTotal` vs `external` vs `rss`, and what each one tells you that the others do not.
- [ ] Flat heap plus growing RSS points to `external`/native memory, and I know the usual causes.
- [ ] I can describe the two-snapshot delta workflow and, crucially, how to read the **retainer path**.
- [ ] There is a CI leak test: N create/destroy cycles, forced GC, an assertion that the heap returns to baseline.
- [ ] Alerts are on the **slope** of post-GC heap, not on the level; `--max-old-space-size` is a limit, not a fix.
- [ ] I know `async_hooks`' four ids and four hooks, and that `destroy` is required or my own `Map` leaks.
- [ ] Request context uses `AsyncLocalStorage.enterWith`/`run` deliberately, and I know `enterWith` can leak context into a later request.
- [ ] Worker pools are bounded with a queue cap, and a timeout kills a worker that misses its job.
- [ ] I know `os.availableParallelism()` is the correct pool-size input inside a container.

## Express: routing, middleware, errors

- [ ] Literal routes are registered **before** parameterised ones, and I can say why (first match wins, in registration order).
- [ ] I know `app.use` is a **prefix** match for any method, and `app.METHOD` is an exact match â€” and that `/api` also matches `/api-key`.
- [ ] `req.params` / `req.query` / `req.body` / `req.path` / `req.baseUrl` / `req.originalUrl` are all distinct and I know which to log.
- [ ] I can explain the onion model and prove it with logging on both sides of `next()`.
- [ ] `next()` vs `next(err)` vs sending a response are the three ways a layer ends, and `next(err)` skips every non-error middleware.
- [ ] The error handler has **exactly four** declared parameters and is registered **last**.
- [ ] Every error handler starts with `if (res.headersSent) return next(err)`.
- [ ] Async handlers cannot throw uncaught in the chosen Express version: either a wrapper, `express-async-errors`, or Express 5.
- [ ] `next()` in an async middleware is the last statement, on the success path only.
- [ ] A 404 handler exists after all routes and returns JSON, not Node's default HTML.
- [ ] Errors are logged **once**, centrally, with the request id, the route, and the user; 4xx at `warn`, 5xx at `error`.
- [ ] 5xx bodies contain no internals and do contain a `traceId`.

## Middleware order, parsing, validation

- [ ] The order in `app.js` is: request id â†’ logger â†’ helmet â†’ CORS â†’ compression â†’ body parsers â†’ rate limit â†’ auth â†’ routes â†’ static/SPA â†’ 404 â†’ errors.
- [ ] I can state the **failure** each ordering rule prevents, not just the rule.
- [ ] CORS is before routes, before auth, and before rate limiting, so preflight is never rejected by them.
- [ ] Body parsers are before anything that reads `req.body`, and the raw-body route for webhooks is **before** `express.json()`.
- [ ] Every parser has a `limit`, and large uploads are capped by a streaming byte counter, not by `Content-Length`.
- [ ] The rate limiter runs before expensive authentication, and `trust proxy` is set to a hop count â€” not `true`.
- [ ] The SPA catch-all is after the API routes and excludes `/api`.
- [ ] Order-dependent invariants have integration tests (a preflight test, an async-rejection test, an unknown-route test).
- [ ] Validation happens **once at the boundary**, with Zod or Joi, and the *parsed* value flows inward.
- [ ] `params` and `query` are validated too, with bounds, defaults, and allowlisted sort fields.
- [ ] I know the Express 5 changes that matter: path syntax, the query parser, `res.send(status)`, `app.del`, `redirect('back')`, promise forwarding.
- [ ] Mass assignment is impossible: `.strict()` / `additionalProperties: false` or an explicit field allowlist.

## Structure, config, security, observability

- [ ] Layering is controller â†’ service â†’ repository, with the domain importing nothing from HTTP or SQL, enforced by a linter.
- [ ] Services depend on **interfaces**, so a unit test needs no mocking library.
- [ ] Authorisation is checked on the **object** in the service, not only on the route (IDOR).
- [ ] Transactions are owned by the service and span repositories via an injected `Tx`.
- [ ] `package.json` has `exports`, `type`, `engines`, `files`, `sideEffects` understood and deliberate.
- [ ] The lockfile is committed and CI uses `npm ci`; the image installs with `--omit=dev` and runs as non-root.
- [ ] Config is a Zod-validated `process.env` parsed **once at boot**, failing fast with the variable names; no other file reads `process.env`.
- [ ] Secrets come from the environment/secret manager, are never logged, and are redacted in the logger.
- [ ] `helmet()` is on, CSP is deployed report-only with a monitored endpoint, and then enforced.
- [ ] CORS is an explicit origin allowlist with `credentials: true` â€” never `origin: true`.
- [ ] Cookies are `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`, host-only.
- [ ] Pino has `redact` paths, a validated level, and a request id on every line via `mixin`/`AsyncLocalStorage`; `pino-pretty` is dev-only.
- [ ] The access log captures status and duration from `res.on('finish')`, and a log flush runs on shutdown.
- [ ] `healthz` is unrate-limited, unauthenticated, and excluded from log sampling.
- [ ] Compression is mounted before routes, has a `threshold` and a content-type filter, sets `Vary`, and only one layer (app or proxy) compresses.
- [ ] Templates use escaping-by-default syntax, raw-output tags are grepped in CI, and rich text is sanitised with an allowlist **on write**.
- [ ] I can say why Express, Fastify, or Hono, naming the mechanism rather than a benchmark.

## Interview readiness

- [ ] I can narrate the event loop without notes, including the guaranteed and the racy orderings.
- [ ] I can classify any given Node API as main-thread, pool, or kernel-async.
- [ ] I can walk a real memory leak from symptom to snapshot delta to retainer path to fix to regression test.
- [ ] I can present a shutdown sequence with the deadline arithmetic.
- [ ] I can explain `pipeline` vs `pipe`, backpressure, and `highWaterMark` without a diagram.
- [ ] I can explain why an Express error handler sometimes "does not run", naming arity and order.
- [ ] I can list the ordering rules and the incident each one prevents.
- [ ] I can state the trade-off, not just the choice, for every decision above.

**Reading list, by name (no URLs, by design).** The Node.js documentation for `process`, `timers`, `events`, `stream`, `buffer`, `fs`, `worker_threads`, `child_process`, `cluster`, `async_hooks`, `diagnostics_channel`, `perf_hooks`, and `v8`; the libuv design document; the V8 blog posts on hidden classes, the interpreter/JIT tiers, and deoptimisation; RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics); RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching); RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs); RFC 7540/7541 (HTTP/2) for the streaming and header limits that bite on `compression` and `res.write`; RFC 793 and the BREACH paper (compression plus secrets); the BREACH attack paper's mitigation guidance for TLS; the Express, Fastify, Hono, Zod, Joi, Helmet, `cors`, Pino, and `pino-http` documentation sets; and the OpenTelemetry specification's Node.js SDK notes on context propagation.

**Practice order.** Do the ten MUST-IMPLEMENT problems in order, because each introduces exactly one new idea: pub/sub semantics (1), flow control (2), ordering (3), the pool (4), parallelism (5), incremental parsing (6), context propagation (7), the HTTP pipeline end to end (8), lifecycle (9), and leak detection (10). Then the eighteen traces, in order, until you can narrate each one aloud without running it. Then the debugging scenarios, because they map the same ten ideas onto production conditions. Finish with the rapid-fire set until the one-line answers come out without hesitation.

questions.text: Why use NestJS instead of Express?
questions.answer: Coordination cost (many engineers, many modules, cross-cutting concerns) vs framework tax; a DI container gives substitutability, boot-time validation and one place for enhancers; costs are reflection, decorators, a learning curve, and ~10-30% throughput. Be honest that layered Express (5.2) is often better for small services

questions.text: What do imports and exports in a module do?
questions.answer: imports grants access to other modules' exports; providers are module-private unless exported. Importing a module does not expose its internals â€” the visibility rule behind every DI error

questions.text: useClass vs useExisting vs useValue vs useFactory?
questions.answer: useClass constructs a new instance; useExisting aliases an already-registered class (no new instance, so state is shared); useValue is a literal; useFactory builds it from injected deps, sync or async

questions.text: When and why is a dynamic module useful?
questions.answer: When a module's configuration varies per application or per feature: forRoot once, forRootAsync when it needs ConfigService, forFeature per feature. A convention, not framework law â€” nothing stops you calling forRoot twice

questions.text: How do you fix a circular module dependency?
questions.answer: forwardRef(() => X) in imports and @Inject(forwardRef(() => X)), or ModuleRef.get(X, {strict:false}) lazily. But say the better answer: extract the shared provider into a third module â€” forwardRef defers a resolution error, it does not fix the design

questions.text: What are the three injection scopes?
questions.answer: DEFAULT (singleton per module), REQUEST (per inbound request), TRANSIENT (new per consumer). Plus durable transient. Explain bubbling: scope propagates up the consumer chain, so one @Inject(REQUEST) deep in a service makes the whole subgraph request-scoped

questions.text: Why is Scope.REQUEST a performance problem?
questions.answer: New instance graph per request, a separate injector, lost singleton caches, extra GC and WeakMap lookups, and constructor work repeated per request. Rule: keep default scope; get request data from AsyncLocalStorage or an explicit parameter

questions.text: What is a durable transient provider for?
questions.answer: One instance cached *on the consumer* â€” per-consumer decorators/wrappers (retry, logging, metrics) around a singleton, without bubbling the scope

questions.text: What exactly do you lose with @Res()?
questions.answer: With no passthrough, the framework stops handling the response for that handler: response interceptors do not run, ClassSerializerInterceptor does not apply, automatic finalization is off. With passthrough: true you set headers and Nest still serializes and awaits

questions.text: Put the NestJS request pipeline in order.
questions.answer: middleware â†’ guards â†’ interceptors â†’ pipes â†’ handler â†’ (reverse) interceptors â†’ filters (exceptions only). Middleware has no DI and no route awareness; filters do not catch errors thrown in app.use() middleware

questions.text: Guard vs middleware vs interceptor vs pipe vs filter?
questions.answer: Guards decide *whether* (authorization, can short-circuit); interceptors *wrap* (logging, timing, response shape, caching); pipes transform/validate *arguments*; filters map a thrown error to a response; middleware is platform-level plumbing with no DI; decorators attach metadata for the others to read

questions.text: Why do DTOs need to be classes rather than interfaces?
questions.answer: Interfaces are erased â€” no runtime information. A class gives a constructor, emitDecoratorMetadata design-time types (so @Type(() => Nested) works), and one place for validation + OpenAPI metadata. Types are not validation

questions.text: What do whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted do?
questions.answer: whitelist strips properties with no validation decorator (the mass-assignment fix); forbidNonWhitelisted turns a strip into a loud 400. Both together catch client bugs and block privilege escalation via role/orgId

questions.text: Why does nested validation need @Type(() => NestedDto)?
questions.answer: class-transformer cannot know the runtime class of a plain nested object without the hint, so ValidateNested has nothing to instantiate
It coerces loosely â€” "false" becomes truthy in places, empty strings become numbers â€” so prefer explicit @Type(() => Number) per field and leave it off

questions.text: Why doesn't a timeout interceptor stop the work?
questions.answer: rxjs's timeout unsubscribes from the observable, but an async handler's promise keeps running â€” the query, the write, the third-party call all continue and may commit. Real cancellation needs an AbortSignal plumbed into the I/O layer

questions.text: Why must ClassSerializerInterceptor be ordered before an envelope interceptor?
questions.answer: Serialization must strip @Exclude()d fields *before* the value is wrapped in { data, meta }; otherwise the secret is already inside the envelope

questions.text: âš« How do you migrate a working Express service to NestJS without a rewrite?
questions.answer: Strangler: extract domain logic into framework-free modules first, add a shared contracts package, mount a Nest app alongside the Express one for new features, forbid cross-imports, and migrate endpoints as they are touched. Explain why a big-bang rewrite loses a quarter of delivery capacity and mixes framework learning with business change

questions.text: âš« When does NestJS's cost/benefit turn positive?
questions.answer: When coordination cost dominates runtime cost: many engineers, many features needing the same conventions, many cross-cutting concerns, and generated docs. Negative for few engineers, few endpoints, edge runtimes, and latency-critical paths

questions.text: âš« Why do you avoid module-level DataLoaders in GraphQL, even though it is NestJS?
questions.answer: Loaders must be request-scoped so their cache dies with the request; a module-level loader is a singleton whose cache spans users and tenants â€” that is a data-leak bug, not a performance one. Build them in the createContext/factory, and keep them out of the DI graph or explicitly request-scoped

Resources. Plural nouns, no verbs, â‰¤2 levels of nesting. Sub-resources are nouns; state transitions are POST /orders/{id}/cancel, not PATCH {status} â€” because status is a state machine, and a settable field invites illegal transitions

questions.text: When do you flatten a nested URL?
questions.answer: When the parent is only an authorization scope, when the child has its own identity elsewhere, past two levels, or when you want a shareable link. Keep nesting only when the child cannot exist without the parent

questions.text: Safe vs idempotent: define and list methods
questions.answer: Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. Idempotent: safe + PUT, DELETE. POST and PATCH are neither (PATCH is idempotent only if its *document* is). Consequences: safe methods may be re-requested by browsers/crawlers/CDNs; idempotent methods can be auto-retried by clients and proxies; a timed-out POST is ambiguous, which is why idempotency keys exist

400 = the server could not understand the request (unparseable JSON, a query param that is not a number). 422 = understood, refused on domain/validation grounds. Different audiences: client bug vs user-fixable form error. Be consistent, and provide field-level detail on 422

questions.text: 401 vs 403 vs 404 for a private resource?
questions.answer: 401 = not authenticated (include WWW-Authenticate); 403 = authenticated but not allowed; and for a resource that must not be revealed to exist, return 404 for both missing and forbidden â€” that is the standard IDOR defence
409 = the request conflicts with the current state: duplicate unique key, illegal transition, version mismatch, idempotency key reuse. 400 = the request is malformed in isolation
428 says "I require a precondition" (send If-Match); 412 says "your precondition failed â€” the resource changed" and should include the current ETag so the client can rebase

questions.text: Which redirects preserve the HTTP method?
questions.answer: 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) preserve method and body. 301/302 historically rewrote to GET; 303 forces GET. Use 308 for a permanent API move, 307 for a temporary redirect of a POST

Retry-After (delta-seconds or date) plus the limit headers: RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, optionally RateLimit-Policy, and a Link to the docs. Emit the limit headers on 200s too, so clients throttle proactively. X-RateLimit-* for legacy clients

questions.text: When is keyset pagination strictly better than offset, and what does it cost?
questions.answer: Strictly better for large, live, ordered data: no duplicates/skips under concurrent writes, and constant cost per page. Costs: no random page jumps, requires a unique sort key (add a tiebreaker), the WHERE and ORDER BY must match the index, and the sort must be on immutable columns

questions.text: Why is COUNT(*) expensive and what do you return instead?
questions.answer: On a large filtered table it is a scan that cannot use most indexes well. Return hasMore from the limit + 1 trick; expose totals on a separate, explicitly-expensive endpoint or as a cached estimate

questions.text: How do you make a cursor opaque and safe?
questions.answer: Sign a versioned JSON payload (sort key + scope) with an HMAC, verify before parsing, reject a bad cursor loudly rather than resetting to page 1, and keep decoding old versions or expire deliberately

questions.text: Why must every sort have a unique tiebreaker?
questions.answer: SQL does not guarantee a total order unless the ORDER BY is unique. Ties on the sort key let the plan return rows in any order, so a keyset boundary skips or repeats them. Append id and match its direction

questions.text: Why PATCH is not automatically idempotent
questions.answer: Idempotency depends on the *document*: {"status":"x"} sets (idempotent), {"quantity":{"$inc":1}} and add /tags/- accumulate (not). The method gives no protection; the document's semantics must

Merge Patch (RFC 7396): one partial document, null deletes, absent leaves alone, objects merge, arrays replace. JSON Patch (RFC 6902): an operation array with JSON Pointers, can address array elements, has move/copy, and test for atomic optimistic concurrency. Pick Merge Patch for simple public updates, JSON Patch when you need array addressing or test

Client generates per intent (not per attempt) â†’ server reserves atomically (SET NX / unique insert) â†’ stores a fingerprint of method+path+canonical body â†’ same key + same body replays the stored response byte-for-byte â†’ same key + different body is 409 â†’ concurrent in-flight gets 409 + Retry-After â†’ TTL â‰¥ the client's retry window â†’ propagate the upstream provider's key when you call out. Also: dedupe webhooks on the event id

questions.text: Why must the top-level status of a bulk endpoint be 200?
questions.answer: A 4xx means "this request was rejected, do not resend" to every generic client, so retries re-submit the whole batch and duplicate the successes. The request succeeded; per-item outcomes belong in the body. Alternative: an all-or-nothing bulk endpoint in a single transaction

Rarely. It is the WebDAV multi-status code, but many client libraries, gateways and monitoring tools treat non-2xx as an error. Most public APIs use 200 with a per-item results array including an index or the client's own key

questions.text: âš« How do you introduce cursor pagination without breaking clients?
questions.answer: Ship both: ?cursor= present â†’ keyset path, absent â†’ legacy offset path, both supported for the deprecation window. Because changing the sort order is breaking for every stored cursor, keep the default order stable, version the cursor payload, and measure per-client usage before removing the offset path (see the Deprecation/Sunset answer)

questions.text: âš« How do you verify a webhook securely?
questions.answer: HMAC-SHA256 over ${timestamp}.${rawBody} with a constant-time compare, a Â±5 minute timestamp tolerance for replay, the raw bytes (re-serializing breaks the signature), no signature in a URL, per-secret signature values for rotation, and â€” for the receiver side â€” atomic dedupe on the event id with a unique constraint, plus version tolerance because delivery is unordered and at-least-once

questions.text: âš« What belongs in a 202 long-running-operation contract?
questions.answer: 202 + Location for a job resource + Retry-After; a cheap status resource with queued/running/succeeded/failed and progress; terminal states only; a TTL with 410 afterwards; results as a presigned reference; Idempotency-Key on create; and cancellation as a modelled transition (cancelling â†’ cancelled or completed), because you cannot preempt work preemptively

questions.text: âš« Design the error contract for ten services
questions.answer: One shared package: application/problem+json with the RFC 9457 core, a stable machine-readable code per condition, field errors as JSON Pointers, a traceId in the body, the header and the log. title constant per problem type, detail per occurrence, 4xx specific and 5xx information-free. Never 200 with an error body, never a stack trace. Assert the shape in CI per service

questions.text: Why is no-cache not "do not cache"?
questions.answer: no-cache = may store, must revalidate before use. no-store = do not store. Conflating them is the most common caching bug; the distinction is what lets a browser keep a copy of a permissions response and still revalidate it every time

questions.text: What is a Vary bug and how does it look to a user?
questions.answer: Returning a representation that varies with a request header without declaring it in Vary, so a shared cache serves Brotli to a client that cannot decode it, or CSV to a client that asked for JSON. The user sees a parse error. Over-broad Vary (a per-request nonce) is the opposite failure: hit rate collapses to zero
Over-fetching and under-fetching; the real cost is *round trips*, not bytes, so collapsing 3 sequential requests into 1 is the win. Move the complexity to the server, where you can optimize it once

Authorization (every field is a decision), CDN caching (POST), N+1 (easier to write, not harder), query cost, operational simplicity, and stable cacheable URLs. It can easily be *slower* than the REST equivalent

questions.text: How is nullability a design decision?
questions.answer: Non-null is a promise with a large blast radius: a throw in a non-null field propagates up and can null the whole data. Use nullable at every boundary, non-null only for guaranteed values, and nullable for legitimately absent ones. Also [String!]! vs [String!] vs [String]! encode different promises

questions.text: Input types vs output types vs payload types?
questions.answer: Separate because reads and writes evolve differently; reusing one type forces every read field to exist on writes. Mutations take one input object and return a payload type, which is where the typed error array lives

questions.text: When do you need a custom scalar vs a wrapper type?
questions.answer: Custom scalar for genuine primitives (timestamp, decimal). Wrapper type (Money { amountMinor, currency }) when you want self-documentation and the ability to add fields without a breaking change. Never Float for money, never ID parsed by clients

questions.text: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL, and what is the fix?
questions.answer: A field resolver runs once per object in the response, so 100 orders â†’ 101 queries. Fix with a request-scoped DataLoader: one batched set-based query per selection level, with a per-request cache for duplicate keys

questions.text: How does DataLoader batching actually work?
questions.answer: load(key) returns a cached promise or enqueues the key; a microtask at the end of the current tick dispatches the batch function once with all queued keys; results are distributed to the individual promises. maxBatchSize caps the list; errors are per key; failures are not cached

questions.text: Why must DataLoaders be per request?
questions.answer: The cache is a request-local memo. A module-level loader is a cross-request cache with no invalidation â€” and it leaks one user's data to the next. Cross-request caching is a *cache* problem (TTL/event invalidation), not a DataLoader problem

questions.text: Why are connections edges + node + cursor rather than a list?
questions.answer: A cursor is a *position in a sort*, which is edge metadata, not node metadata (a node can appear at several positions). A bare list cannot express hasNextPage without an out-of-band channel, and a normalized client cache duplicates or loses rows when a page re-returns a node

questions.text: Why is offset pagination wrong for GraphQL?
questions.answer: Infinite scroll has no page number, so a cursor is needed anyway; a normalized additive cache duplicates/skips with offsets; offsets are just a number and get replayed against a changed filter; and the cost grows with depth exactly as in REST

questions.text: How do you prevent N+1 in production?
questions.answer: Count database queries per request and alert on the p99 of that count, not the total; count resolver invocations per type; and assert a query-count ceiling in the test suite for every query in your integration tests. That last one is the highest-value GraphQL test

questions.text: What is the "N+1 authz check" trap?
questions.answer: A per-row permission check in a field resolver is a database query per row. The tempting fix â€” check once for the list and apply it to all rows â€” is a data leak, because the list is authorized and the individual objects are not. Batch per-key checks, or filter unauthorized rows out in SQL

questions.text: Why is a field count a bad complexity measure?
questions.answer: Cost is multiplicative through lists. orders(first:100){items(first:100){variants(first:100){price}}} has ~5 fields and up to 10^6 rows. Estimate by multiplying effective list sizes, add a depth limit, and convert cost into a token budget

questions.text: What is the strongest protection for a public GraphQL API?
questions.answer: An allowlist of persisted queries (plus introspection off, depth/complexity limits, per-operation rate limiting, disabled field suggestions, and no HTTP batching of operations). Allowlists turn the flexible endpoint into a fixed set of operations â€” which is an honest thing to say in a design review

questions.text: Why is a GraphQL response hard to cache at a CDN?
questions.answer: No URL: the shape is client-chosen, the request is a POST, and even as a GET the whole document would be in the key (formatting-sensitive, leaks into logs, breaks URL length limits). Persisted queries fix key stability but remove arbitrary queries

questions.text: What are the trade-offs of the Apollo normalized cache?
questions.answer: Field-level updates and cross-component reactivity for free; but object identity by id + __typename means the raw nested JSON is unrecoverable, keyArgs/merge are easy to get wrong (filter pollution, duplicate rows on append), and knowing *which object* changed does not tell you *which queries* depended on which of its fields

graphql-ws (not the deprecated protocol), auth in connection_init because browsers cannot set headers on a WebSocket, connectionInitWaitTimeout, ping/pong keepalive, cleanup on disconnect, per-event authorization, and pub/sub fan-out across instances. Always re-sync on reconnect â€” subscriptions are an optimization over polling, never the source of truth

questions.text: When is GraphQL the wrong choice?
questions.answer: Metered/bandwidth-constrained clients, simple CRUD with cacheable GETs, a public API with unknown clients, a team without schema governance, a need for real HTTP semantics (status codes, ETag, CDN), and low operational maturity. A BFF is usually the right-sized answer

Contract (OpenAPI / schema / .proto / TS types); transport (HTTP+JSON / HTTP POST / HTTP/2+protobuf / HTTP+JSON); caching (first class / hard / none / limited); tooling (universal / mature but narrower / excellent / TS-only); code reuse (shared package / codegen / codegen everywhere / perfect in TS); N+1 risk (low / high by default / low / low). gRPC wire details are in PHASE 7

questions.text: What is tRPC, and what disqualifies it?
questions.answer: TypeScript RPC where the server router *is* the contract â€” no schema, no resolver map, no codegen, with Zod in .input() giving both validation and inference. Disqualified for any non-TypeScript consumer: no schema, no generated SDK, and a hand-written wire-format client gets none of the benefits and drifts silently

questions.text: âš« A team wants GraphQL for their B2B SaaS. What questions do you ask?
questions.answer: (1) Does a screen actually need more than one round trip? (2) Can we afford a query planner, cost analysis, persisted queries, resolver observability, and a named schema owner? (3) Who are the clients â€” first-party (we control the query shapes) or unknown third parties (a POST that accepts arbitrary documents is a liability)? Then recommend concretely, and name the measurement that would prove the choice wrong. A BFF is very often the right answer, and saying so is a stronger answer than defending GraphQL

questions.text: âš« Design an API for a marketplace with four kinds of consumer
questions.answer: Public REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract; a BFF for the web app; GraphQL for first-party mobile if round trips dominate; gRPC or REST service-to-service. Explain that "one style everywhere" is a sign the analysis was not done, and sequence the rollout: REST first, then add a style where a *measured* constraint demands it

(2) Can we afford a query planner, cost analysis, persisted queries, resolver observability, and a named schema owner? (3) Who are the clients â€” first-party (we control the query shapes) or unknown third parties (a `POST` that accepts arbitrary documents is a liability)? Then recommend concretely, and name the measurement that would prove the choice wrong. A BFF is very often the right answer, and saying so is a stronger answer than defending GraphQL |
| 66 | âš« Design an API for a marketplace with four kinds of consumer | Public REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract; a BFF for the web app; GraphQL for first-party mobile if round trips dominate; gRPC or REST service-to-service. Explain that "one style everywhere" is a sign the analysis was not done, and sequence the rollout: REST first, then add a style where a *measured* constraint demands it |

Each scenario: **symptom â†’ hypotheses â†’ instrumentation â†’ fix â†’ prevention**. The habit being tested is narrowing with evidence before changing code, and the interview answer always ends at *prevention*, not at *the one-line fix*.

practice.title: Scenario 1 â€” N+1 queries in a GraphQL resolver
practice.afterTopic: tRPC: End-to-End Type Safety
practice.signal: Distinguishing "N+1" from "pool exhaustion" from "slow query" without guessing, and knowing that the *fix for a DataLoader registered in the wrong scope* is a registration move, not a batching rewrite.
symptoms: A Query.orders endpoint is fast with three orders and times out (or hits a DB connection ceiling) with 300. CPU on the database host is high; p99 latency scales with the number of orders returned; the GraphQL response is roughly the right size.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) the batched set-based query against real row counts.

2. A `listSizeHint` is missing, so `orders(first: 100)` is priced as 1 and cost-based throttling never engages.
