practice.title: INTERVIEW Q&A
practice.afterTopic: Deprecation, Versioning, and Killing a Feature Safely
items: Where do config values live, in order of precedence?
What are the log levels and what belongs in each?
How do you correlate logs across services?
How do you keep secrets out of logs?
What is cardinality in logging, and why does it matter?
Where do you validate, and in what order?
What is mass assignment and how do you prevent it?
Why does offset pagination skip and duplicate rows?
Why must the sort have a unique tiebreaker?
Why is the cursor opaque and signed?
What is the trade-off of soft delete?
What breaks when you soft-delete with a plain unique index?
What must an audit log record?
Why before *and* after, not just field names?
How do you make an audit log tamper-evident?

questions.answer: Codebase; dependencies; config in env; build/release separation; release vs run; stateless processes; port binding; process model; disposability; dev/prod parity; logs as event streams; admin tasks as one-off processes. Factors III, V, IX, and XI are the ones that come up in backend interviews

Config baked into the code or image â€” a flag, a host, a credential, a URL. Anything that differs per environment must be injected at run time, so one artifact promotes unchanged from staging to prod

questions.text: Where do config values live, in order of precedence?
questions.answer: Code defaults, shared base file, env file, per-environment secret, process environment, CLI/flags, and dynamic flag service. The rule that matters: the environment wins over the file, and per-request values are *not* config â€” they are flags or tenant settings

A missing required variable should stop the process before it accepts traffic, with an aggregated error naming every problem. Booting successfully and failing on first use converts a deploy-time error into a 3am incident
process.env.PORT || 3000 turns PORT=0 into 3000, and RETRY=0 into the default. 0 is a meaningful value for both. Use ??, and use schema coercion with explicit bounds

questions.text: What are the log levels and what belongs in each?
questions.answer: trace/debug for developer detail (off in production), info for significant normal events, warn for something unexpected that was handled, error for a failed operation someone may care about, fatal for the process exiting. The discipline: info must be safe at volume; error must be rare enough to read
Values stay values, so you can query and aggregate them; a log message with interpolated values is unquotable and needs a regex to parse. Structured logs turn "grep for a user id" into a field query

questions.text: How do you correlate logs across services?
questions.answer: A request id (and a trace id) created or honoured at the edge, propagated in headers and attached to every log line via AsyncLocalStorage, returned in the response header, and included in job payloads so async work stays correlated

questions.text: How do you keep secrets out of logs?
questions.answer: Path-based redaction configured on the logger (auth headers, cookies, password, token, card fields), a safe Error serialiser so an axios error does not drag along config.headers, a lint rule against logging req.body, and a periodic scan of the log store for known secret formats

Volume arithmetic: ~300 bytes/line Ã— 2 lines Ã— 100 rps â‰ˆ 5 GB/day. Mitigate with one completion line per request, debug for success detail, sampling of successes (never errors), and metrics for anything you need to count

questions.text: What is cardinality in logging, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The number of distinct values a field takes. A field named userId is fine; a field *named* after the user id creates thousands of fields and ruins the index. Metrics need bounded label sets; logs need bounded field names

Validation returns a boolean and leaves the caller to re-derive meaning. Parsing returns a typed value â€” a Date, a coerced number, a narrowed enum â€” so the boundary produces the trusted type and nothing downstream re-parses or re-checks

questions.text: Where do you validate, and in what order?
questions.answer: At the boundary, once: body, query, params, headers, queue payloads, webhook bodies. Order: authenticate, authorise coarsely, parse, then authorise on the loaded object â€” the last step is what prevents IDOR and needs the parsed id

questions.text: What is mass assignment and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Spreading a client-supplied object into a model, so a role or tenantId field in the body gets written. Prevent with a schema allowlist (.strict() to reject, .strip() to drop) â€” which also becomes your OpenAPI source and your test fixture

No. Injection is prevented by parameterisation; validation bounds and shapes input, and output encoding prevents XSS. Saying "we validate, so we don't need prepared statements" is the wrong answer and it is asked deliberately

questions.text: Why does offset pagination skip and duplicate rows?
questions.answer: The offset is a *position*, and positions shift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. Insert a row before page 2 and every later row shifts one place, so one row repeats and another is never seen

Anchoring on the last row's sort values instead of a position: where (created_at, id) < ($anchor, $anchorId) order by created_at desc, id desc. Inserts do not shift the window, and deep pages stay O(log n)

questions.text: Why must the sort have a unique tiebreaker?
questions.answer: Because the sort column is not unique. Rows sharing the anchor's created_at are excluded by created_at < anchor, so they are silently skipped. Adding id to the comparison makes it a total order and makes the tuple comparison correct

questions.text: Why is the cursor opaque and signed?
questions.answer: Opaque so clients cannot depend on its contents or hand-edit it; signed so a tampered or foreign cursor is rejected with a clean 400 instead of returning an arbitrary window. It also binds the cursor to the filter set, which prevents replaying it against a different query

questions.text: What is the trade-off of soft delete?
questions.answer: You keep recoverability and history, and pay a query tax, a partial-unique-index subtlety, and unbounded growth. It is also what makes a wrong bulk delete survivable â€” which is the strongest argument for it

questions.text: What breaks when you soft-delete with a plain unique index?
questions.answer: Re-creating a row with the same value fails: the deleted row still occupies the key. The fix is a partial unique index where deleted_at is null, so only live rows must be unique

Soft delete hides a row; it does not remove it, and it does not remove it from backups either. Erasure is a separate, auditable process, and where a legal retention obligation exists the resolution is anonymisation â€” replace identifying fields, keep the record, log the erasure

questions.text: What must an audit log record?
questions.answer: Who (human, service, or system â€” with the session for privileged actions), what (a verb from a closed vocabulary), which entity (type, id, tenant), when (RFC 3339 UTC from a synchronised clock), and before/after values. Plus a request id so the entry joins to logs and traces

questions.text: Why before *and* after, not just field names?
questions.answer: Because "changed" is useless in a dispute. The values are the evidence; the field names only tell you where to look

questions.text: How do you make an audit log tamper-evident?
questions.answer: Three layers: permissions (revoke update/delete/truncate), a hash chain so an edit is *located*, and an external anchor of the head hash to WORM storage so a full database compromise cannot rewrite history silently. Each layer alone is defeatable

Shared schema: one table with tenant_id, simplest and cheapest, weakest isolation, noisy neighbours, trivial cross-tenant analytics. Schema-per-tenant: same tables in a namespace, medium isolation, migrations run N times. Database-per-tenant: strongest isolation, N pools and N migrations, cross-tenant queries need federation. Most teams land on shared schema with strict scoping plus dedicated databases only for named enterprise tenants

questions.text: What makes a kill switch different from a feature flag?
questions.answer: Availability and latency. A kill switch must stop something harmful immediately, so it cannot depend on the subsystem it disables and cannot sit behind a long cache. Feature flags can be slow, targeted, and removed; kill switches are permanent and global

Liveness answers "is this process wedged?" and failing it restarts the container, so it must check only the process â€” never a dependency, or one slow database restarts the whole fleet. Readiness answers "can this instance serve traffic?" and failing it removes the instance from the pool without restarting it

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Factor III in one line? | Config in the environment â€” never baked into the code or image |
| 2 | Why fail fast at boot? | A bad config should stop the process before it serves traffic, not on first use |
| 3 | `||` or `??` for defaults? | `??` â€” `\|\|` turns `0` and `''` into the default |
| 4 | Aggregate or report the first validation error? | Aggregate: one boot tells you everything that is wrong |
| 5 | Env var or flag for "enable new checkout"? | A flag â€” an env change is a restart |
| 6 | Env var or flag for a database URL? | Env â€” it is config; it changes per deployment, not per request |
| 7 | What is factor V? | A release is an immutable artifact plus config; a process is a running release |
| 8 | Secret or config? | A secret is a config value that must never be readable, logged, or committed â€” and must be rotatable |
| 9 | Where do logs go in a container? | stdout/stderr as an event stream (factor XI), never a file |
| 10 | Most common config bug? | Name drift between the schema and the platform (`DB_URL` vs `DATABASE_URL`) |

## Logging

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | Six levels? | trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal |
| 12 | Production default level? | info; debug on demand for one instance |
| 13 | Which level for a retry that succeeded? | warn â€” something unexpected, handled |
| 14 | Which level for a handled 404? | info or warn with a reason code â€” not error, or the error rate stops meaning anything |
| 15 | Which level for an uncaught exception? | fatal â€” the process is exiting |
| 16 | JSON or string? | JSON; values must stay values |
| 17 | How do you get a request id onto every line? | `AsyncLocalStorage` set in middleware, attached by a logger mixin |
| 18 | Log the URL or the route template? | The route template â€” raw URLs carry unbounded ids and query secrets |
| 19 | Redact how? | Path-based redact list on the logger, plus a safe `Error` serialiser |
| 20 | Bytes per request at 100 rps? | ~5 GB/day for two JSON lines per request |
| 21 | What do you never sample? | Errors and above â€” that is the evidence |
| 22 | Cardinality rule for logs? | Bounded field names; metrics need bounded label values |
| 23 | Where do counts belong? | Metrics â€” logs are for individual events |

## Validation

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 24 | Parse or validate? | Parse â€” return the typed value, not a boolean |
| 25 | Which sources? | body, query, params, headers, queue payloads, webhook bodies |
| 26 | `.strict()` or `.strip()`? | `.strict()` on write/money/identity paths so typos are loud |
| 27 | Unknown query params? | Reject on writes, ignore on reads (forward compatibility) |
| 28 | 400 or 422? | 422 â€” well-formed syntax, invalid semantics |
| 29 | Validate `?sort=`? | Allowlist only â€” it reaches `order by` |
| 30 | Validation vs SQL injection? | Unrelated; parameterisation stops injection, validation bounds input |
| 31 | Mass assignment fix? | A schema allowlist, so unknown keys never reach the model |
| 32 | Body size limit? | A parser limit plus a 413; a schema with `.max()` is not enough |
| 33 | Validation vs authorisation? | Different things; validation never prevents IDOR |
| 34 | Normalise unicode where? | At the boundary, to NFC, before any uniqueness comparison |

## Pagination and soft deletes

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 35 | Offset vs keyset? | Offset for bounded random access, keyset for large or unstable lists |
| 36 | Keyset predicate? | `(sort_col, id) < ($anchor, $anchorId)` â€” row-wise comparison with a unique tiebreaker |
| 37 | Why `limit + 1`? | It gives `hasNextPage` with no `COUNT`, which can be a full scan |
| 38 | Why sign the cursor? | To reject tampered and foreign cursors with a clean 400 instead of a wrong window |
| 39 | What invalidates a cursor? | A changed sort, collation, or filter set â€” hence version and filter hash |
| 40 | Soft delete + unique index? | Make it partial: `unique â€¦ where deleted_at is null` |
| 41 | Restore collisions? | Surface them as a conflict; never silently overwrite |
| 42 | Restore and sessions? | Revoke credentials on delete; never resurrect them on restore |
| 43 | Is soft delete GDPR erasure? | No â€” and backups still contain the data |

## Multi-tenancy, idempotency, jobs, and ops

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 44 | Most common cross-tenant leak? | A cache key without the tenant prefix |
| 45 | RLS needs what two things? | `with check` for writes, and `force row level security` to cover the table owner |
| 46 | Where must `set_config` run? | Inside the transaction on the held connection (`â€¦ , true`) |
| 47 | Per-tenant `new Pool()`? | Fine at ~50 tenants, impossible at thousands â€” use a router or LRU-evicted pools |
| 48 | Idempotency key scope? | `(tenant, user, endpoint, key)` â€” never the key alone |
| 49 | Same key, different body? | Refuse with 422 `idempotency_key_reuse` â€” never replay |
| 50 | Concurrent duplicate? | Atomic claim on a unique index; the loser gets 409 with `Retry-After` |
| 51 | Where does the idempotency record commit? | In the same transaction as the side effect |
| 52 | Three replicas and a cron? | It runs three times â€” use a dedicated scheduler or an advisory lock |
| 53 | DST and a 02:30 job? | 02:30 may not exist, or may occur twice; key the run record on the logical period |
| 54 | Flag vs config? | Flags change without a deploy and are evaluated per request; config changes on deploy |
| 55 | Kill-switch requirement? | It must not depend on the subsystem it disables, and it must not sit behind a long cache |
| 56 | Sticky bucketing? | A deterministic hash of a stable id, not `Math.random()` |
| 57 | Liveness may check the database? | Never â€” that converts a slow query into a fleet-wide restart storm |
| 58 | 404 or 410 after a deprecation? | 410 Gone, with the replacement â€” self-diagnosing for the client |
| 59 | What is an error budget? | `1 âˆ’ SLO`; the currency you spend on releases, with a written freeze policy |
| 60 | Alert on CPU at 80%? | No â€” alert on symptoms, not causes |

practice.afterTopic: Deprecation, Versioning, and Killing a Feature Safely

practice.reference:
Print this. Every line is something a reviewer should be able to answer "yes" to before the design is approved.

## Configuration (5.10.1)

- [ ] I can name the twelve factors and say which two govern day-to-day backend work.
- [ ] Config is loaded once, validated with a schema, frozen, and never re-read.
- [ ] The schema has types and bounds, so `PORT=abc` fails at boot instead of producing a NaN bind.
- [ ] Cross-field rules are enforced (a dev secret cannot reach production).
- [ ] Boot order is: validate config â†’ logger â†’ connect and verify dependencies â†’ migrate â†’ listen â†’ install shutdown.
- [ ] A missing optional dependency does not crash the service; a missing required one does.
- [ ] I use `??`, not `||`, and I can explain why (`0` is a meaningful value).
- [ ] Secrets come from a secret manager, are never logged, and are redacted in any rendered config.
- [ ] Per-request values are flags or tenant settings, not env vars.
- [ ] There is a CI check that diffs variable *names* across environments.

## Logging (5.10.2)

- [ ] I can name the levels and give a real, defensible example of each.
- [ ] `info` is safe at volume; `error` is rare enough that reading errors is feasible.
- [ ] Logs are JSON with stable keys, and errors are serialised to `{message, stack, code}`.
- [ ] Every line carries a request id and, where available, a trace id, via `AsyncLocalStorage`.
- [ ] Redaction is path-based and covers auth headers, cookies, passwords, tokens, and PII fields.
- [ ] I do not log `req.url` at info, and I do not log request or response bodies on auth/payment routes.
- [ ] I can do the volume arithmetic: bytes/line Ã— lines/request Ã— rps Ã— retention.
- [ ] Sampling applies to successes only, and never to errors.
- [ ] Metrics carry bounded label values; log *field names* are bounded.
- [ ] There is a `log_replay`-safe way to debug one instance without disabling redaction.

## Input validation (5.10.3)

- [ ] Validation happens at every trust boundary, including queue payloads and webhooks.
- [ ] I parse rather than validate, and the parsed value replaces the raw one.
- [ ] Every string has a max length and every array a max size; the body parser has a byte limit.
- [ ] `.strict()` (or an explicit allowlist) on write, money, and identity endpoints.
- [ ] `sort`, `order`, and filter fields are allowlisted, never interpolated.
- [ ] Errors are RFC 9457 problem details with field paths and machine-readable codes, and never echo the submitted value.
- [ ] Coercion is bounded; I know that `"1e5"`, `"  "`, and `"0x10"` all surprise you.
- [ ] `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` keys are rejected, and nesting depth is limited.
- [ ] Order is: authenticate â†’ coarse authorise â†’ parse â†’ authorise on the loaded object.
- [ ] I can state clearly that validation does not replace parameterisation or output encoding.

## Pagination (5.10.4)

- [ ] I can explain offset instability with a concrete insert/delete example.
- [ ] Keyset predicates use row-wise comparison with a unique `id` tiebreaker.
- [ ] The composite index matches the tenant filter and the sort direction.
- [ ] `hasNextPage` comes from `limit + 1`, not from `COUNT(*)`.
- [ ] Cursors are opaque, signed, versioned, and bound to the filter set.
- [ ] A tampered or foreign cursor returns a clean `400`, not a wrong result or a 500.
- [ ] I never sort by a nullable column with a cursor, and I know why.
- [ ] Deep offsets are capped, with a documented alternative.
- [ ] Exports take a snapshot rather than paging a moving target.
- [ ] A concurrency test proves each row appears exactly once while rows are being written.

## Soft deletes and retention (5.10.5)

- [ ] Soft-deletable tables use partial unique indexes for live-row uniqueness.
- [ ] The live-row predicate lives in one place â€” a repository, a scope, or RLS â€” not in every query.
- [ ] Deletes record `deleted_at` and `deleted_by`, and every one is audited.
- [ ] Delete revokes sessions and API keys immediately, not at purge time.
- [ ] Restore surfaces uniqueness conflicts and does not resurrect credentials.
- [ ] Retention windows exist per table class and are enforced by a job.
- [ ] The purge job is batched, keyset-paginated, uses `skip locked`, rate-limits, and is resumable.
- [ ] `legal_hold` is a per-record flag checked by the purge job, not a disabled job.
- [ ] Erasure is anonymisation where retention applies, and the erasure itself is audited.
- [ ] I can state that backups still contain deleted data, and what the procedure does about it.

## Audit logs (5.10.6)

- [ ] Entries carry actor (type, id, session), action from a closed vocabulary, entity, tenant, request id, and UTC timestamps.
- [ ] Before *and* after values are stored, with secrets scrubbed.
- [ ] The table is append-only by database permission, not by convention.
- [ ] Hash chaining exists, and concurrent writers are serialised so the chain is total.
- [ ] The head hash is anchored externally on a schedule.
- [ ] Verification recomputes the chain and reports the *first* break.
- [ ] Service-account actions store the delegation record, so "who" resolves to a human.
- [ ] Clock synchronisation is monitored, and the clock source is recorded per entry.
- [ ] There is an audit-coverage test: privileged routes cannot be reached without an audit call.
- [ ] Retention exceeds the dispute window and is documented.

## Multi-tenancy and isolation (5.10.7, 5.10.8)

- [ ] I can compare shared schema, schema-per-tenant, and database-per-tenant on isolation, cost, migrations, and cross-tenant queries.
- [ ] The tenant id comes from a signed claim or a verified gateway header â€” never from a body field or an unverified header.
- [ ] Every tenant-scoped repository method requires a tenant; there is no unscoped export.
- [ ] RLS is enabled with `force row level security` and `with check`, and the app connects as a non-superuser.
- [ ] `set_config(..., true)` runs inside the transaction on the held connection.
- [ ] Cache keys, job payloads, idempotency keys, and object paths are all tenant-prefixed by construction.
- [ ] `tenant_id` is `NOT NULL` and the leading column of every composite index; test fixtures are never `null`.
- [ ] Per-tenant migrations have a version ledger and a lock budget; `CONCURRENTLY` is used for large tables.
- [ ] Break-glass access is explicit, audited, time-boxed, and alerted on.
- [ ] The route-table-driven isolation matrix runs in CI and asserts both id and value absence.

## API design review (5.10.9)

- [ ] I can state the nine blocking classes a review must catch.
- [ ] Naming conventions are followed: plural nouns, hierarchy, no verbs, opaque ids, RFC 3339 UTC, integer minor units for money.
- [ ] `PATCH` distinguishes absent, `null`, and a value, and the choice is documented.
- [ ] The additive-change table is written down, and enum additions are treated as dangerous.
- [ ] A CI gate fails on non-additive public API changes.
- [ ] Consumer-driven contract tests exist for service-to-service boundaries.
- [ ] Deprecation headers are part of the contract from day one.
- [ ] Every endpoint defines its failure responses, not just its happy path.
- [ ] The most expensive possible request per endpoint has been considered.

## Idempotency (5.10.10)

- [ ] I can list which methods are idempotent by definition and where keys are required.
- [ ] Keys are scoped to `(tenant, user, endpoint, key)` and bounded in length.
- [ ] The request fingerprint detects the same key with a different body, and returns 422.
- [ ] The claim is atomic (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` + `RETURNING`), never select-then-insert.
- [ ] Concurrent duplicates get 409 with `Retry-After`; completed ones get a byte-identical replay.
- [ ] The record commits in the same transaction as the side effect.
- [ ] External side effects receive the key from the provider too.
- [ ] There is a reaper for stale `in_progress` rows and a purge for expired ones.
- [ ] Retries use exponential backoff with full jitter, and only for idempotent requests.
- [ ] The key table has an erasure policy, because it stores request bodies.

## Background jobs (5.10.11)

- [ ] Every job has a name, an owner, a purpose, a schedule with an explicit timezone, a timeout, and a DLQ owner.
- [ ] Schedules live in one place with a single-execution guarantee (dedicated scheduler and/or advisory lock on a dedicated connection).
- [ ] Every handler is idempotent, keyed on a logical period or a business key.
- [ ] A run-record exists and is the authority for "did this period already run".
- [ ] DST is handled by keying on the logical period, not the instant.
- [ ] Concurrency policy is explicit (skip, queue, or replace) with a depth alert for `queue`.
- [ ] Destructive jobs have a dry-run mode, a reason field, and an expected-count assertion.
- [ ] Backfills are batched, resumable, rate-limited, and have a kill switch.
- [ ] A `last_success` alert exists for every job â€” the alert that catches a silently dead cron.
- [ ] Job payloads are versioned and re-validated at the worker.

## Feature flags (5.10.12)

- [ ] Flags and config are distinguished: deploy-time global vs per-request dynamic.
- [ ] Flag kinds are distinguished: release, kill switch, permission, experiment, config â€” with different removal rules.
- [ ] Kill switches do not depend on the subsystem they disable, and have a fast path plus an env-var backstop.
- [ ] Every flag has an owner and an expiry date, enforced by the flag store.
- [ ] Bucketing is a deterministic hash of a stable identifier.
- [ ] Rollout compares the flag-on cohort against the control cohort, and measures exposure.
- [ ] Failure mode is per flag: release/kill switches fail open, permission flags fail closed.
- [ ] CI detects drift in both directions: a code reference to a deleted flag, and a stored flag no code reads.
- [ ] No data migration is behind a flag without an expand/contract plan.
- [ ] Flag changes are audited and treated as deployment-class events.

## Health checks and operational readiness (5.10.13, 5.10.14)

- [ ] Liveness checks only the process, including real event-loop responsiveness, and never a dependency.
- [ ] Readiness checks critical dependencies with explicit timeouts, and records non-gating ones without gating.
- [ ] Deep readiness results are cached so probes do not add measurable load.
- [ ] `startupProbe` covers the worst-case cold start including dependency timeouts.
- [ ] The drain flips readiness first, keeps liveness green, waits for endpoint propagation, then closes and drains with a hard deadline.
- [ ] In-flight work is tracked on both `finish` and `close`.
- [ ] `/livez` and `/readyz` are unauthenticated, unrate-limited, untraced, and expose nothing sensitive.
- [ ] SLIs have a written measurement definition; the SLO is agreed by the people who must live with it.
- [ ] Alerting is multi-window burn-rate, on symptoms, with a runbook link in the alert text.
- [ ] The pre-launch checklist is gated: flags default off, rollback rehearsed, runbook written, business metric defined, first-48-hours owner named.
- [ ] Alerts are on queue depth *and* oldest message age, not depth alone.
- [ ] A game day has been run against this service by someone who did not build it.

## Deprecation (5.10.15)

- [ ] I can compare URL versioning, header versioning, additive-only, and internal-only versioning and say which applies to a public vs internal API.
- [ ] Deprecation follows the five steps: decide, announce, measure, migrate, enforce â€” with usage telemetry before any of it.
- [ ] `Deprecation`, `Sunset`, and `Link rel="deprecation"` headers are sent, and the sunset date is real.
- [ ] Post-sunset responses are 410 Gone with a pointer, not 404 and not a 200 warning body.
- [ ] Data migration is planned and validated, because removing code is the easy part.
- [ ] The kill order is: stop new usage â†’ communicate â†’ migrate data â†’ freeze â†’ remove code and the "off" path.
- [ ] Internal deprecations produce a compiler warning and a build-time usage report.
- [ ] I can name the rollback for the migration, not just the plan.

**Reading list, by name (no URLs, by design).** The 12-factor methodology; RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics) for method safety and idempotency and status-code selection; RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs); RFC 8594 (Sunset) and the `Deprecation` header specification; the OpenAPI 3.1 specification and its schema-object rules; JSON Schema 2020-12; the Pino documentation (redaction paths, transports, serializers, stdSerializers); the OWASP cheat sheets for logging, input validation, mass assignment, authorisation, and multi-tenancy; the PostgreSQL documentation on row-level security (including `FORCE`), `set_config`, advisory locks, partial indexes, `SKIP LOCKED`, and `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`; the Prisma middleware and `$extends` documentation; PgBouncer's transaction-mode pooling documentation and its list of session-state features; the Google SRE workbook chapters on SLOs, error budgets, and alerting on symptoms; the Prometheus multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerting runbook; Kubernetes documentation on liveness, readiness, and startup probes and termination behaviour; the Stripe API reference sections on idempotency and webhook signature verification; the GDPR articles on erasure, rectification, and records of processing; the LaunchDarkly and Unleash documentation on flag lifecycles, streaming evaluation, and kill switches; the OpenTelemetry specification's context-propagation and log-correlation notes.

**Practice order.** Do the eight MUST-IMPLEMENT problems in order, because each builds on the last: config (1) feeds the logger (2), which the validation layer (3) uses for its error envelope, which paginates (4), which soft-deletes (5) and audits (6), which are both tenant-scoped (7) and made retry-safe (8). Then work the ten debugging scenarios in order â€” they map the same practices onto production conditions, and the isolation-matrix scenario is the one that finds the most expensive bug. Then the rapid-fire set until every answer comes out in one breath and in the right order.

topics.title: The event loop: phases, microtask vs macrotask ordering
topics.description: The event loop is libuv's scheduler: a fixed sequence of *phases* that run once per "tick", with a microtask queue drained completely between every single phase, and between every individual callback. Node's own process.nextTick queue is drained *before* the microtask queue.
keyConcepts: The phases, in order, one tick
The two drain queues, and their exact relationship
The canonical demonstration, and how to read it
What the poll phase actually blocks on

Microtask (await, queueMicrotask): work that must happen *before* the program does anything else observable â€” unwinding a chain of state updates, writing a value that the next synchronous reader must see, batching within one turn. It is the default for "sequence-dependent continuation".

Timer (setTimeout(fn, 0)): deliberately yielding to the event loop so *other* work (I/O, other callbacks) can proceed. A zero-delay timer is not "immediately"; it is "after at least one turn of the loop, and in practice no sooner than 1 ms".

A common mistake that is also a common pattern: awaiting a resolved promise in a loop that awaits other promises. Each await is a microtask, so the whole chain drains before any I/O, even if the loop body is I/O-shaped. If you *need* to let I/O interleave, you need a macrotask boundary (setImmediate).

Microtasks give ordering guarantees but are un-preemptible; a runaway microtask chain starves the loop, and the loop is the only place your I/O completions can be delivered. There is no "interrupt" in JavaScript.
Timers give fairness but are imprecise (clamped, and never earlier than the requested delay) and cost a bit more per scheduling.
setImmediate is the correct tool for "do this after the current I/O batch, before yielding to timers", e.g. kicking off work right after draining a socket.

Never schedule a timer to represent "a duration in the future" if a single long timer would do (setTimeout(fn, 3600_000) vs 3,600,000 one-second timers). A large timer list is real memory and a real epoll bookkeeping cost.
Timers are not cancelled by garbage collection if a reference remains. clearTimeout in the teardown path of long-lived objects (request handlers, subscriptions) is not optional.
commonMistakes: Claiming setTimeout(0) always fires before setImmediate. It does not, at the top level of a module.
Claiming process.nextTick and promises interleave. They do not; nextTick fully drains first.
Using queueMicrotask for a heavy loop and calling it "async". It blocks the loop exactly like a for loop, with fewer debugging tools.
Assuming a pending timer keeps the process alive. Only the *unref'd* case is subtle: timer.unref() lets the process exit even though the timer is registered.

topics.title: process.nextTick vs setImmediate vs setTimeout(0) vs promises
topics.description: Four ways to defer work, with three distinct positions in the tick and one genuinely different mechanism (nextTick is a Node-specific queue drained ahead of everything, not a libuv phase).
keyConcepts: The one table to memorise
nextTick vs a promise, on the question of stacks
To schedule application work. It is a V8-adjacent ordering tool, not a scheduler.
Inside a library that runs in someone else's process. nextTick runs before the *caller's* continuation, which will surprise them.
To "yield". It does not yield to I/O. If you want to yield, you want setImmediate or setTimeout(0).
In a EventEmitter handler or a request handler, process.nextTick work happens before the current request's response can be flushed â€” that is the *point*, and also the risk if the work is heavy.
Never use nextTick to schedule a retry with a backoff; use setTimeout (or a real queue). A microtask "retry" against a condition that is still false produces a permanent 100% CPU spin.
setTimeout in Node returns a Timeout object with unref()/ref(). unref()'d timers do not keep the process alive â€” useful for keep-alive probes in a CLI, dangerous for a business timer.
Under load, "check phase runs every tick" means setImmediate callbacks can be starved by a poll phase that always has work. There is no fairness guarantee between phases.

"Order these six callbacks, and tell me which ordering is guaranteed and which is a race." The guaranteed set is: sync code â†’ all nextTick â†’ all promises â†’ then *one* of timer/immediate. Saying that precisely is the whole answer.

"Is recursive nextTick a stack overflow?" â€” no. The stack unwinds between callbacks, so it never reaches a RangeError; the real failure is starvation, because the queue drains before the loop advances and I/O and timers never run. Yield with setImmediate.
"How do you schedule a function after the current I/O batch but before the next timers phase?" â€” setImmediate.
commonMistakes: process.nextTick(() => reject(e)) inside an async function, where the function's own rejection already covers it. Now you have an unhandled rejection and a double-settle.
Using setTimeout(fn, 0) and claiming it runs "before promises".
Assuming nextTick and queueMicrotask are interchangeable. They are ordered differently, and libraries depend on the difference.
Using queueMicrotask to spawn concurrent work: microtasks run *before* the promise you returned is even observed, so a caller can never get control between them.

Explain nexttick vs a promise, on the question of stacks and when you would use it.

topics.title: libuv and the thread pool: what runs off the main thread
topics.description: libuv is the C event-loop and cross-platform I/O library under Node's core. It provides the loop, the async I/O primitives (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), the thread pool, and cross-platform abstractions. Node's JavaScript runs on one thread; the actual blocking work happens in the pool.
keyConcepts: The pool
The knob, and its classic bug
Sizing the pool, honestly
The default of 4 is conservative and appropriate for a service that is mostly *network*-bound: most of a typical service's "async" work is socket I/O, which does not touch the pool at all.
Raise it when you can *measure* pool saturation. Raising it costs memory (each thread has a stack and a libuv request) and adds contention.
Never raise it as a substitute for moving the work out of the process. If compression or PBKDF2 is saturating the pool, the answer is a worker thread or a different architecture, not 64 pool threads.
Measure with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 as a diagnostic: if throughput barely changes, the pool was not your bottleneck, and you have saved yourself a tuning mistake.
zlib is the most common hidden pool consumer. compression and sharp/sharp-adjacent pipelines and brotli all land here. If you gzip, prefer doing it once at a proxy, or accept the pool cost knowingly.

crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt are the most dangerous, because the work factor is attacker-controllable in the sense that a login endpoint *always* runs them. Node 18+ and the WebCrypto API give you off-thread variants; a dedicated worker or an async KDF in a separate process is the robust answer for high login rates.

dns.lookup vs dns.resolve is a real production footgun: lookup is getaddrinfo, which is in the pool, and a slow DNS server then stalls unrelated fs calls. Use dns.resolve4/resolveAny (c-ares, loop-based) for high-volume outbound calls, or set dns.setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first') to reduce the A+AAAA double lookup.
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE must be set before anything requires libuv â€” setting it in application code after boot is a no-op. Put it in the Dockerfile ENV or the process manager's environment.
"Which of these 10 fs/network/zlib operations use the thread pool?" â€” expect you to classify all ten.
commonMistakes: Believing sockets use the thread pool. They do not.
Believing fs.promises means "not the thread pool". It means "the pool, but with a promise instead of a callback".
"We raised UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64 and p99 got worse" â€” plausible: more context switches, more memory, and more contention on the same data structures.
Using fs.readFileSync in a migration script that runs concurrently with serving traffic.
Assuming async crypto/zlib work does not block. It blocks *the pool*, which is a shared, finite resource â€” a different kind of blocking, with a different blast radius.


- Believing `fs.promises` means "not the thread pool". It means "the pool, but with a promise instead of a callback".

- Using `fs.readFileSync` in a migration script that runs concurrently with serving traffic.
- Assuming async `crypto`/`zlib` work does not block. It blocks *the pool*, which is a shared, finite resource â€” a different kind of blocking, with a different blast radius.

- "How would you hash a password without blocking?" â€” async `crypto.scrypt`/`pbkdf2` (still pool-bounded), a worker thread, an external auth service, or a separate process; and the argument that the *right* answer is often to not roll your own password hashing at all.

topics.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O, and the CPU-bound trap
topics.description: Blocking I/O stops execution until the operation completes; non-blocking I/O returns immediately and delivers completion later via a callback/promise/stream event. Node is a *non-blocking by design* runtime, which means every synchronous operation you write is a bug waiting for traffic.
keyConcepts: The trap, stated precisely
The three correct fixes, and what each costs
The classification rule interviewers like
I/O-bound (waiting on a socket, disk, DNS, a queue): async/await, keep the work on the main thread, and let the loop overlap it with other requests. Concurrency comes free.

CPU-bound (parsing a 40 MB payload, image transforms, crypto on large buffers, JSON stringify of a giant graph, a tight loop): a worker thread or a process, plus backpressure so the queue does not become its own outage.

Ambiguous (a database query: network I/O, but the *driver* may block): assume the driver is async, but verify. Some drivers do synchronous DNS or synchronous certificate validation. Check the driver's await coverage and its connection-pool behaviour before you claim a route is non-blocking.
When NOT to reach for a worker thread
The work is under about 1 ms. Message-passing overhead and structured-clone/transfer cost exceed the work itself.
The work is a "blocking" library call you can replace with an async one. fs.readFileSync â†’ fs.promises.readFile is nearly always better than wrapping readFileSync in a worker.
You can push the work downstream: an image resize belongs in a job queue, not in the API request.
Every synchronous API in the standard library has a rule: sync in the *startup* path, async in the *request* path. readFileSync for config at boot is idiomatic and correct.
--max-old-space-size does not make main-thread compute faster; it only delays the OOM. Treat a raised heap limit as a symptom, not a fix.
commonMistakes: Marking a function async and believing that made it non-blocking. It changed the *signature*, not the *execution*.
Awaiting a promise chain that never actually suspends (1000 iterations of await Promise.resolve(1)) and calling it "concurrent". It is 1000 microtasks and zero overlap.
Reading a 20 MB file into memory per request with readFile, then JSON.parseing it â€” two main-thread stalls per request.
Using a while loop to poll for a condition instead of a timer or an event, producing a 100%-CPU spin.
Assuming a rate limiter or a queue in front of a CPU-bound endpoint makes the CPU work cheaper. It only makes the queue longer.

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 5.1.1

**Definition:** Blocking I/O stops execution until the operation completes; non-blocking I/O returns immediately and delivers completion later via a callback/promise/stream event. Node is a *non-blocking by design* runtime, which means every synchronous operation you write is a bug waiting for traffic.

**The trap, stated precisely**

Node's concurrency model assumes your work is *waiting*, not *computing*. When you compute, there is no event loop progress: no other request, no other connection, no timer. There is no preemption in JavaScript. The only defences are: do less work, move work to another thread, or move work to another process.

```js
// The CPU-bound trap in its purest form: 3,000 concurrent requests, one core.
app.get('/hash', async (req, res) => {
  // Looks async. Is not. This is 80 ms of hard block per call.
  res.json(sha256(req.query.input));
});
// With 200 concurrent requests: ~16 seconds for the last one, and every other
// route on the same process is frozen the whole time. Health checks time out.
// The orchestrator restarts the pod. The incident is "random 502s".
```

The diagnostic signature is important to state: **p99 explodes while p50 stays fine**, and the failure is *correlated with concurrency*, not with payload size. A slow *dependency* also produces a p99 spike, so the way you tell them apart is the event loop delay histogram and CPU utilisation:

| Symptom | CPU at 100%? | Event loop delay histogram | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU-bound handler | Yes, one core | Fat tail, hundreds of ms | Main-thread compute |
| Slow database | No, idle | Fat tail | Off-process wait |
| GC pressure | Yes, spiky | Periodic spikes | Allocation rate / heap growth |
| `fs` pool saturation | No, low | Long but *bunched* | Thread pool contention |

**The three correct fixes, and what each costs**

```js
// 1. Make the work cheaper. Best first move: measure before optimising.
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';                 // native, fast, but still main-thread
const cached = new Map();                                  // memoise idempotent work
function hash(s) { const hit = cached.get(s); if (hit) return hit;
  const h = createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex'); cached.set(s, h); return h; }

// 2. Move it to a worker thread. (See 5.1.8 for the full pattern.)
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';
const pool = new WorkerPool(4, new URL('./hash-worker.js', import.meta.url));

// 3. Move it to another process. (See 5.1.9.)
```

**The classification rule interviewers like**

- **I/O-bound** (waiting on a socket, disk, DNS, a queue): async/await, keep the work on the main thread, and let the loop overlap it with other requests. Concurrency comes free.
- **CPU-bound** (parsing a 40 MB payload, image transforms, crypto on large buffers, JSON stringify of a giant graph, a tight loop): a worker thread or a process, plus backpressure so the queue does not become its own outage.
- **Ambiguous** (a database query: network I/O, but the *driver* may block): assume the driver is async, but verify. Some drivers do synchronous DNS or synchronous certificate validation. Check the driver's `await` coverage and its connection-pool behaviour before you claim a route is non-blocking.

**When NOT to reach for a worker thread**

- The work is under about 1 ms. Message-passing overhead and structured-clone/transfer cost exceed the work itself.
- The work is a "blocking" library call you can replace with an async one. `fs.readFileSync` â†’ `fs.promises.readFile` is nearly always better than wrapping `readFileSync` in a worker.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 5.1 introduction

**Definition:** A `Buffer` is Node's view over a chunk of raw memory, a fixed-length byte array backed by an off-heap allocation. It is how Node represents binary data, and it is deliberately *not* a JavaScript string: strings are UTF-16 code-unit sequences, which cannot represent arbitrary bytes.

**The mental model: bytes vs characters**

```
A string in JS  : "Ã©"            â†’  1 code point, 1 UTF-16 code unit (U+00E9), 2 UTF-8 bytes
A string in JS  : "ðŸ˜€" (U+1F600) â†’  2 UTF-16 code units, 4 UTF-8 bytes, length === 2
A Buffer        : <Buffer e9>    â†’  1 byte, length === 1, no notion of "character"

Node strings are UTF-16. If you write a fixed-width parser against string.length,
you are reading UTF-16 code units, not characters, and not bytes.
```

```js
'ðŸ˜€'.length;                 // 2
Buffer.from('ðŸ˜€', 'utf8');   // <Buffer f0 9f 98 80>  length 4
'Ã©'.length;                  // 1
Buffer.from('Ã©', 'latin1');  // <Buffer e9>  length 1
Buffer.from('Ã©', 'utf8');    // <Buffer c3 a9>  length 2
```

That last pair is the classic bug: reading a latin1/binary file with `utf8` (or vice versa) does not throw â€” it produces *mojibake*, and sometimes produces a string that is a different *length*, which corrupts any offset-based seek. Decoding errors must be surfaced, not silently replaced.

**Allocating and reading**

```js
import { Buffer, constants, transcode } from 'node:buffer';

// Allocate; note that Buffer.alloc is ZERO-FILLED and Buffer.allocUnsafe is NOT.
const a = Buffer.alloc(16);                 // 16 zero bytes, guaranteed
const b = Buffer.allocUnsafe(16);           // 16 bytes of whatever was there â€” may contain secrets
const c = Buffer.from('hello');             // from a string
const d = Buffer.from([0xde, 0xad, 0xbe, 0xef]);
const e = c.toString('base64url');
const f = Buffer.from('aGVsbG8=', 'base64');

// Conversion cost note (this is the thing people forget):
const bytes = Buffer.from(str, 'utf8');     // ALWAYS copies
const shared = Buffer.from(str);            // shares str's memory (fast) â€” do not mutate
console.log(shared.byteOffset, shared.buffer.byteLength, shared.length);

// Check capacity, not just the view.
console.log(c.buffer.byteLength);           // 8192 â€” the pool slab, not 5
// Buffer.poolSize>>>1 controls the slab; Buffer.allocUnsafe uses the pool,
// Buffer.alloc (for sizes < poolSize/2) and Buffer.from(string) allocate fresh.
```

`Buffer.allocUnsafe` is a security issue, not a performance one. Any uninitialised byte you do not fully write is a byte from a previous request's data, and it leaves the process. Its legitimate uses are narrow: filling the whole buffer immediately with `buf.fill()`, or `buf.write()` returning bytes you have verified.

```js
// The genuinely dangerous shape:
const b = Buffer.allocUnsafe(4096);
const n = socket.read(b);                    // only n bytes are meaningful
fs.writeFile('out.bin', b);                  // leaks up to 4096-n bytes of other users' memory
// Correct: b.subarray(0, n)
```

**The pool slab, `subarray` vs `slice`, and mutation**

```js
const slab = Buffer.allocUnsafe(8192);
const view  = slab.subarray(0, 16);   // SAME memory, no copy
const copy  = slab.slice(0, 16);      // new Buffer, copied
view[0] = 0xff;
console.log(slab[0]);                 // 255 â€” they are the same bytes
```

This is a real source of subtle bugs: `Buffer.concat`, `Buffer.from` and `subarray` mix copy and no-copy semantics in the same expression, and a held `subarray` keeps the whole slab alive (a memory leak that looks like nothing at all in a heap snapshot).

**Reading: three methods, three meanings**

```js
const buf = Buffer.from('hÃ©llo', 'utf8');

buf.toString();                        // 'hÃ©llo'  â€” whole buffer, utf8
buf.toString('utf8', 0, 3);            // 'hÃ©'    â€” byte range 0..2 (may split a char!)
buf.subarray(0, 3).toString();         // 'hÃ©'    â€” same, but the subarray is a view
buf.length;                            // 6 â€” BYTES, not characters
buf.byteLength;                        // 6
String(buf).length;                    // 5 â€” characters; a confusing source of "why doesn't this match?"
```

For fixed-width binary formats, the tool that removes all guesswork is `DataView`, which is explicit about endianness and offsets and does not inherit Buffer's pooling:

```js
function readHeader(b) {
  const dv = new DataView(b.buffer, b.byteOffset, b.byteLength);
  return {
    magic:   dv.getUint32(0, false),   // false = big-endian (network order)
    version: dv.getUint16(4, true),    // true  = little-endian
    length:  dv.getUint32(6, false),
  };
}
```

**Encoding choice matters for the wire**

| Encoding | Bytes/char (ASCII) | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `utf8` | 1 | Default. Interoperable, handles all of Unicode |
| `latin1` / `binary` | 1 | Legacy binary blobs, and it maps bytes 0-255 â†’ U+0000-U+00FF losslessly. Do not use as a UTF-8 substitute |
| `ascii` | 1 | Rarely; historically stripped the high bit, which now throws on non-ASCII |
| `hex` | 2 | Debugging, checksums, keys in config |
| `base64` | 4/3 | Transports, JWTs, data URIs |
| `base64url` | 4/3 | JWT and URL-safe, `-` and `_`, no padding |
| `ucs2`/`ucs4`/`utf16le` | 2/4 | Only for legacy Windows UTF-16 files; doubles or quadruples size on the wire |

`Buffer.from(s, 'base64')` is *lenient*: it silently ignores characters outside the alphabet. If the input is attacker-controlled, validate the encoding explicitly or use `base64url` plus a length check, because "invalid base64 becomes a shorter valid string" is a real bypass surface for signature checks (see **PHASE 7 â†’ Cryptography**).

**Streams of bytes: the `Buffer` â†’ `Stream` relationship**

Every stream chunk in object mode off is a Buffer (or a string if `encoding` is set). Streams are the right abstraction for any data whose size you do not know up front; Buffers are right for data you *do* know, and for wire formats you parse by hand.

```js
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';
// 4 MB file: one 4 MB Buffer (peak memory = file size)
// 4 MB file, 64 KB chunks: peak memory ~= 64 KB + downstream buffers
createReadStream('./big.csv', { highWaterMark: 64 * 1024 });
```

**When to use a Buffer vs a string vs a stream vs a typed array**

- **Buffer**: file I/O, network frames, crypto input, anything you will hand to a native API.
- **String**: text you are parsing, printing, or putting in JSON. Convert at the boundary, not in the middle of logic.
- **Stream**: size unknown, or you want constant memory while processing.
- **`Uint8Array` / `DataView`**: when you share memory with a worker via transfer, or when interoperating with a browser-side buffer, or when you want explicit endianness control. `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array` subclass, so it interoperates, but `Buffer` allocates from the slab.

**Trade-offs**

- Strings are convenient and universally understood by libraries; Buffers are exact and allocation-cheap. Converting between them costs a copy every time. Pick one representation per layer and convert at the boundary.
- `latin1` is 1 byte per char and lossless for bytes, which makes it a fast intermediate for binary parsing â€” but the moment you `toString('utf8')` it you are decoding, and a mis-split multi-byte sequence becomes U+FFFD. Parse *bytes*, then decode the field.
- Buffers off-heap: they are invisible to the V8 heap in heap snapshots. A Buffer leak shows up as growing RSS with a flat heap â€” which is exactly the diagnostic in 5.1.12.

**Production considerations**

- Set a size cap at every trust boundary. `Buffer.from(hugeBase64)` on an unbounded request body is a one-line memory DoS.
- `Buffer.concat(list, totalLength)` computes the total for you; forgetting `totalLength` makes it re-sum the list (O(n) instead of O(1)) and can allocate twice.
- Never log a Buffer containing credentials or session material. `console.log(buf)` prints the whole thing, including zero bytes.
- Watch for slab retention: a cached `subarray` pins an 8 KB slab indefinitely. If you cache anything, cache a copy (`Buffer.from(view)`).
- If you build many small Buffers per request, you are creating GC pressure on the external memory path; `Buffer.alloc` + a fill is cheaper than repeated `Buffer.concat` of tiny pieces.

**Common mistakes**
- `buf.toString('utf8', 0, len)` where `len` was computed from a string's `.length` â€” string length is UTF-16 units, buffer length is bytes.
- Treating a truncated multi-byte sequence as a bug in the data when it is a bug in the framing.
- `Buffer.from(str)` (no encoding) instead of `Buffer.from(str, 'utf8')` â€” identical for ASCII, and a trap the moment the string is not ASCII.
- Using `base64` for a token that goes in a URL (should be `base64url`, or the `+`/`/` and `=` get percent-encoded or rejected).
- Mutating a Buffer you received from a stream chunk and being surprised when the source's data changes.

**What an interviewer probes**
- "Why does `Buffer.from('Ã©')` have length 2 but `String(Buffer.from('Ã©'))` have length 1?" â€” UTF-8 bytes vs characters.
- "How do you detect a byte-order mark and what do you do with it?" â€” read the first 3 bytes; `ef bb bf` is UTF-8 BOM and must be stripped or your JSON parse fails with a character you cannot see.
- "Your image endpoint returns null bytes in the first 200 KB." â€” `allocUnsafe` not fully written, or a length field written in the wrong endianness, or a latin1/utf8 mismatch.

```js
createReadStream('./big.csv', { highWaterMark: 64 * 1024 });
```

**When to use a Buffer vs a string vs a stream vs a typed array**

- **Buffer**: file I/O, network frames, crypto input, anything you will hand to a native API.
- **String**: text you are parsing, printing, or putting in JSON. Convert at the boundary, not in the middle of logic.
- **Stream**: size unknown, or you want constant memory while processing.
- **`Uint8Array` / `DataView`**: when you share memory with a worker via transfer, or when interoperating with a browser-side buffer, or when you want explicit endianness control. `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array` subclass, so it interoperates, but `Buffer` allocates from the slab.

**Trade-offs**

- Strings are convenient and universally understood by libraries; Buffers are exact and allocation-cheap. Converting between them costs a copy every time. Pick one representation per layer and convert at the boundary.
- `latin1` is 1 byte per char and lossless for bytes, which makes it a fast intermediate for binary parsing â€” but the moment you `toString('utf8')` it you are decoding, and a mis-split multi-byte sequence becomes U+FFFD. Parse *bytes*, then decode the field.
- Buffers off-heap: they are invisible to the V8 heap in heap snapshots. A Buffer leak shows up as growing RSS with a flat heap â€” which is exactly the diagnostic in 5.1.12.

**Production considerations**

- Set a size cap at every trust boundary. `Buffer.from(hugeBase64)` on an unbounded request body is a one-line memory DoS.
- `Buffer.concat(list, totalLength)` computes the total for you; forgetting `totalLength` makes it re-sum the list (O(n) instead of O(1)) and can allocate twice.
- Never log a Buffer containing credentials or session material. `console.log(buf)` prints the whole thing, including zero bytes.
- Watch for slab retention: a cached `subarray` pins an 8 KB slab indefinitely. If you cache anything, cache a copy (`Buffer.from(view)`).
- If you build many small Buffers per request, you are creating GC pressure on the external memory path; `Buffer.alloc` + a fill is cheaper than repeated `Buffer.concat` of tiny pieces.

**Common mistakes**
- `buf.toString('utf8', 0, len)` where `len` was computed from a string's `.length` â€” string length is UTF-16 units, buffer length is bytes.
- Treating a truncated multi-byte sequence as a bug in the data when it is a bug in the framing.
- `Buffer.from(str)` (no encoding) instead of `Buffer.from(str, 'utf8')` â€” identical for ASCII, and a trap the moment the string is not ASCII.
- Using `base64` for a token that goes in a URL (should be `base64url`, or the `+`/`/` and `=` get percent-encoded or rejected).
- Mutating a Buffer you received from a stream chunk and being surprised when the source's data changes.

**What an interviewer probes**
- "Why does `Buffer.from('Ã©')` have length 2 but `String(Buffer.from('Ã©'))` have length 1?" â€” UTF-8 bytes vs characters.
- "How do you detect a byte-order mark and what do you do with it?" â€” read the first 3 bytes; `ef bb bf` is UTF-8 BOM and must be stripped or your JSON parse fails with a character you cannot see.
- "Your image endpoint returns null bytes in the first 200 KB." â€” `allocUnsafe` not fully written, or a length field written in the wrong endianness, or a latin1/utf8 mismatch.

topics.description: EventEmitter is Node's pub/sub primitive, and the base of nearly every Node API you use: streams, HTTP request/response objects, the process object, most libraries. It is synchronous, unbounded, and it has one special rule: emitting 'error' with no listener throws.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: none

**Definition:** `package.json` is both a manifest (name, version, entry points, dependencies) and a set of **executable contracts with the tooling** â€” the `exports`/`imports` maps, `type`, `engines`, `sideEffects`, `files`. The fields that bite production incidents are almost never `dependencies`.

**The fields that matter, and what each one actually does**

| Field | Effect | Getting it wrong means |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | `"module"` or `"commonjs"` for **your** `.js` files; defaults to `commonjs` | Silent `require is not defined` / `module is not defined` |
| `main` | CJS entry point | Deep imports become your public API |
| `module` | Non-standard bundler hint | Ignored by Node; relied on by bundlers, inconsistently |
| `exports` | The public API of a **package**; a map of subpath â†’ target | `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`, or accidentally exporting internals |
| `imports` | The public API of **your own package's internals** (`#alias`) | Monorepo-internal imports stop working in a published build |
| `files` | What goes in the tarball | Shipping tests, fixtures, `.env`, source maps you did not mean to publish |
| `sideEffects` | Tells bundlers which modules can be dropped if unused | A CSS import or a polyfill silently disappears in production |
| `engines` | A warning, **never** an enforcement | Deployment runs on the wrong major and fails at runtime |
| `bin` | Executables linked into `node_modules/.bin` | A global install that does nothing |
| `scripts` | Aliases; also the hook points CI uses | `npm test` that does not run the tests |
| `private` | Blocks publish | An accidental public release of an app |
| `packageManager` | Pins pnpm/yarn via Corepack | Different lockfile behaviour per developer and in CI |
| `overrides`/`resolutions` | Force a transitive version | A patched-but-incompatible dependency, invisibly |

**The module system, in one table**

```jsonc
{
  "type": "module",            // .js is ESM. Use .mjs/.cjs to override per file.
  "main": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS entry
  "module": "./dist/index.js",  // bundler hint (not a Node contract)
  "exports": {                 // THE public API. Nothing outside is importable.
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "import": "./dist/index.js",     // ESM consumers
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS consumers
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    },
    "./package.json": "./package.json",  // required for tools that read the manifest
    "./sub": "./dist/sub.js"
  },
  "imports": {                 // YOUR package's internal aliases. '#' prefix is mandatory.
    "#db": "./src/db/index.js",
    "#config": { "node": "./src/config.node.js", "default": "./src/config.js" }
  },
  "files": ["dist", "README.md"],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"],
  "engines": { "node": ">=20.11" },
  "packageManager": "pnpm@9.12.0"
}
```

Three consequences worth saying out loud:

- **`exports` is a hard wall.** `require('mypkg/src/internal')` fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` once `exports` exists. That is a feature: it is how you can refactor internals without a breaking release. It is also why "just import the deep path" is a bug report waiting to happen.
- **`exports` also controls types.** A package with a `types` condition inside `exports` gives TypeScript the right declaration; one with only a top-level `types` field breaks under `moduleResolution: "bundler"`/`"node16"`.
- **`"imports"` with `#` is not optional.** A bare `"#db"` key or a non-`#` key is invalid and the resolution fails at load time, not install time.

**Dependencies, correctly**

```jsonc
{
  "dependencies":    { "pg": "8.13.1" },                     // exact: you control it
  "devDependencies": { "typescript": "^5.6.3" },             // range: you tolerate churn
  "peerDependencies": { "react": "^18 || ^19" },
  "optionalDependencies": { "fsevents": "^2.3.3" }          // failure is tolerated
}
```

- **`dependencies` should be exact or caret-minus, but the lockfile is the real pin.** Commit `package-lock.json` / `pnpm-lock.yaml` and use `npm ci` (or `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) in CI. `npm install` in CI can silently change versions, which is how "it worked yesterday" incidents happen.
- **`peerDependencies`** means "the host must provide this", which is right for React plugins and wrong for libraries that just want a version range. Getting this wrong produces a *nested duplicate* of a singleton library, and duplicate singletons are a real bug class (see **PHASE 4 â†’ micro-frontends**).
- **`optionalDependencies`** is a genuine "best effort": a platform-specific binary that must not break the install on the wrong OS. It is also the standard way to ship `fsevents`.
- **A runtime dependency imported inside a `try` in an optional code path is still a hard dependency for bundlers.** If a package is truly optional, do not import it statically.

**Lockfiles and reproducibility**

```bash
npm ci                       # CI: exact, from the lockfile, fails if the lock is stale
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
yarn install --immutable
node -p "process.versions"    # what you actually run

# Audit and provenance
npm audit --omit=dev         # production tree only; dev vulns rarely matter at runtime
npm ls --all                 # who is pulling in lodash 3?
npm explain express
npm outdated --long
```

`npm audit` is a CVE database join, not a reachability analysis (see **PHASE 7 â†’ Supply Chain**). The high-signal command is `npm explain <pkg>` for *why* a package is present, and reviewing whether the vulnerable code path is reachable at all.

**Publishing and install artefacts**

```bash
npm publish --dry-run         # shows exactly what goes in the tarball
npm pack --dry-run            # same, tarball form
npm pkg get name version      # read manifest fields via the CLI
npx node-gyp rebuild          # native addon, if it is yours
```

```dockerfile
# Multi-stage, and the install step is the one people get wrong.
FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # deps only, no build tools needed

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                         # dev deps needed to build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node                            # never run as root
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]         # no npm/npx in the entrypoint: PID 1 signal delivery
```

`CMD ["node", ...]` rather than `CMD ["npm", "start"]` is not a style preference: npm forwards signals inconsistently, so `SIGTERM` may never reach your process and every graceful shutdown in 5.1.11 silently becomes a `SIGKILL`.

**Monorepo package managers**

| Tool | Model | Notable |
|---|---|---|
| npm workspaces | Symlinked `node_modules`, hoisted | Simplest, least strict |
| pnpm | Content-addressed store, **strict** by default | No phantom dependencies; smaller install; the strictness is the feature |
| Yarn (berry) | Plug'n'Play or node_modules | `yarn constraints`; good for constraints-heavy teams |
| Nx / Turborepo | Task graph, caching, affected-only builds | Build-time optimisation, not installation |

The single most valuable behaviour to know: **pnpm's strictness makes an undeclared dependency an error rather than an accident that works locally** because of hoisting. If a package imports something not in its own `package.json`, npm/Yarn will often let it work and pnpm will not. That is a bug caught in CI instead of in production.

**Trade-offs**

- Exact pins in `dependencies` make upgrades deliberate and patch work manual; ranges make security patches automatic and introduce nondeterminism. The lockfile-plus-`npm ci` answer is: **ranges in the manifest, exact in the lockfile, `ci` in CI, plus a scheduled dependency PR bot.**
- `"type": "module"` is the correct modern default. It costs a migration (no `require` in your own code, `__dirname` gone) and buys real ESM: live bindings, top-level await, and `import`/`exports` symmetry.
- Monorepos buy atomic cross-package changes and one CI bill; they cost a build-system tax, a publish-ordering problem, and a temptation to create a `utils` dumping ground.
- Dual-publishing ESM and CJS is real work (two builds, two `exports` branches, a `types` condition per branch) and it is what every well-behaved library does, because one of your consumers is always on the other system.

**Production considerations**

- Commit the lockfile. Run `npm ci` (or the equivalent) in CI and in the Docker build. A `npm install` in a build step makes builds non-reproducible.
- `NODE_ENV=production` in the image, `--omit=dev` in the install.
- Run as a non-root user, and set `--max-old-space-size` in the entrypoint if the container limit is known.
- `engines` is advisory; if you need enforcement, do it in the Dockerfile or a preflight check.

**Common mistakes**

- `npm install` in CI or in a Dockerfile instead of `npm ci`.

- Duplicated singleton packages because a `peerDependency` was declared as a regular `dependency` in one of your dependencies.

topics.bodyMarkdown:
ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: none

**Definition:** `package.json` is both a manifest (name, version, entry points, dependencies) and a set of **executable contracts with the tooling** â€” the `exports`/`imports` maps, `type`, `engines`, `sideEffects`, `files`. The fields that bite production incidents are almost never `dependencies`.

**The fields that matter, and what each one actually does**

| Field | Effect | Getting it wrong means |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | `"module"` or `"commonjs"` for **your** `.js` files; defaults to `commonjs` | Silent `require is not defined` / `module is not defined` |
| `main` | CJS entry point | Deep imports become your public API |
| `module` | Non-standard bundler hint | Ignored by Node; relied on by bundlers, inconsistently |
| `exports` | The public API of a **package**; a map of subpath â†’ target | `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`, or accidentally exporting internals |
| `imports` | The public API of **your own package's internals** (`#alias`) | Monorepo-internal imports stop working in a published build |
| `files` | What goes in the tarball | Shipping tests, fixtures, `.env`, source maps you did not mean to publish |
| `sideEffects` | Tells bundlers which modules can be dropped if unused | A CSS import or a polyfill silently disappears in production |
| `engines` | A warning, **never** an enforcement | Deployment runs on the wrong major and fails at runtime |
| `bin` | Executables linked into `node_modules/.bin` | A global install that does nothing |
| `scripts` | Aliases; also the hook points CI uses | `npm test` that does not run the tests |
| `private` | Blocks publish | An accidental public release of an app |
| `packageManager` | Pins pnpm/yarn via Corepack | Different lockfile behaviour per developer and in CI |
| `overrides`/`resolutions` | Force a transitive version | A patched-but-incompatible dependency, invisibly |

**The module system, in one table**

```jsonc
{
  "type": "module",            // .js is ESM. Use .mjs/.cjs to override per file.
  "main": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS entry
  "module": "./dist/index.js",  // bundler hint (not a Node contract)
  "exports": {                 // THE public API. Nothing outside is importable.
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "import": "./dist/index.js",     // ESM consumers
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS consumers
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    },
    "./package.json": "./package.json",  // required for tools that read the manifest
    "./sub": "./dist/sub.js"
  },
  "imports": {                 // YOUR package's internal aliases. '#' prefix is mandatory.
    "#db": "./src/db/index.js",
    "#config": { "node": "./src/config.node.js", "default": "./src/config.js" }
  },
  "files": ["dist", "README.md"],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"],
  "engines": { "node": ">=20.11" },
  "packageManager": "pnpm@9.12.0"
}
```

Three consequences worth saying out loud:

- **`exports` is a hard wall.** `require('mypkg/src/internal')` fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` once `exports` exists. That is a feature: it is how you can refactor internals without a breaking release. It is also why "just import the deep path" is a bug report waiting to happen.
- **`exports` also controls types.** A package with a `types` condition inside `exports` gives TypeScript the right declaration; one with only a top-level `types` field breaks under `moduleResolution: "bundler"`/`"node16"`.
- **`"imports"` with `#` is not optional.** A bare `"#db"` key or a non-`#` key is invalid and the resolution fails at load time, not install time.

**Dependencies, correctly**

```jsonc
{
  "dependencies":    { "pg": "8.13.1" },                     // exact: you control it
  "devDependencies": { "typescript": "^5.6.3" },             // range: you tolerate churn
  "peerDependencies": { "react": "^18 || ^19" },
  "optionalDependencies": { "fsevents": "^2.3.3" }          // failure is tolerated
}
```

- **`dependencies` should be exact or caret-minus, but the lockfile is the real pin.** Commit `package-lock.json` / `pnpm-lock.yaml` and use `npm ci` (or `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) in CI. `npm install` in CI can silently change versions, which is how "it worked yesterday" incidents happen.
- **`peerDependencies`** means "the host must provide this", which is right for React plugins and wrong for libraries that just want a version range. Getting this wrong produces a *nested duplicate* of a singleton library, and duplicate singletons are a real bug class (see **PHASE 4 â†’ micro-frontends**).
- **`optionalDependencies`** is a genuine "best effort": a platform-specific binary that must not break the install on the wrong OS. It is also the standard way to ship `fsevents`.
- **A runtime dependency imported inside a `try` in an optional code path is still a hard dependency for bundlers.** If a package is truly optional, do not import it statically.

**Lockfiles and reproducibility**

```bash
npm ci                       # CI: exact, from the lockfile, fails if the lock is stale
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
yarn install --immutable
node -p "process.versions"    # what you actually run

# Audit and provenance
npm audit --omit=dev         # production tree only; dev vulns rarely matter at runtime
npm ls --all                 # who is pulling in lodash 3?
npm explain express
npm outdated --long
```

`npm audit` is a CVE database join, not a reachability analysis (see **PHASE 7 â†’ Supply Chain**). The high-signal command is `npm explain <pkg>` for *why* a package is present, and reviewing whether the vulnerable code path is reachable at all.

**Publishing and install artefacts**

```bash
npm publish --dry-run         # shows exactly what goes in the tarball
npm pack --dry-run            # same, tarball form
npm pkg get name version      # read manifest fields via the CLI
npx node-gyp rebuild          # native addon, if it is yours
```

```dockerfile
# Multi-stage, and the install step is the one people get wrong.
FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # deps only, no build tools needed

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                         # dev deps needed to build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node                            # never run as root
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]         # no npm/npx in the entrypoint: PID 1 signal delivery
```

`CMD ["node", ...]` rather than `CMD ["npm", "start"]` is not a style preference: npm forwards signals inconsistently, so `SIGTERM` may never reach your process and every graceful shutdown in 5.1.11 silently becomes a `SIGKILL`.

**Monorepo package managers**

| Tool | Model | Notable |
|---|---|---|
| npm workspaces | Symlinked `node_modules`, hoisted | Simplest, least strict |
| pnpm | Content-addressed store, **strict** by default | No phantom dependencies; smaller install; the strictness is the feature |
| Yarn (berry) | Plug'n'Play or node_modules | `yarn constraints`; good for constraints-heavy teams |
| Nx / Turborepo | Task graph, caching, affected-only builds | Build-time optimisation, not installation |

The single most valuable behaviour to know: **pnpm's strictness makes an undeclared dependency an error rather than an accident that works locally** because of hoisting. **Trade-offs**

- Exact pins in `dependencies` make upgrades deliberate and patch work manual; ranges make security patches automatic and introduce nondeterminism. The lockfile-plus-`npm ci` answer is: **ranges in the manifest, exact in the lockfile, `ci` in CI, plus a scheduled dependency PR bot.**

- Importing a `devDependency` from runtime code and shipping with `--omit=dev`.
- `CMD ["npm", "start"]` breaking signal delivery.
- Duplicated singleton packages because a `peerDependency` was declared as a regular `dependency` in one of your dependencies.

topics.title: Node vs Bun vs Deno
topics.description: Three runtimes that execute the same language with different defaults: Node (V8 + libuv + npm, the incumbent), Bun (JavaScriptCore + a bundled toolchain, prioritising startup time and built-ins), Deno (V8 + Rust + deno-native permissions, prioritising a secure-by-default web runtime).
keyConcepts: The comparison, on the axes that actually decide it
Where each genuinely wins
The migration cost, stated honestly

Node â†’ Bun: usually "works", with four recurring costs. (1) Some node: built-ins are shimmed with different semantics (dns, net TLS options, child_process signals). (2) N-API addons generally work but must be rebuilt for Bun's platform target. (3) Bun's event loop has a "should we await this?" heuristic that changes performance characteristics for certain sync/async mixes, and it is not bug-free. (4) The production runbook â€” your APM, your log shipper, your crash reporter â€” may not have a Bun integration.

Node â†’ Deno: the node: compat layer covers a lot, but node: coverage is not complete and the differences around streams, Buffer, and error cause semantics bite. The bigger cost is ecosystem: most of your dependencies are distributed for node_modules.
Both: you lose the LTS guarantee and the LTS conversation. In a regulated or large-organisation setting, "what is your support plan" is a procurement question, not an engineering one.
When to choose what â€” the honest heuristic

Bun's headline number is startup time and bundling speed. Both matter enormously for CLIs and serverless, and not at all for a long-running service, where steady-state throughput and ecosystem integration dominate. Saying "Bun is faster" without qualifying *what* is the mistake.

Deno's permissions are a real security improvement and a real operational cost: every new capability is a prompt or a flag, and flags are easy to over-broaden (--allow-all is the default in some tooling and the exact thing you did not want).
Node's "boring" is an asset. Predictable semantics, LTS, an enormous body of production knowledge, and no surprises at 3 a.m.
Every runtime's TypeScript story is a *transpile-only* story except Deno's deno check; neither Node nor Bun type-checks by default, and neither will catch a type error that exists only in types.

Benchmark your actual workload, not a synthetic one. Startup time, p99 under a realistic request mix, and a memory profile are three different numbers and Bun's advantage is concentrated in the first.
