topics.title: Controllers: Routing Decorators and the @Res Caveat
topics.description: A controller is a class whose decorated methods map HTTP routes to handlers. It is deliberately thin: parse input, delegate, shape output.
keyConcepts: Handler rules that matter

Return a value, a Promise, an Observable (converted with lastValueFrom internally), or a StreamableFile/Buffer for downloads. Returning a promise is fully supported; you do not need async just to be safe, though async is clearer.
Route order matters. Static segments must be declared before parameter segments, otherwise search is matched as :idOrSlug. This is a common production bug.
@Body() with the app's body-parser limit, @Query(), @Param(), @Headers(), @Req(), @Ip(), @Session() (needs the session middleware) are the parameter decorators.

@Header('X-Request-Id', id), @Redirect(url, status), @Render(template), @HttpCode(status), @UseGuards, @UseInterceptors, @UsePipes, @UseFilters complete the set. @UseGuards/@UseInterceptors registered on a controller apply to every handler; registered on a method only to that one; app.useGlobalGuards to all.
Headers are case-insensitive; use @Headers('x-request-id').
The @Res() caveat â€” the single most common NestJS surprise
With @Res() (no passthrough): ClassSerializerInterceptor will not strip @Exclude()d fields, logging/timing interceptors will not see the result, and the route will hang if you forget to send/finish.
Nest's docs say to use @Res() only when you need a library that requires the raw object (@Res() + passthrough: true is the escape hatch that keeps the pipeline).
Streaming responses
commonMistakes: using @Res() "just to set a header"; expecting interceptors to run; returning a promise from a handler that also used @Res() without passthrough; declaring search after :id; putting business logic in the controller instead of the service; changing status codes in the service layer.
practiceTasks: build a controller with twelve routes, then add: a ListOrdersQueryDto, a route that returns a CSV stream, a route that returns a 204, and one route using @Res({ passthrough: true }) to set an ETag. Then inject a logging interceptor and prove the @Res() (non-passthrough) handler never logs â€” and fix it.

interviewQuestions.text: What do you lose when you use `@Res()` without `passthrough`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: someone injected @Res() to set a header and then wondered why their @Exclude()d password field appeared in the response. Decision: treat @Res() as an opt-out from the framework's response pipeline, and use it only when a third-party library needs the raw Express/Fastify object. Reasoning: the presence of the response object is how the framework knows you took over, so it stops doing the things it would otherwise do â€” running the response interceptors, applying class serialization, and finalising the response for you. With passthrough: true you get the best of both: you set headers yourself, Nest still awaits your return value and serialises it, and exceptions still reach the filters. Trade-offs: passthrough still means you are responsible for Content-Type and for not calling send() yourself, and mixing the two styles in one handler is a good way to produce a double-send bug. Failure scenario: a Stripe SDK integration calls res.raw in an interceptor; every response in that controller now skips the logging interceptor, and support cannot find the request id in logs. Alternative: put the library behind an adapter class that exposes a plain method, and keep the response object inside the adapter â€” the controller never touches it."

interviewQuestions.text: Why must static routes be declared before parameterized ones?
How do you stream a large file from a controller?
What is the default status code for `POST`, and how do you change it?
Controller or service: who decides the HTTP status code?

topics.title: Guards vs Middleware vs Interceptors vs Pipes vs Filters vs Decorators
topics.description: Six extension points in the NestJS request lifecycle. Confusing them is the single most common NestJS interview and debugging failure, so this section is a reference, not a summary.
keyConcepts: Execution order
Ordering rules worth memorising
Interceptors wrap in reverse order of declaration: the first-registered outermost interceptor's next() callback is entered first, and its post-processing runs last.
Global enhancers run *before* controller-level ones.
A guard returning false throws ForbiddenException automatically; a guard that throws its own exception can return any status.

Exception filters do not reliably catch errors thrown in app.use() middleware, because middleware runs before Nest's exception layer exists. Wrap middleware bodies in try/catch or add a platform-level error handler.
Worked example 1 â€” Guard (authorization)
Worked example 2 â€” Pipe (validation + transformation)
The important limitation
Worked example 4 â€” Filter (uniform error body)
Worked example 5 â€” Custom decorator (metadata + behaviour)
commonMistakes: putting authorization in middleware (no DI, no route awareness); using a guard to transform the response; expecting @Res() handlers to pass through interceptors; assuming exception filters cover middleware; thinking decorators execute code (they mostly attach metadata); forgetting that interceptor post-processing runs in reverse order.
practiceTasks: build one of each â€” a guard, a pipe, an interceptor, a filter, a middleware and a custom decorator â€” on the same route. Then instrument the pipeline with a log line in each and hit the endpoint, so you can state the exact order from memory. Then deliberately throw an error inside a middleware and observe which filter (if any) catches it.

interviewQuestions.text: Put the six extension points in execution order and say what each can change.
Why can't middleware use DI?
What does a guard returning `false` do, and how do you return a custom status?
Why doesn't a timeout interceptor actually stop work?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a report endpoint started timing out at 30s, and after a few minutes the database showed hundreds of still-running queries, even though clients had already received 503. Decision: treat the timeout interceptor as a *client-facing* deadline and implement real cancellation separately. Reasoning: rxjs's timeout operator unsubscribes from the observable chain, but the handler is usually an async function whose promise is already executing inside the database driver. Unsubscribe does not send pg_cancel_backend or abort a fetch â€” the work continues and may commit after the client is gone, which is worse than slow: you get partial side effects with no client to receive the result. Trade-offs: real cancellation means threading an AbortSignal through the service and repository signatures, which touches a lot of code and needs driver support (node-postgres AbortSignal, pg cancellation, fetch's signal). Failure scenario: a batch job cancels 10,000 rows client-side and every cancellation still performed the write, so the retry logic double-charged customers. Alternative: two deadlines â€” a short timeout interceptor for the HTTP response, plus a long, enforced job-level timeout inside the worker that actually owns the work, with idempotent operations so an ambiguous outcome can be retried safely (see 5.4.4)."

interviewQuestions.text: Do exception filters catch errors thrown in middleware?
What's the difference between `@UseInterceptors(A, B)` and `@UseInterceptors(B, A)`?

topics.title: DTOs and Validation: The Actual Security Boundary
topics.description: A DTO is a class that describes the shape of an input at runtime. Because it is a class, class-validator decorators become real runtime constraints, and class-transformer can coerce and nest plain JSON into typed instances.
keyConcepts: Why a class and not a TypeScript interface
interface is erased at compile time â€” zero runtime information.

class emits both a runtime constructor and (with emitDecoratorMetadata) design-time type metadata (design:type), which is how @Type(() => OrderItemDto) can be applied automatically to nested properties.
DTO classes give you one place for OpenAPI metadata, validation rules, defaults, and documentation of what the client may send.

They give a compile-time type you can import in the controller signature *and* a runtime check â€” which is the whole point of "types are not validation" (see PHASE 1 TypeScript and 5.2's Zod discussion: Zod is the other valid answer, and a codebase should pick one).
Global pipe configuration

whitelist: true alone is the mass-assignment fix, because a property with no decorator is dropped. forbidNonWhitelisted: true turns "dropped silently" into a loud 400, which catches client bugs. Enable both; they are complementary.

transform: true is required for the handler to receive a CreateOrderDto instance, not a plain object, which matters as soon as you use class methods, nested @Type() conversion, or ClassSerializerInterceptor.

enableImplicitConversion will happily convert "true", "12", and â€” dangerously â€” anything truthy-looking. Prefer explicit @Type(() => Number) / @Type(() => Boolean) per field and leave implicit conversion off, then convert query DTOs explicitly.

Response validation exists too: new ValidationPipe({ ... }) on responses is opt-in per handler (@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe(...)) plus a response DTO class) and is mostly useful for preventing internal objects from leaking private fields.
Query DTOs need explicit conversion
Array pipes and other built-ins
commonMistakes: interfaces for DTOs; forgetting @Type(() => NestedDto); enableImplicitConversion on globally; @Expose() on a password field; echoing value back in validation errors; running an async validator per row in a loop (N+1 on validation); assuming the DTO's TS type protects the DB write.
practiceTasks: build a ValidationPipe configuration, then attack it: send role: 'admin', send an unknown field, send limit=99999999999999999999, send items as an object instead of an array, send items[] with 51 entries, and send totalCents with a string. Record the status code and body for each, and confirm none of them reaches the database. Then swap the stack to Zod and diff the two error shapes.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must a DTO be a class rather than an interface?
What do `whitelist` and `forbidNonWhitelisted` each do, and why both?
Why does nested validation need `@Type()`?
What breaks with `enableImplicitConversion: true`?
Explain the mass-assignment risk in three sentences.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a signup endpoint takes a JSON body, and a DTO that declares only email and password still carries whatever else the client sent. Decision: run a global ValidationPipe with whitelist: true and forbidNonWhitelisted: true on every body, and treat the DTO as the only thing allowed to reach the persistence layer. Reasoning: the request body is untrusted input, so every property that is not explicitly declared and validated must not exist. Without whitelisting, an attacker who guesses a field name â€” or reads it from the public JavaScript bundle â€” can set role: 'admin', orgId of another tenant, or an internal creditBalance, because data: req.body forwards all of it to the ORM. That is mass assignment, and it is a privilege-escalation bug, not a data-validation nit. Trade-offs: forbidNonWhitelisted turns silent drops into 400s, so older clients that send extra fields (a stale SDK sending nulls) start failing â€” which is a feature if you version the API, and an incident if you do not. Failure scenario: a mobile client version 3.2 sends a removed field for eight months because the store keeps old builds alive, and the fix is server-side leniency for known-old fields, not removing the whitelist. Alternative: derive the persistence input explicitly â€” create(dto) { return prisma.user.create({ data: pick(dto, ['email','passwordHash']) }) } â€” which protects you even if the pipe is misconfigured, and pair it with a schema library whose output type is derived from the validator (Zod) so the allowed keys are visible in the type."

interviewQuestions.text: When would you use Zod instead of class-validator?

topics.title: Interceptors: Logging, Envelopes, Timeouts, Caching
topics.description: An interceptor wraps handler execution. It receives the execution context and a next handle, and returns an RxJS Observable of the result â€” so it can transform the value, time it, swap it, or fail it.
keyConcepts: 1. Structured request logger
2. Response envelope
The honest opinion
3. Timeout
4. Caching interceptor (per-request memo, not a shared cache)
Caveats that make this mostly a teaching example
Composing them
commonMistakes: logging the request body or Authorization; ordering serializers after the envelope; caching non-GET or error responses; using a process-wide cache interceptor in a clustered deployment; returning of(value) synchronously for a slow value (it lies about duration); assuming interceptors see WebSocket/RPC contexts the same way.
practiceTasks: stack logging, timeout, envelope and serializer interceptors, hit five routes (including one with @Res() and one with a thrown HttpException), and log from inside each interceptor so you can draw the true order. Then swap the cache interceptor to request scope and re-measure a duplicate-heavy endpoint.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must a logger interceptor log on completion rather than on entry?
Why does `ClassSerializerInterceptor` have to be ordered before the envelope interceptor?
What does a per-request cache interceptor buy you, and what is unsafe about a process-wide one?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a controller fetches the same configuration row 40 times inside one request, because 40 branches of the request each need it. Decision: a request-lifetime memo, not a shared cache. Reasoning: within a single HTTP request the data cannot change underneath you if it was read once from the primary, so a Map keyed on the request gives you free deduplication with zero risk of staleness, invalidation or cross-tenant leakage â€” the failure modes that make process-wide or Redis caches dangerous. A process-wide interceptor is a different animal entirely: it is per-instance, so the same URL can return different data from different pods, it never expires, and unless the key includes the principal and tenant it will serve one user's data to another. Trade-offs: request scope means the memo has to be instantiated per request, which in NestJS means a request-scoped provider â€” precisely the scope that bubbles (5.3.4) â€” so the correct shape is a provider constructed in a middleware or created explicitly per request rather than a global singleton. Failure scenario: a singleton cache interceptor in a 20-pod deployment, a user updates their display name, and for up to the TTL (or forever) 19 of 20 pods serve the old name, so the bug is intermittent and looks like a replica-lag problem. Alternative: push the dedupe down to the query layer with a per-request identity map or a DataLoader, which gives batching as well as caching and keeps the cache lifetime tied to the request by construction."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is an envelope response format a debatable choice?
How do you skip an interceptor for one handler?

topics.title: Exception Filters: Mapping Domain Errors to HTTP
topics.description: An ExceptionFilter is the boundary where a thrown value becomes a status code and a body. Its job is to make every failure in the system look the same to a client, and to make sure internal details never leak.
keyConcepts: The three layers of error
Domain exceptions â€” OrderNotFound, PaymentDeclined, InsufficientInventory. They know nothing about HTTP. They are thrown from services and unit-tested without a server.

HTTP exceptions â€” HttpException and its subclasses (NotFoundException, ConflictException, ForbiddenException, UnauthorizedException, PayloadTooLargeException, UnprocessableEntityException, TooManyRequestsException, ServiceUnavailableException, ...). They carry a status and a response body.
Unknown errors â€” TypeError, driver errors, ECONNREFUSED, third-party SDK faults. They become 500 with a generic message and a trace id.
HttpException vs custom exceptions
Filter that uses the mapper and emits RFC 9457
Rules that keep error bodies consistent across services

Same media type and same shape everywhere: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, instance, plus code and traceId. Generate it from one shared package so ten services cannot drift.
A stable machine-readable code (ORDER_NOT_FOUND) is the contract; detail is for humans and may change; title is a short human phrase. Clients branch on code (or status), never on detail.
5xx bodies are uniform and information-free: same type and title for every internal error, a traceId, and the real cause only in logs. Never return stack traces, SQL, file paths, or upstream URLs.
4xx bodies are specific and may include field-level errors, because the client can act on them.

A filter registered with app.useGlobalFilters(new X()) applies to unhandled routes too (it is registered as the platform's terminal error handler), but not to errors thrown in app.use() middleware â€” wrap those yourself.
commonMistakes: extending HttpException in domain services (couples the domain to HTTP and makes unit tests need HTTP types); using the exception message as the client contract; returning different shapes for 400 vs 500 vs exceptions; logging 4xx at error level (it destroys signal in the logs â€” 5xx and unhandled are errors, expected 4xx are info/debug); forgetting host.getType() !== 'http' in a hybrid app.
practiceTasks: write a DomainExceptionMapper covering ten domain errors and six database error codes, plus a global filter, and unit-test the whole table. Then deliberately leak a stack trace, run a linter/grep over your repo for res.json(e) patterns, and count how many you find.

interviewQuestions.text: Should a domain exception extend `HttpException`? Why or why not?
What is the single mapping point for error â†’ status, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: five services each hand-rolled catch (e) { res.status(500).json({ error: e.message }) }, so clients had to special-case each service. Decision: one tiny shared package exporting domainErrorToHttp(err) plus one problemFrom(status, ...) builder, and a global filter in every service that uses them. Reasoning: the mapping from a domain failure to an HTTP status is a *contract decision*, so it deserves tests and one owner, not five independent if chains. Centralizing it means the same INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY produces 422 with the same code and the same application/problem+json body in every service, so a client can write one error handler. It also lets me unit-test the entire mapping table â€” a pure function from error object to HTTP exception â€” with no HTTP, no database, and no framework, which is far stronger coverage than asserting on responses. Trade-offs: a shared package couples services together, so it must stay dependency-free and boring, and it must be versioned carefully because a status change is a breaking change for clients. Failure scenario: a new service skips the shared filter, and one 500 response leaks e.message containing a connection string with the password; the leak is discovered by a customer reading their own error body. Alternative: if you cannot run a shared package, generate the OpenAPI error schema per service and assert in CI that the emitted application/problem+json schema matches the reference â€” a spec-level contract that catches the same drift without a runtime dependency."

interviewQuestions.text: What must never appear in a 5xx body?
Where do validation errors fit in the error contract?
Do global filters handle errors thrown in middleware?
How do you test error mapping without starting a server?

topics.title: Configuration: @nestjs/config with Validation
topics.description: Configuration is external, typed, validated at boot, and per-environment. Reading process.env.DATABASE_URL in twenty files is the failure mode.
keyConcepts: Typed access
Per-environment config
.env.development checked in, .env.test in CI, production values only from the platform's secret store.

Secrets never in the image, never in git, never in logs. Load from the environment (or a mounted secret file), redact in the logger, and give each environment a distinct key so a production key leak does not unlock staging.
Feature flags belong in config too, but read them through a typed flag service so FEATURE_X is a union type, not a string compared with 'true' in nine places.
Never branch on NODE_ENV for behaviour that should be a flag. NODE_ENV is for error verbosity and optimizations, not product decisions.
Validation options
commonMistakes: reading process.env in feature code; config.get('KEY') with no default and no infer (silent undefined); committing .env; putting secrets in build args; using one giant APP_CONFIG object with everything any; branching on NODE_ENV for product behaviour.
practiceTasks: add a Zod-validated config to a NestJS app with six variables (two required in prod only), then write a script that boots the app with each variable missing/empty/wrong-type and confirms it exits with a non-zero code and a readable message. Type the config so a misspelled key is a compile error.

interviewQuestions.text: Why validate configuration at boot instead of lazily?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a service deployed with a missing REDIS_URL booted fine, served 200s for 40 minutes because Redis was only used by one feature, then failed every request that touched the cache. Decision: validate the entire environment against a schema in ConfigModule.forRoot({ validate }) so the process exits non-zero at boot. Reasoning: configuration is a dependency of the whole application, not of the code path that happens to read it. Lazy validation converts a deployment error into a partial, hard-to-diagnose runtime error, and it fails *late* and *intermittently*, which is the worst combination. Boot-time validation is also cheap insurance for the specific production failure that causes the most pain: an environment variable that was renamed in CI, is absent in the manifest, or has an invalid shape. Trade-offs: a strict schema means you cannot deploy with a partially new configuration, and adding an env var becomes a deploy-ordering concern since the old version must tolerate its absence; that is a real constraint but a good one, because it forces the migration order to be explicit. Failure scenario: the app validates fine locally because a developer's .env.local has a value CI never sets, so the first production deploy with the new schema fails after the migration has already been announced. Alternative: if a hard fail is unacceptable for a read-only replica or a worker that can degrade, split the schema into critical (must have, exit on failure) and optional (validated, warned, defaulted), and have the degraded paths check the parsed result rather than assuming it is present."

interviewQuestions.text: `registerAs` and namespaces â€” what problem do they solve?
How do you keep secrets out of logs and images?
When is `NODE_ENV` the wrong thing to branch on?
How do you type configuration so a typo is a compile error?

topics.title: Testing NestJS: Unit with Mocks, E2E with Supertest
topics.description: Two levels that matter. Unit tests instantiate a provider with hand-made or framework-provided fakes and assert behaviour. E2E tests boot the whole HTTP application in-process and assert the real contract: routing, pipes, guards, filters, serialization and the database.
keyConcepts: Unit test â€” no framework needed
TestingModule â€” when you need the container
overrideProvider(TOKEN).useValue(fake) and overrideProvider(TOKEN).useClass(Fake) are the standard overrides.
moduleRef.init() is required only if something in the graph calls onModuleInit.
.compile() and .resolve() return promises â€” forgetting await is the most common cause of a mysteriously empty test.
jest.resetModules() / per-test module creation causes Nest to warn about duplicate module instances; create the module once in beforeAll, or use testingModule.get() inside each test.
E2E â€” the real contract
What to test where
commonMistakes: testing only services and never HTTP; new NestFactory in tests instead of the module; forgetting await app.init() before getHttpServer(); not closing the app (open handles hang CI); mocking repositories in e2e; asserting on res.body shapes that come from an interceptor that e2e never registered.
practiceTasks: write three unit tests with hand-rolled fakes, one TestingModule integration test for a module's wiring, and four supertest e2e tests covering 201, 400-whitelist, 404 problem details, and idempotent replay. Extract configureApp() so the global pipe cannot be forgotten, and prove it by deleting the pipe registration and watching two tests fail.

interviewQuestions.text: When do you need `TestingModule` rather than `new Service(fake)`?
Why must the E2E test apply the same global pipes as `main.ts`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an e2e test for POST /users asserted a 400 for an oversized payload and passed â€” but only because a route-level pipe was set in the test module. The controller had no @UsePipes, and the global pipe was only ever registered in main.ts, which the test never ran. Decision: extract the entire bootstrap into a configureApp(app: INestApplication) function that both main.ts and the e2e test call, and forbid any app.useGlobalX call outside that function. Reasoning: an e2e test that builds a differently-configured application is not testing the application's contract, it is testing a convenient fiction. Every global concern â€” the ValidationPipe with whitelisting, the exception filter, the global prefix, versioning, CORS, and body-parser limits â€” is part of the observable API, so all of it must be present in the test. Centralising the configuration also means a new global concern cannot be added to production and forgotten in tests, which is exactly the class of bug that makes staging behave differently from CI. Trade-offs: sharing the function means a test that *wants* different global settings must reconfigure deliberately, which needs app.useGlobalPipes to be idempotent or the test to call configureApp then override â€” slightly more ceremony, but explicit. Failure scenario: a security team asks whether a role field in a signup body is rejected; the e2e suite says yes because the test module had a pipe, while production had the pipe added in a file that no test imports, so the answer was no. Alternative: a lighter-weight guard against the same class of bug is an e2e assertion that boots the real entry point (import('../src/main')) behind a flag, or a contract test that generates the OpenAPI doc from the real app and diffs it in CI."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the most common `TestingModule` bug?
What should never be mocked in an E2E test?
How do you test a guard that reads `Reflector` metadata?

topics.title: Microservices: Transports, Patterns, and Operational Cost
topics.description: @nestjs/microservices adds a second transport to a NestJS application so it can call or be called by other processes over TCP, Redis, RabbitMQ, NATS, MQTT or Kafka.
keyConcepts: The three patterns
Client registration and transports

Transport.TCP is a Nest-specific JSON-over-TCP protocol. It is fast and has no broker, but it is not interoperable, has no persistence, and needs a load balancer plus a service registry. It is a poor default for anything you intend to keep for years.
Transport.RMQ is the most feature-complete (durable queues, DLQ via deadLetterQueue, priority, publisher confirms, separate queues per event type). Use it when delivery guarantees matter.
Transport.REDIS is fast pub/sub but has no built-in delivery guarantee â€” a subscriber that is down misses messages.
Transport.NATS and MQTT are excellent for fan-out events; NATS JetStream adds persistence.
Transport.KAFKA (via kafkajs) is for high-throughput event streams and partitioned replay.
ClientProxyFactory.create() builds an ad-hoc client; @InjectClient('NAME') is the module-registered, lifecycle-managed way (always prefer it, so the client is connected and closed with the app).
Serialization
Retries, timeouts, and correlation
Timeouts must be enforced on both sides or a slow consumer causes an unbounded queue.
Retries need idempotent handlers â€” a broker redelivers. See 5.4.4 and the outbox pattern in PHASE 5 Background Processing.
commonMistakes: choosing TCP for anything you need to keep; assuming pub/sub delivery is exactly-once; forgetting the timeout on the client side; using Date or BigInt over the default JSON serializer; running microservices without a DLQ and an alert; extracting services before you have CI, migrations and on-call; sharing one database across services and calling it decomposition.
practiceTasks: stand up a TCP-based users service and an HTTPâ†’RPC hybrid gateway, then add a Redis-pub/sub event consumer. Kill the consumer, publish an event, restart the consumer, and observe which transport lost the message. Then add a DLQ, a retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and an idempotency key in the handler, and re-run the test.

interviewQuestions.text: `@MessagePattern` vs `@EventPattern` â€” what is the real difference?
Which transport would you pick and why? What does each one give up?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a Node.js platform team needs to decouple order processing from the HTTP API, with at-least-once delivery and independent deploys. Decision: RabbitMQ over the TCP transport, for the RPC-ish request paths and durable event fan-out. Reasoning: my hard requirement is that a consumer that was down must still get the message after it restarts, and that I need a dead-letter queue I can alert on. RabbitMQ gives durable queues, publisher confirms, per-message priority, and a first-class DLX, and the Nest RMQ client exposes all of it. TCP is faster but has no persistence and no DLQ, so a restart silently drops in-flight work; Redis pub/sub drops messages for any subscriber that is not currently connected; NATS with JetStream is the strongest alternative but has a smaller operational footprint in most companies and requires more setup for per-message priority. Trade-offs: RabbitMQ is another stateful system to run, monitor, upgrade and page on, and a broker outage becomes an API outage unless you decouple with an outbox and a local queue. Failure scenario: I choose TCP because it benchmarked 30% faster, then a rolling deploy drops 4,000 queued order.created events, and the warehouse never learns about the orders â€” nobody noticed for a day because there was no DLQ to alert on. Alternative: for pure internal fan-out with high volume and replay needs, Kafka is the right answer instead; for a handful of internal services that could be functions, I would skip the broker entirely and use HTTP with a proper client library, and reserve the broker for genuinely asynchronous work."

interviewQuestions.text: What happens to an `@EventPattern` handler's error?
Why must RPC handlers be idempotent?
What does `@nestjs/microservices` not give you?
When is a microservice split actively harmful?

topics.title: Express vs Fastify vs NestJS vs Hono vs Next.js Route Handlers
topics.description: Five ways to serve HTTP from Node, differing in how much structure they impose, how they validate and serialise, and where they run. The decision is about the cost of the framework versus the cost of coordination.
keyConcepts: There is no best one. The honest conclusion
Express wins on ecosystem and total familiarity. Its weakness is that structure is a matter of discipline, so teams drift â€” that is the exact gap NestJS fills.
Fastify wins on throughput and on schema-first design; plugin encapsulation is a real architectural tool. Reach for it when you want Express-like freedom with a performance budget.

NestJS wins when *coordination* is the bottleneck. It costs roughly 10-30% throughput versus Fastify and adds a learning curve, and it is the wrong choice for edge runtimes and trivial services. Its real deliverables are a uniform pipeline, automatic DI, a module graph you can reason about, and first-class OpenAPI generation.
Hono wins where portability matters â€” the same handler runs on Node, Bun, Deno, workers and edge. Small surface, Web-standard APIs, no container.

Next.js route handlers win when the API exists to serve one frontend. You get auth helpers, cookies, and one deploy unit. They are a poor fit for a public API consumed by many clients, for long-running work, and for anything that needs streaming responses with fine control.
commonMistakes: claiming a framework is faster without measuring; choosing NestJS for an edge function; using Next.js route handlers as a public API platform; assuming Fastify's schema is only validation (it also drives serialization and docs); forgetting that decorator metadata requires specific tsconfig settings and can break some bundlers.
practiceTasks: implement the same four endpoints (list with cursor pagination, get, create with idempotency, delete) in Express, Fastify, NestJS and Hono. Compare: LOC, dependencies, time to add a new endpoint, unit-test setup, and autocannon p99 at 200 rps. Write down which you'd pick for a 3-person team and which for a 30-person team, and why the answers differ.

interviewQuestions.text: Which of these would you pick for a public API consumed by 40 internal clients, and why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a domain API with about 60 endpoints, 40 internal consumers across six teams, an in-house generated SDK, and a requirement that the schema is enforced in CI. Decision: NestJS on Node, with a code-first OpenAPI document and a CI breaking-change diff. Reasoning: my bottleneck is not throughput â€” it is that six teams will each interpret 'create an order' slightly differently. NestJS gives me the things that actually reduce that cost: a module graph with enforced boundaries, one global validation pipe so every body is whitelisted and typed, one error filter so every failure is a problem+json document, and a code-first spec generated from the same DTO classes the runtime validates against, which removes the drift that hand-written docs always develop. Trade-offs: I accept roughly 10-30% lower throughput than Fastify, which is irrelevant at 400 rps, and I accept the decorator learning curve and a heavier test setup. Failure scenario: a reviewer adds a new endpoint without a DTO class, so the generated spec omits it and the client generator produces nothing for it, and the contract test does not catch it because the generator reads the spec rather than the code. Alternative: Fastify with JSON-Schema definitions as the single source of truth, which is faster and arguably more honest, at the cost of losing the container and the DI-driven test seams; if my team were smaller, that is what I would pick."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is schema validation a first-class feature of Fastify but a middleware in Express?
What do you give up by choosing NestJS for an edge-deployed function?
When is Next.js route handlers the wrong choice?
Is a framework choice ever reversible? What would make it so?

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** Five ways to serve HTTP from Node, differing in how much structure they impose, how they validate and serialise, and where they run. The decision is about the cost of the framework versus the cost of coordination.

| Dimension | Express | Fastify | NestJS | Hono | Next.js Route Handlers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mental model | Middleware + router, you assemble | Plugin/encapsulation (avvio) + schema-first | Modules + DI + a fixed pipeline | Web-standard `Request`/`Response`, tiny | React framework; HTTP is a feature of the deployment |
| DI | None built in; hand-rolled factories | `fastify-plugin` + decorators, or manual | Full container: tokens, scopes, lifecycle | `hono/context` + middleware factories | `Request`/`NextRequest`, `cookies()`, React context; no container |
| Validation | `joi`/`zod`/`express-validator` middleware | JSON-Schema-native, compiles a validator (fast) | `class-validator` via pipes (or Zod) | `@hono/zod-validator`, built-in `zValidator` | Hand-rolled, or a shared schema in the handler |
| Structure | Convention, none enforced | Encapsulation, moderate | **Enforced** module graph | Minimal, composable | File-system routes, React conventions |
| Raw performance | Slowest; regex routing | Fastest of the Node set (JSON-Schema compile, serialization) | Slower than Fastify (decorators, reflection, enhancers) | Very fast; runs on Bun/Node/edge | Irrelevant â€” includes React SSR/RSC |
| Edge / serverless | Needs adapters | Limited | Poor fit (container, metadata, Node-only) | First-class (Web standard APIs) | Native (edge runtime) |
| Ecosystem maturity | Largest; everything supports it | Large and growing | Large, opinionated, heavy | Small but fast-moving | Huge (React) |
| Error handling | `(err, req, res, next)` middleware | `setErrorHandler`, typed errors | Exception filters | `app.onError` | Return `Response`; `error.tsx` for UI |
| Observability hooks | Middleware, `AsyncLocalStorage` | Hooks (`onRequest`, `onResponse`, `onTimeout`) | Middleware + interceptors | Middleware | Middleware, `instrumentation.ts` |
| Best fit | Small/medium services, anything bespoke, maximum control | Performance-sensitive services, schema-first teams, plugins | Larger teams, many modules, conventions + generated docs (OpenAPI) | Edge functions, CLIs, small services, Bun | BFF / full-stack apps where the UI and API ship together |

**There is no best one. The honest conclusion:**
- **Express** wins on ecosystem and total familiarity. Its weakness is that structure is a matter of discipline, so teams drift â€” that is the exact gap NestJS fills.
- **Fastify** wins on throughput and on schema-first design; plugin encapsulation is a real architectural tool. Reach for it when you want Express-like freedom with a performance budget.
- **NestJS** wins when *coordination* is the bottleneck. It costs roughly 10-30% throughput versus Fastify and adds a learning curve, and it is the wrong choice for edge runtimes and trivial services. topics.title: Scale and Team Considerations: When NestJS Pays Off and What It Costs
topics.description: The question is not "does NestJS scale" but "for how many engineers, how many modules, and how much governance does this team have, and what does the framework cost per request?" Both sides of that ledger, stated concretely.
keyConcepts: Where it pays off
Many engineers touching one service. The module graph plus enforced boundaries means "who is allowed to import this" is answered by the container, not by a code-review convention.
Many similar features. A new feature is copy-structure: module, controller, service, DTOs, tests. Consistency across 40 features is the product.
Cross-cutting concerns are numerous and must be uniform â€” authN/authZ, validation, logging with trace ids, error format, audit, rate limits. Registering each once is a genuine win.
Generated API documentation from the same types that validate at runtime. This kills spec drift.
Mixed transports (HTTP + microservice + GraphQL) in one codebase with one DI graph.
Onboarding: a documented module layout means a new engineer knows where things go.
Where it costs you

Reflection and metadata overhead: container resolution on the request path, emitDecoratorMetadata emitting design:paramtypes for every decorated class, and decorator function-call overhead at definition time. Real but modest â€” measure before arguing about it.

Readability: a controller method with @UseGuards, @UseInterceptors, @UsePipes, @UseFilters and five parameter decorators is hard to scan, and IDE "go to definition" is less direct than reading a plain function.
Bundle and cold-start size â€” matters for serverless; less so for a long-lived container.
Learning curve â€” the enhancer/scope/module vocabulary is a real ramp, and the failure modes are confusing.
commonMistakes: introducing a framework to "modernize" without a named problem; letting the domain layer import Nest decorators; using request scope for convenience; assuming the DI graph is automatically a good architecture rather than just a visible one; planning a rewrite instead of a strangler; running a @nestjs/config validation that fails in one environment only.
practiceTasks: take a 3-module Express service. (1) Draw its dependency graph by hand, then with a tool. (2) Convert one module to NestJS as a hybrid mount, keeping the domain folder framework-free. (3) Import the domain use case into a plain Node test with no Nest at all and prove it works. (4) Measure cold start and p99 for both stacks.

interviewQuestions.text: When does NestJS's cost/benefit turn positive?
How do you keep a NestJS codebase portable?
Why is request scope a scale problem rather than a style problem?
What is the incremental cost of a heavy NestJS app at 5,000 rps?
How would you introduce NestJS into an existing Express service without a rewrite?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a 40-endpoint Express service with 25 engineers, drifting structure, and no plan for a rewrite. Decision: a strangler migration â€” new feature modules go into NestJS alongside the existing Express app, and existing routes stay until they are touched. Reasoning: the value of NestJS is conventions and a validated DI graph, and neither is delivered by a big-bang rewrite; a rewrite loses a quarter of delivery capacity, mixes framework-learning cost with business change, and risks a silent regression in an API that 40 clients depend on. Coexisting two frameworks is ugly for about two months and then the old surface shrinks to nothing. Practical mechanics: one repository, two main.ts entry points or one entry that mounts both an Express app and a Nest application on different prefixes, a shared packages/contracts package for DTO types and the error format, and a lint rule that forbids a Nest module from importing anything from the legacy routes/ tree. Trade-offs: two HTTP stacks, two test setups, and duplicated infrastructure code (logging, tracing, health checks) until the migration completes, so I would extract that shared infrastructure into plain libraries first. Failure scenario: the new Nest path handles orders and the legacy path handles refunds, and the shared Order model evolves in the Nest DTO only, so refunds silently read a stale shape from a different serializer. Alternative: if the pain is purely 'no one enforces boundaries' rather than 'no DI', a much cheaper fix is ESLint import-boundary rules plus Zod validation in the existing Express app, and that is genuinely enough for many teams."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** The question is not "does NestJS scale" but "for how many engineers, how many modules, and how much governance does this team have, and what does the framework cost per request?" Both sides of that ledger, stated concretely.

**Where it pays off**
- **Many engineers touching one service.** The module graph plus enforced boundaries means "who is allowed to import this" is answered by the container, not by a code-review convention.
- **Many similar features.** A new feature is copy-structure: module, controller, service, DTOs, tests. Consistency across 40 features is the product.
- **Cross-cutting concerns are numerous and must be uniform** â€” authN/authZ, validation, logging with trace ids, error format, audit, rate limits. Registering each once is a genuine win.
- **Generated API documentation** from the same types that validate at runtime. This kills spec drift.
- **Mixed transports** (HTTP + microservice + GraphQL) in one codebase with one DI graph.
- **Onboarding:** a documented module layout means a new engineer knows where things go.

**Where it costs you**
- **Reflection and metadata overhead:** container resolution on the request path, `emitDecoratorMetadata` emitting `design:paramtypes` for every decorated class, and decorator function-call overhead at definition time. Real but modest â€” measure before arguing about it.
- **Readability:** a controller method with `@UseGuards`, `@UseInterceptors`, `@UsePipes`, `@UseFilters` and five parameter decorators is hard to scan, and IDE "go to definition" is less direct than reading a plain function.
- **Bundle and cold-start size** â€” matters for serverless; less so for a long-lived container.
- **Learning curve** â€” the enhancer/scope/module vocabulary is a real ramp, and the failure modes are confusing.
- **The magic tax:** debugging "why didn't my guard run" is a recurring tax, and NestJS's error messages are not always obvious.
- **Framework-coupled tests:** with heavy DI, unit tests can start looking like container tests, which is slower and less clear than `new Service(fake)`.
- **Opinionated upgrade cadence:** major versions change bootstrapping, and staying current costs migration work. Being framework-agnostic at the domain layer keeps this cheap.

**How it interacts with microservices**
- A **hybrid app** (HTTP + microservice in one process) lets you extract a module into a service gradually â€” you change the transport, not the domain code, because the domain services do not know about HTTP.
- **Keep the domain free of framework imports.** A `use-cases/` or `domain/` folder that imports neither `express` nor `@nestjs/*` can be moved into any service, tested with no framework, and understood by non-Node developers. This is the single highest-value structural decision in a NestJS codebase, and the most frequently skipped.
- **The DI graph becomes your dependency map** â€” which is exactly why request scope (5.3.4) and circular imports (5.3.2) matter so much at scale: they are the graph's structural defects.
- **Microservices replace in-process DI with network failure.** Every provider call you turn into an RPC becomes a call that can time out, retry, and partially fail. Rule of thumb: keep in-process modules tightly coupled (they are cheap), and make the boundary between *services* coarse and few.

**The senior framing for an interview:** "NestJS is a bet that coordination cost will dominate runtime cost. That bet pays off with many engineers and many modules, and loses with few engineers, few endpoints, and latency-sensitive paths. I would not introduce it to a working codebase without a concrete problem it solves, and I would keep my domain layer framework-agnostic so the bet is reversible."

**Questions**
1. When does NestJS's cost/benefit turn positive?
2. How do you keep a NestJS codebase portable?
3. Why is request scope a scale problem rather than a style problem?
4. What is the incremental cost of a heavy NestJS app at 5,000 rps?
5. How would you introduce NestJS into an existing Express service without a rewrite?

**Model answer, Q5:** "Context: a 40-endpoint Express service with 25 engineers, drifting structure, and no plan for a rewrite. Decision: a strangler migration â€” new feature modules go into NestJS alongside the existing Express app, and existing routes stay until they are touched. Reasoning: the value of NestJS is conventions and a validated DI graph, and neither is delivered by a big-bang rewrite; a rewrite loses a quarter of delivery capacity, mixes framework-learning cost with business change, and risks a silent regression in an API that 40 clients depend on. Coexisting two frameworks is ugly for about two months and then the old surface shrinks to nothing. Practical mechanics: one repository, two `main.ts` entry points or one entry that mounts both an Express app and a Nest application on different prefixes, a shared `packages/contracts` package for DTO types and the error format, and a lint rule that forbids a Nest module from importing anything from the legacy `routes/` tree. Trade-offs: two HTTP stacks, two test setups, and duplicated infrastructure code (logging, tracing, health checks) until the migration completes, so I would extract that shared infrastructure into plain libraries first. Failure scenario: the new Nest path handles orders and the legacy path handles refunds, and the shared `Order` model evolves in the Nest DTO only, so refunds silently read a stale shape from a different serializer. Alternative: if the pain is purely 'no one enforces boundaries' rather than 'no DI', a much cheaper fix is ESLint import-boundary rules plus Zod validation in the existing Express app, and that is genuinely enough for many teams."

**Mistakes:** introducing a framework to "modernize" without a named problem; letting the domain layer import Nest decorators; using request scope for convenience; assuming the DI graph is automatically a good architecture rather than just a visible one; planning a rewrite instead of a strangler; running a `@nestjs/config` validation that fails in one environment only.

**Mini task:** take a 3-module Express service. (1) Draw its dependency graph by hand, then with a tool. (2) Convert one module to NestJS as a hybrid mount, keeping the domain folder framework-free. (3) Import the domain use case into a plain Node test with no Nest at all and prove it works. (4) Measure cold start and p99 for both stacks.

topics.title: Resource Naming and URL Design
topics.description: A REST API models the *domain* as addressable resources. URLs name things; HTTP methods say what to do with them. A good URL is boring, predictable, and tells a developer what exists without documentation.
keyConcepts: The rules that hold up in practice
Plural nouns for collections: /orders, /users, /products. Singular is for a single instance's sub-resources: /orders/{id}.
No verbs in URLs. The method is the verb. /orders/create is wrong because the operation was already a POST to /orders.
Nesting is a last resort. One level is usually the most a human can hold in their head; two is the practical maximum.
The path identifies the resource, the body and query carry the rest. If it fits in a URL, it is probably a filter.
Lowercase, hyphen-separated (/purchase-orders). Case-sensitive in principle, inconsistent in practice.
No trailing slashes. /orders/ and /orders are different keys to a cache, an analytics funnel and a router.

Nesting depth and when to denormalize
Denormalize (flatten) when
Sub-resource vs action endpoint
An action endpoint is justified when
commonMistakes: verbs in URLs; mixing singular and plural; three or four levels of nesting; PUT on a collection; casing and trailing-slash inconsistency; PII in query strings; a /doSomething catch-all; treating every business operation as a PATCH of a status field.
practiceTasks: design the URL surface for a blog (posts, comments, tags, authors, media). Then draw the nesting, then flatten half of it, and justify each choice in one sentence. Then decide for each of six operations whether it is CRUD or an action, and defend the two hardest calls.

interviewQuestions.text: Why no verbs in URLs?
When do you flatten a nested URL?
Why is `PATCH /orders/{id} {status: "cancelled"}` a bad design?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a client sets order status directly, and support reports orders in illegal states â€” CANCELLED after SHIPPED, SHIPPED with no payment. Decision: make status transitions action endpoints (POST /orders/{id}/cancel, /ship, /fulfil), and keep PATCH /orders/{id} for the fields that are genuinely free-form (delivery notes, tags, internal notes). Reasoning: status is not a field, it is the output of a state machine whose legal transitions depend on payment state, inventory reservation and cancellation windows. Exposing it as a settable attribute means the client is now responsible for the transition table, and the server has lost the only place where the rules live. That produces exactly the corruption we saw, and it is unrecoverable because the invalid transitions are already committed. The action endpoint names the transition, keeps the precondition checks in one place, gives the operation a first-class audit entry, and makes the request idempotent by naming. Trade-offs: you lose generic field-level updates, so a legitimate status change that is not in the enum needs a new endpoint, and the API surface grows with the state machine â€” which is fine, because the state machine is bounded and the domain owns it. Failure scenario: a bulk import tool that legitimately needs to set several fields and a status in one call has to make N+1 requests, so someone adds PATCH /orders/{id}/status 'just for the import' and the state machine is bypassed again. Alternative: keep PATCH but require an explicit transition object with a precondition â€” { from: 'PAID', to: 'CANCELLED' } â€” so the server can validate the from state atomically. That works, but it leaks the machine into the wire format and still needs server-side validation, so the action endpoint is clearer."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** A REST API models the *domain* as addressable resources. URLs name things; HTTP methods say what to do with them. A good URL is boring, predictable, and tells a developer what exists without documentation.

**The rules that hold up in practice**
- **Plural nouns for collections**: `/orders`, `/users`, `/products`. Singular is for a single instance's sub-resources: `/orders/{id}`.
- **No verbs in URLs.** The method is the verb. `/orders/create` is wrong because the operation was already a `POST` to `/orders`.
- **Nesting is a last resort.** One level is usually the most a human can hold in their head; two is the practical maximum.
- **The path identifies the resource, the body and query carry the rest.** If it fits in a URL, it is probably a filter.
- **Lowercase, hyphen-separated** (`/purchase-orders`). Case-sensitive in principle, inconsistent in practice.
- **No trailing slashes.** `/orders/` and `/orders` are different keys to a cache, an analytics funnel and a router.
- **Don't put secrets or PII in URLs** â€” they end up in access logs, browser history, and `Referer` headers.

**Nesting depth and when to denormalize**
```
/organizations/{orgId}/projects/{projectId}/tasks/{taskId}/comments
```
That is four levels. The problems: every level's id must be validated for authority (otherwise IDOR), every level must exist or you need a policy for a non-existent parent, the URL is a *composite key* that must stay stable forever, and clients memorize it. The standard fix is to make the most important resource addressable on its own and pass the scope as a filter:
```
GET /tasks?projectId={projectId}                        âœ… flat, cacheable, filterable
GET /organizations/{orgId}/projects/{projectId}/tasks   âš ï¸ acceptable when the parent is a hard scope
```

```

POST  /orders/{id}/cancel             âœ… an operation on the resource
```
The test: *if the thing you are doing is a transition in the domain's state machine, it is not a field update â€” it is an action.* `PATCH {status: 'cancelled'}` invites the client to set `CANCELLED` from `SHIPPED`, which is illegal. `POST /orders/{id}/cancel` names the legal transition and lets the server enforce the machine. 1. Why no verbs in URLs?
2. When do you flatten a nested URL?
3. Why is `PATCH /orders/{id} {status: "cancelled"}` a bad design?
4. Give five legitimate reasons for an action endpoint.
5. How deep should nesting go?

**Model answer, Q3:** "Context: a client sets order status directly, and support reports orders in illegal states â€” `CANCELLED` after `SHIPPED`, `SHIPPED` with no payment. Decision: make status transitions action endpoints (`POST /orders/{id}/cancel`, `/ship`, `/fulfil`), and keep `PATCH /orders/{id}` for the fields that are genuinely free-form (delivery notes, tags, internal notes). Reasoning: `status` is not a field, it is the output of a state machine whose legal transitions depend on payment state, inventory reservation and cancellation windows. Exposing it as a settable attribute means the client is now responsible for the transition table, and the server has lost the only place where the rules live. That produces exactly the corruption we saw, and it is unrecoverable because the invalid transitions are already committed. The action endpoint names the transition, keeps the precondition checks in one place, gives the operation a first-class audit entry, and makes the request idempotent by naming. Trade-offs: you lose generic field-level updates, so a legitimate status change that is not in the enum needs a new endpoint, and the API surface grows with the state machine â€” which is fine, because the state machine is bounded and the domain owns it. Failure scenario: a bulk import tool that legitimately needs to set several fields and a status in one call has to make N+1 requests, so someone adds `PATCH /orders/{id}/status` 'just for the import' and the state machine is bypassed again. Alternative: keep `PATCH` but require an explicit transition object with a precondition â€” `{ from: 'PAID', to: 'CANCELLED' }` â€” so the server can validate the `from` state atomically. That works, but it leaks the machine into the wire format and still needs server-side validation, so the action endpoint is clearer."

topics.title: HTTP Methods: Safety and Idempotency
topics.description: Safe methods are read-only by definition â€” the client did not request a change and the server is not obligated to log anything. Idempotent means the intended effect of *N* identical requests is the same as one.
keyConcepts: Why the distinction has real consequences

Safe methods are cacheable and re-requestable. Browsers, crawlers, CDNs and proxies may repeat them freely. That is why "GET must not change state" is a rule and not a style guideline: a prefetch that charges a card, or a crawler that archives a page and logs a user out, is a production incident.

Idempotent methods are safely retryable by infrastructure. Load balancers, mobile clients, and SDKs retry on timeouts and 502s. If DELETE is idempotent, a retry is harmless. This is the property that makes safe auto-retry policies possible.

POST is the dangerous one. A timeout on POST /payments means *you do not know* whether the charge happened. This ambiguity is the whole reason idempotency keys exist (5.4.4). There is no protocol-level fix: HTTP has no "request id" concept, so the client must supply one.
A non-idempotent DELETE would break everything, which is why "deleting an already-deleted resource" must return 204 (or 404 if you have chosen strict semantics, but you must be consistent).

Proxies and crawlers are conservative. Search engines re-crawl GETs; link checkers follow GETs; service meshes and API gateways retry idempotent methods. Non-standard methods like PURGE often get dropped or mapped by intermediaries.
Rules that follow

GET with a body is legal but broken in practice: intermediaries may strip it, and caches key on the URL, not the body. If a search needs many parameters, use POST /search (documented as non-cacheable) rather than a GET with a body.
PUT to a URI that does not exist creates it â€” a real, under-used 201 case.

DELETE on a collection (DELETE /orders?createdBefore=2026-01-01) is legal and genuinely idempotent, but it is dangerous: it is irreversible, uncacheable, and has no natural idempotency key. Prefer an explicit, named, asynchronous operation.
Never use POST for a read *except* for POST /search-style queries, and document it as such.
commonMistakes: mutating state in GET (a "GET to toggle" endpoint); treating PATCH as automatically idempotent; putting search parameters in a GET body; assuming a timeout means failure; using DELETE for reversible operations; non-standard methods without documenting proxy behaviour.
practiceTasks: build six endpoints, then run a checklist against each: safe? idempotent? cacheable? retryable by the client? what is the idempotency strategy? Then write a small script that fires 10 concurrent identical POST /payments with and without an Idempotency-Key and count the charges.

interviewQuestions.text: Is `PATCH` idempotent?
Why does it matter that `GET` is safe?
What happens if a `POST /payments` times out?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a mobile checkout calls POST /payments and the response times out after 30 seconds at the client. The server may have charged the card, or may not have â€” the client cannot tell. Decision: the client must send an Idempotency-Key, and the server must make the operation safely retryable and its outcome queryable. Reasoning: the ambiguity is inherent to the network, not to my implementation. At-least-once retry without a key means a double charge; refusing to retry means an unknown state that the user has to resolve by phoning support. So the design is: the client generates a stable key per user intent (generated once when the checkout screen loads, reused on every retry of that intent, and a *new* key for a genuinely new attempt), the server reserves the key atomically, executes at most once, stores the response, and replays it on a repeat. To make the unknown state recoverable, the key is also attached to the payment record, so GET /payments/by-idempotency-key/{key} answers the question after the fact. Trade-offs: the store is now in the request path (so it must be fast, have a TTL, and never be a single point of failure), concurrency needs a real compare-and-set rather than a get-then-set, and non-keyed requests are harder to reason about during an incident. Failure scenario: the client library regenerates the key inside the retry loop, so each retry is a fresh request, the server correctly charges each time, and the double-charge bug appears in production while every server-side test passes. Alternative: for a provider that supports it, use the payment processor's own idempotency key and expose the processor's key as the API key, so ambiguity is resolved upstream."

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Request body allowed | Typical response | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | âœ… | âœ… | Discouraged (undefined by spec) | `200` + representation | The only method caches reliably |
| `HEAD` | âœ… | âœ… | No | `200`, headers identical to `GET`, no body | Cheap availability/latency check |
| `OPTIONS` | âœ… | âœ… | No | `204` + `Allow`, CORS headers | "What can I do here?" â€” browser uses it for preflight |
| `TRACE` | âœ… | âœ… | No | `200` echo | Usually disabled (cross-site tracing / credential theft) |
| `POST` | âŒ | âŒ | âœ… | `201` + `Location` (create) or `200`/`202` | The only method that creates a new subordinate resource |
| `PUT` | âŒ | âœ… | âœ…, full representation | `200`/`204` (update), `201` (create if absent) | Replaces the whole representation |
| `PATCH` | âŒ | âŒ* | âœ… partial document | `200`/`204` | *Idempotent only if the patch document is idempotent* |
| `DELETE` | âŒ | âœ… | Discouraged | `204`, or `200` + the deleted object | Repeating it must not error; "already gone" is success |

topics.title: Status Codes: The Full List and When Each Is Correct
topics.description: The status code is the primary machine-readable channel for the outcome of a request. Choosing it correctly is what lets a client, a proxy, a cache, and a monitoring system each react appropriately without parsing your body.
keyConcepts: The classes
1xx informational. 100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols (WebSocket upgrade), 102 Processing, 103 Early Hints (preload hints before the body).
2xx success. 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 203 Non-Authoritative Information (proxy-modified), 204 No Content, 205 Reset Content, 206 Partial Content (range requests, Content-Range).
3xx redirection. 300 Multiple Choices, 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 303 See Other, 304 Not Modified, 307 Temporary Redirect, 308 Permanent Redirect.
4xx client error. The request is wrong; fix it and retry â€” the identical request will fail identically.
5xx server error. The request may be fine; retrying the identical request is legitimate (with backoff).
The nuanced ones, stated once each
201 + Location: the new resource's canonical URI. Send the representation in the body too (that is allowed and common), but Location is the contract.

204 rules: absolutely no body, and per RFC 9110 it must not include content; some clients (and buggy proxies) mis-handle a Content-Length on a 204, so omit it. 205 Reset Content is the one that *requires* Content-Length: 0.

400 vs 422: 400 = the server could not understand or parse the request (bad JSON, ?limit=abc that fails parsing, wrong content encoding). 422 = the server understood it and the DTO/business rules rejected it. Clients handle these differently: a 400 is usually a client bug, a 422 is usually user-fixable data. This is the single most argued-about choice in API design; be consistent and document it.

401 vs 403: 401 means *who are you* failed and includes a WWW-Authenticate challenge. 403 means *we know who you are and no*. If the answer must not reveal existence, return 404 for both missing and forbidden (the standard defence against IDOR enumeration).
404 vs 409: 404 = the resource does not exist. 409 = it exists but the request conflicts with its current state (duplicate email, edit a deleted row, concurrent version).

topics.title: Idempotency: Keys, Storage, Fingerprints, and Replay
topics.description: Idempotency is the property that repeating a request has the same effect as making it once. HTTP gives it to safe and idempotent methods for free (5.4.2). For POST, the client supplies the guarantee with an Idempotency-Key header, and the server enforces it.
keyConcepts: Which operations need it
The design, end to end

Client generates the key for an *intent*, not a request attempt: a UUIDv4 created when the user opens the checkout, reused on every retry of that checkout, regenerated when the user deliberately starts over. A key generated inside the retry loop defeats the entire mechanism.
Server reserves the key atomically before doing any work â€” a compare-and-set insert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, or SET key value NX EX). Never GET then SET.

Server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key: a hash over method, path, and canonicalized body (and usually the tenant/principal). If the same key arrives with a *different* fingerprint, the client made a programming error; reject with 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED rather than silently returning the wrong cached response.

Server stores the response â€” status, selected headers, and body â€” on completion, and replays it byte-for-byte on subsequent requests with the same key and fingerprint. Replaying the *exact* response (not re-executing) is what makes the guarantee real.

Concurrency: a second request with the same key while the first is in flight must not execute. Options: return 409 with Retry-After (simple, honest), or wait briefly on a short poll (nicer clients), or make the underlying operation itself idempotent so a double execution is harmless and just let both run. The third option is the most robust and the most work.

TTL: at least as long as the client's maximum retry window. 24 hours is a common default; payments and orders should be as long as your business's duplicate-detection policy (often 7 days). Store the TTL on the key so it can be tuned per endpoint â€” and consider keeping a *minimal* fingerprint-only record much longer to detect "this key was used a month ago".

Storage: Redis with a TTL, or a relational table with UNIQUE(key) and a cleanup job. Redis is fast and self-expiring; a table is transactional with your own data, which matters when the key insert and the business write must commit together.
Interaction with at-least-once delivery

Webhooks and queue consumers are at-least-once by nature. Idempotency keys are the standard way to convert an at-least-once channel into an effectively-once side effect: the *consumer* generates or derives the key from the message id and calls your idempotent endpoint.

The outbox pattern (see PHASE 5 Background Processing) solves the other half: a message can be delivered zero times if the transaction that would have enqueued it rolls back. Idempotency does not fix at-most-once; the outbox does. You need both for exactly-once *effects*.
commonMistakes: generating the key per attempt; GET-then-SET instead of an atomic reserve; no fingerprint, so a reused key returns another request's response; replaying by *re-executing* instead of returning the stored response; a TTL shorter than the client's retry window; not documenting the header in the OpenAPI spec; assuming the key protects against a client that generates a new key each time.
practiceTasks: implement idempotency for POST /payments with an atomic reserve, a fingerprint, a 24h TTL, response replay, and a 409 on key reuse with a different body. Then test it: 10 concurrent identical requests (must charge once), the same key with a changed amount (must be 409), a retry after completion (must replay with the identical body), a retry after TTL expiry (must execute again), and a store outage (must fail closed with 503).

**Which operations need it**
| Operation | Needs a key? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /payments`, `POST /orders` (money, stock, notifications) | **Yes** | The client cannot distinguish a timeout from a failure; retrying may double-charge |
| Webhook handlers you expose to third parties | **Yes** (or equivalent dedupe) | Receivers retry on their own schedule, at least once |
| `POST /imports`, `POST /batch-jobs` | **Yes** | Expensive, and the client's only recourse after a timeout is to retry |
| `POST /users` signup | **Yes** | A retried signup is a confusing "email already registered" |
| `POST /search` | No | Safe to duplicate; it only costs a query |
| Any `GET` | No | Already idempotent |
| `DELETE`, `PUT` | No | Already idempotent by method (but see `PUT` + increment-style payloads) |
| Third-party call you make *from* a handler | **Yes, propagated** | Your own retry needs the same guarantee; and if you retry the upstream, the upstream's key should be your key so the chain stays de-duplicated |

**The design, end to end**
1. **Client generates the key** for an *intent*, not a request attempt: a UUIDv4 created when the user opens the checkout, reused on every retry of that checkout, regenerated when the user deliberately starts over. A key generated inside the retry loop defeats the entire mechanism.
2. **Server reserves the key atomically** before doing any work â€” a compare-and-set insert (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, or `SET key value NX EX`). Never `GET` then `SET`.
3. **Server stores a fingerprint** of the request alongside the key: a hash over method, path, and canonicalized body (and usually the tenant/principal). If the same key arrives with a *different* fingerprint, the client made a programming error; reject with `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` rather than silently returning the wrong cached response.
4. **Server stores the response** â€” status, selected headers, and body â€” on completion, and replays it byte-for-byte on subsequent requests with the same key and fingerprint. Replaying the *exact* response (not re-executing) is what makes the guarantee real.
5. **Concurrency:** a second request with the same key while the first is in flight must not execute. Options: return `409` with `Retry-After` (simple, honest), or wait briefly on a short poll (nicer clients), or make the underlying operation itself idempotent so a double execution is harmless and just let both run. The third option is the most robust and the most work.
6. **TTL:** at least as long as the client's maximum retry window. 24 hours is a common default; payments and orders should be as long as your business's duplicate-detection policy (often 7 days). Store the TTL on the key so it can be tuned per endpoint â€” and consider keeping a *minimal* fingerprint-only record much longer to detect "this key was used a month ago".
7. **Storage:** Redis with a TTL, or a relational table with `UNIQUE(key)` and a cleanup job. Redis is fast and self-expiring; a table is transactional with your own data, which matters when the key insert and the business write must commit together.

**Interaction with at-least-once delivery**
- Webhooks and queue consumers are at-least-once by nature. Idempotency keys are the standard way to convert an at-least-once channel into an effectively-once side effect: the *consumer* generates or derives the key from the message id and calls your idempotent endpoint.
- **The outbox pattern** (see **PHASE 5 Background Processing**) solves the other half: a message can be delivered zero times if the transaction that would have enqueued it rolls back. Idempotency does not fix at-most-once; the outbox does. You need both for exactly-once *effects*.
- **Deriving keys from message ids** is better than generating new ones on redelivery: `{eventId}` is stable across redeliveries, so `Idempotency-Key: <eventId>` works with zero client coordination.

- An idempotency store is now on the critical path: it adds a round trip, and its outage mode is a decision (fail closed and reject, or fail open and risk duplicates). Fail closed for money.

- Storing response bodies can be large; store what is needed to reconstruct the response, or cap the size and store a reference.
- The header name has no standard: `Idempotency-Key` is a de facto convention (also used by payment processors). Document it in your OpenAPI spec, because undeclared headers get stripped by some proxies.

topics.title: PUT vs PATCH and the Patch Formats
topics.description: PUT replaces a resource's state with the body it is given; PATCH applies a partial modification described by a patch document whose *format* â€” merge patch, JSON Patch, or something proprietary â€” determines what the server can and cannot express.
keyConcepts: PUT â€” full replacement
If the URI does not exist, PUT creates it (201 + Location).

PUT is idempotent *only if* the body is: {"counter": 5} is idempotent (it sets); {"counter": 6} sent twice is still idempotent; but a payload like {"quantity": {"$increment": 2}} is not. Any body that expresses a *delta* breaks PUT's idempotency, which is a design smell.

PUT requires the client to hold the whole representation, which is expensive and error-prone for large or frequently-updated resources. It also makes concurrency harder: a PUT from a stale client silently discards changes it never saw.
PATCH â€” partial update
1. JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396)
null means "delete this member" (set to JSON null in the output, or remove it, per the RFC's "remove" recommendation).
An absent key means "leave it alone" â€” this is the crucial distinction from PUT.
Objects merge recursively; arrays are replaced wholesale. {"tags": ["a","b"]} replaces the entire array; you cannot append or remove one element.
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json.
Cannot express "append to array" or "increment".
2. JSON Patch (RFC 6902)
commonMistakes: treating PATCH as a partial PUT (sending null for unchanged fields); assuming null means "unchanged"; using Merge Patch when you need array element edits; add vs replace confusion on arrays; relying on a client-supplied updatedAt for concurrency; returning 409 for a lost update where 412 plus the current ETag is more useful.
practiceTasks: implement all three formats for one resource and test the edges: absent key, null key, nested object partial, array replace, array element update, atomic failure on a bad test op, If-Match stale and fresh, and a lost update under two concurrent PATCHes. Then write the exact Content-Type you require for each and the error you return for a wrong one.

Why is `PATCH` not automatically idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a client retries a PATCH that failed on a flaky connection, and the quantity doubles. Decision: only accept patch documents whose application is idempotent, and move anything additive into a named action endpoint. Reasoning: RFC 9110 defines idempotency as a property of the method *for the intended effect of the request*, and a partial update's intended effect depends entirely on its body. {'status': 'cancelled'} sets a value, so applying it twice equals applying it once. {'quantity': 5} also sets. But {'quantity': {'$inc': 1}}, {'tags': {'$push': 'urgent'}}, and a JSON Patch that appends with add /tags/- all *accumulate*, so a retry after a lost response double-counts. The HTTP method gives no protection here â€” the protection has to come from the document's semantics. Trade-offs: restricting patches to set-style operations limits expressiveness, and clients that genuinely need to append must go through an endpoint, which is more HTTP calls for incremental UI. Failure scenario: a mobile cart sends {items: [...], version: 3} on every keystroke-save; the response is lost, the client retries, and because the endpoint is treated as a safe retry the second apply succeeds and the audit log shows two identical saves with different versions, so reconciliation cannot tell which is authoritative. Alternative: accept additive patches but require the client to send an Idempotency-Key (5.4.4) with each one â€” which is really a statement that if you need additive semantics, the operation is an action, not a document edit, and should be named as such so it can be retried, audited, and rate-limited on its own."
