topics.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling as an API Contract
topics.description: Rate limiting is an advertised contract: the server tells clients what their budget is, what they have left, and when they may retry. The algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window/log) and the shared-store design are in PHASE 6 Caching Layers â€” this section is only about the HTTP surface.
keyConcepts: Headers
Retry-After (RFC 9110) is the one header every client and every HTTP library already understands: either delta-seconds or an HTTP-date. It is mandatory on a 429.

RateLimit-Limit / RateLimit-Remaining / RateLimit-Reset are the IETF-standardized set (from the draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers work). RateLimit-Policy conveys the quota and, optionally, a time until the limit is *raised* and whether the client has breached a penalty tier.

X-RateLimit-* (limit/remaining/reset) plus X-RateLimit-Reset-After is the older de facto convention. Many gateways and SDKs still read only the X- names. Emitting both is common and harmless; a client that reads either works. If you are writing a new public API, emit the standard names and consider the X- names for legacy clients.

Emit the limit headers on successful responses too, not just on 429. A well-behaved client throttles proactively, and the headers are how it knows to. Emitting them only when you refuse is a design mistake.

RateLimit as a single combined field (RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=12) exists in the same draft for multiple simultaneous policies (per-tier, per-policy). Choose one form and be consistent; do not emit conflicting variants.
What to key the limit on
Design notes that matter in production
Fail open vs fail closed when the store is unavailable. Fail open for reads, fail closed for writes and for anything that costs money.
Headers through every layer: if a CDN or gateway sits in front, it may consume your 429 or add its own. Decide which layer is authoritative, and make sure the surviving 429 reaches the client.

Distributed consistency: with N pods and a local counter, a client gets NÃ— the intended limit. A shared store (Redis INCR+EXPIRE, or a Lua script for atomicity) is required â€” the mechanism is in PHASE 6.
Retry-After must be truthful. If you say 30 seconds and the window resets in 1, clients waste time; if you say 1 and it resets in 30, you get a retry storm. Derive it from the actual algorithm state.
commonMistakes: no Retry-After; limit headers only on 429; local counters behind multiple pods; keying on IP only, behind a proxy you trust the X-Forwarded-For of; failing open on a payment endpoint; a fixed-window counter with a boundary burst problem and no smoothing; a 429 swallowed by the CDN.
practiceTasks: implement three layered limits (per API key, per tenant, per route class) with a Redis token bucket, returning correct Retry-After, RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset on both 200 and 429. Test: 10 parallel clients sharing one key (the limit must hold globally, not per pod), a burst of 200 requests against a bucket of 100, a key boundary crossing, and a store outage. Verify the headers on every response and that the values are truthful.

interviewQuestions.text: What headers must a `429` carry, and what do they mean?
Which is authoritative: the gateway or the app?
Fail open or fail closed when the store is down?
Why key on tenant as well as client?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a multi-tenant B2B API on one shared pool of pods; one large customer's nightly batch job saturates the database and every other tenant sees timeouts. Decision: apply a layered limit â€” per API key for partner traffic, per tenant for fairness between tenants, per user as a secondary cap, plus a global concurrency limit on the database pool â€” and count the batch job's tokens at a much higher cost per request than an interactive read. Reasoning: the problem is not a single client misbehaving, it is that tenants share a resource, so a fair share of that resource has to be an explicit part of the contract. Without a tenant dimension, the only lever is a per-client limit, and the batch job is a single client, so a limit high enough for its batch is high enough to hurt everyone. With a tenant dimension, the batch job gets its own bucket sized to what it actually needs, and the interactive traffic of the other 4,000 tenants is unaffected. The concurrency limit is the backstop that protects the database even when every individual bucket says 'allowed', because rate limits are about fairness and concurrency limits are about the downstream resource. Trade-offs: more moving parts, and every layer needs a key, which means every request must already carry a tenant identity â€” so the tenant must be established early in the pipeline and available to all four checks. It also means pricing conversations get real: a cap per tenant is effectively a product decision that needs buy-in. Failure scenario: limits are implemented per API key, and a customer's mobile app and their nightly integration share one key, so the batch job exhausts the budget and every interactive user of that customer gets throttled for the rest of the window â€” one tenant harming themselves, and a support escalation that reads as 'your app is broken'. Alternative: a single weighted token bucket keyed on tenant with different weights per endpoint class, and a separate much larger bucket for the integration's own credentials, so an interactive user and a machine never compete for the same budget."

interviewQuestions.text: Why emit limit headers on `200` responses?
What does a GraphQL API need that REST does not?

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** Rate limiting is an **advertised contract**: the server tells clients what their budget is, what they have left, and when they may retry. The algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window/log) and the shared-store design are in **PHASE 6 Caching Layers** â€” this section is only about the HTTP surface.

**Headers**
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 12                 # seconds until the window resets
RateLimit-Policy: 100;w=60           # limit, window seconds, and optional quota/breach policy
Link: <urn:docs:rate-limits>; rel="describedby"
```
- **`Retry-After`** (RFC 9110) is the one header every client and every HTTP library already understands: either delta-seconds or an HTTP-date. It is mandatory on a `429`.
- **`RateLimit-Limit` / `RateLimit-Remaining` / `RateLimit-Reset`** are the IETF-standardized set (from the `draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers` work). `RateLimit-Policy` conveys the quota and, optionally, a time until the limit is *raised* and whether the client has breached a penalty tier.
- **`X-RateLimit-*`** (limit/remaining/reset) plus `X-RateLimit-Reset-After` is the older de facto convention. Many gateways and SDKs still read only the `X-` names. Emitting both is common and harmless; a client that reads either works. If you are writing a new public API, emit the standard names and consider the `X-` names for legacy clients.
- **Emit the limit headers on successful responses too**, not just on `429`. A well-behaved client throttles proactively, and the headers are how it knows to. Emitting them only when you refuse is a design mistake.
- **`RateLimit` as a single combined field** (`RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=12`) exists in the same draft for multiple simultaneous policies (per-tier, per-policy). Choose one form and be consistent; do not emit conflicting variants.

**What to key the limit on**
| Scope | Key | Use for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per client | API key, OAuth client id | Public APIs, partner integrations | The main one; gives one partner's traffic spike no ability to exhaust everyone |
| Per principal | User id | End-user APIs | Often *in addition* to per-client, since one client hosts many users |
| Per IP | IP (with proxy-aware client IP) | Anonymous and unauthenticated endpoints | Easy to spoof wrongly behind proxies; pair with a fingerprint or a proof-of-work/challenge |
| Per route or class | The route's cost class | Expensive endpoints (search, exports, reports) | A weighted limit: a search costs 10, a read costs 1 |
| Per tenant | Tenant id | Multi-tenant SaaS | The fairness mechanism; prevents one tenant starving the rest |
| Per field/operation | Specific field | GraphQL (see 5.5.11) | Required, because one endpoint can hide arbitrarily expensive work |
| Concurrency | In-flight requests | Protect downstream dependencies | Not a rate limit, but complements one; pairs with a circuit breaker |

**Design notes that matter in production**
- **Fail open vs fail closed** when the store is unavailable. Fail open for reads, fail closed for writes and for anything that costs money.
- **Headers through every layer:** if a CDN or gateway sits in front, it may consume your `429` or add its own. Decide which layer is authoritative, and make sure the surviving `429` reaches the client.
- **Distributed consistency:** with N pods and a local counter, a client gets NÃ— the intended limit. A shared store (Redis `INCR`+`EXPIRE`, or a Lua script for atomicity) is required â€” the mechanism is in **PHASE 6**.
- **Retry-After must be truthful.** If you say 30 seconds and the window resets in 1, clients waste time; if you say 1 and it resets in 30, you get a retry storm. Derive it from the actual algorithm state.
- **Burst vs sustained:** a token bucket allows bursts up to its size, a leaky bucket smooths them. Read endpoints can usually tolerate bursts; writes and expensive operations usually should not.
- **Client-side backoff:** a client that retries immediately on a `429` is a self-inflicted DDoS. Document `Retry-After` plus exponential backoff with jitter, and set the SDK default accordingly.
- **Advertise the policy in the OpenAPI spec and the docs**, and make the numbers separate for reads and writes so clients can plan.

**Questions**
1. What headers must a `429` carry, and what do they mean?
2. Which is authoritative: the gateway or the app?
3. Fail open or fail closed when the store is down?
4. Why key on tenant as well as client?
5. Why emit limit headers on `200` responses?
6. What does a GraphQL API need that REST does not?

**Model answer, Q4:** "Context: a multi-tenant B2B API on one shared pool of pods; one large customer's nightly batch job saturates the database and every other tenant sees timeouts. With a tenant dimension, the batch job gets its own bucket sized to what it actually needs, and the interactive traffic of the other 4,000 tenants is unaffected. The concurrency limit is the backstop that protects the database even when every individual bucket says 'allowed', because rate limits are about fairness and concurrency limits are about the downstream resource. Trade-offs: more moving parts, and every layer needs a key, which means every request must already carry a tenant identity â€” so the tenant must be established early in the pipeline and available to all four checks. It also means pricing conversations get real: a cap per tenant is effectively a product decision that needs buy-in. Failure scenario: limits are implemented per API key, and a customer's mobile app and their nightly integration share one key, so the batch job exhausts the budget and every interactive user of that customer gets throttled for the rest of the window â€” one tenant harming themselves, and a support escalation that reads as 'your app is broken'. **Mistakes:** no `Retry-After`; limit headers only on `429`; local counters behind multiple pods; keying on IP only, behind a proxy you trust the `X-Forwarded-For` of; failing open on a payment endpoint; a fixed-window counter with a boundary burst problem and no smoothing; a `429` swallowed by the CDN.

**Mini task:** implement three layered limits (per API key, per tenant, per route class) with a Redis token bucket, returning correct `Retry-After`, `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` on both `200` and `429`. Test: 10 parallel clients sharing one key (the limit must hold globally, not per pod), a burst of 200 requests against a bucket of 100, a key boundary crossing, and a store outage. Verify the headers on every response and that the values are truthful.

topics.bodyMarkdown:
**Definition:** Rate limiting is an **advertised contract**: the server tells clients what their budget is, what they have left, and when they may retry. The algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window/log) and the shared-store design are in **PHASE 6 Caching Layers** â€” this section is only about the HTTP surface.

**Headers**
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 12                 # seconds until the window resets
RateLimit-Policy: 100;w=60           # limit, window seconds, and optional quota/breach policy
Link: <urn:docs:rate-limits>; rel="describedby"
```
- **`Retry-After`** (RFC 9110) is the one header every client and every HTTP library already understands: either delta-seconds or an HTTP-date. It is mandatory on a `429`.
- **`RateLimit-Limit` / `RateLimit-Remaining` / `RateLimit-Reset`** are the IETF-standardized set (from the `draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers` work). `RateLimit-Policy` conveys the quota and, optionally, a time until the limit is *raised* and whether the client has breached a penalty tier.
- **`X-RateLimit-*`** (limit/remaining/reset) plus `X-RateLimit-Reset-After` is the older de facto convention. Many gateways and SDKs still read only the `X-` names. Emitting both is common and harmless; a client that reads either works. If you are writing a new public API, emit the standard names and consider the `X-` names for legacy clients.
- **Emit the limit headers on successful responses too**, not just on `429`. A well-behaved client throttles proactively, and the headers are how it knows to. Emitting them only when you refuse is a design mistake.
- **`RateLimit` as a single combined field** (`RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=12`) exists in the same draft for multiple simultaneous policies (per-tier, per-policy). Choose one form and be consistent; do not emit conflicting variants.

**What to key the limit on**
| Scope | Key | Use for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per client | API key, OAuth client id | Public APIs, partner integrations | The main one; gives one partner's traffic spike no ability to exhaust everyone |
| Per principal | User id | End-user APIs | Often *in addition* to per-client, since one client hosts many users |
| Per IP | IP (with proxy-aware client IP) | Anonymous and unauthenticated endpoints | Easy to spoof wrongly behind proxies; pair with a fingerprint or a proof-of-work/challenge |
| Per route or class | The route's cost class | Expensive endpoints (search, exports, reports) | A weighted limit: a search costs 10, a read costs 1 |
| Per tenant | Tenant id | Multi-tenant SaaS | The fairness mechanism; prevents one tenant starving the rest |
| Per field/operation | Specific field | GraphQL (see 5.5.11) | Required, because one endpoint can hide arbitrarily expensive work |
| Concurrency | In-flight requests | Protect downstream dependencies | Not a rate limit, but complements one; pairs with a circuit breaker |

- **Burst vs sustained:** a token bucket allows bursts up to its size, a leaky bucket smooths them. Read endpoints can usually tolerate bursts; writes and expensive operations usually should not.
- **Client-side backoff:** a client that retries immediately on a `429` is a self-inflicted DDoS. Document `Retry-After` plus exponential backoff with jitter, and set the SDK default accordingly.
- **Advertise the policy in the OpenAPI spec and the docs**, and make the numbers separate for reads and writes so clients can plan.

1. What headers must a `429` carry, and what do they mean?
2. Which is authoritative: the gateway or the app?

topics.title: Long-Running Operations: 202, Status Resources, Polling, Webhooks
topics.description: Work that takes longer than a request should hold open. The pattern is to acknowledge immediately with 202, expose the work as a resource the client can poll, and optionally deliver the terminal result out of band.
keyConcepts: The problem
The pattern
Rules that make it correct

202 means *accepted for processing*, not "maybe". If you completed the work, return 201/200. Returning 202 and then doing the work synchronously is a lie that produces clients that poll for results that already exist.
The job is a resource, with its own URI, so it can be fetched, referenced, and authorized.
Retry-After on the 202 is a hint for the first poll interval.
Terminal states are succeeded and failed; a client that polls forever is a bug, so give jobs a TTL and return 410 after it.
Expose progress for anything over a few seconds; a progress bar changes user behaviour more than a faster job.
The result should be a reference, not an inline blob. A generated CSV belongs at a presigned URL with its own expiry, not inside a polling response.
GET /jobs/{id} must be cheap and cacheable-ish: read one row, or a cached status. Do not recompute.
Notifications: polling vs webhook vs WebSocket.
Cancellation
commonMistakes: 202 for work already done; polling with no backoff or jitter; no terminal state so the client polls forever; a status endpoint that recomputes; no TTL on job records; inlining a huge result in the status response; claiming cancellation succeeded synchronously; a job that is not idempotent being retried.
practiceTasks: implement POST /exports â†’ 202 + Location, a GET /jobs/{id} status resource with queued/running/succeeded/failed, a POST /jobs/{id}/cancel state machine, Idempotency-Key support, and a Retry-After header. Then write a client that polls with exponential backoff and jitter, and a test that: cancels mid-run, cancels after completion (must be 409), polls an expired job (must be 410), and fires 5 concurrent POST /exports with one key (must create one job).

interviewQuestions.text: What is the difference between `202` and "I did it but slowly"?
Why is the job a resource?
Polling, webhook, or WebSocket?
Why is cancellation a request rather than a command?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a user clicks 'cancel' on a two-hour report generation and the UI immediately says 'Cancelled', but the job was 90% through and the final CSV upload completed anyway, so the file appeared in storage after the user was told it would not. Decision: model cancellation as a state transition the job observes, not a command the API executes â€” running â†’ cancelling â†’ cancelled | completed â€” and have the client poll until it reaches a terminal state. Reasoning: a job doing real work cannot be preempted safely at an arbitrary instruction boundary. It may be mid-write, holding a lock, waiting on a third party, or past the point where side effects (a billing event, a stored file) are already visible. The only honest contract is: we will stop at the next safe checkpoint, and until then the outcome is genuinely unknown. Claiming success immediately is not a simplification, it is a false statement about work that is still running, and the resulting 'cancelled but present' artifacts are exactly the kind of bug that takes a week to reproduce. The safe-checkpoint design means the job checks a cancellation flag between chunks, and the work it has already done is written to a staging location that is only promoted atomically, so cancelling before promotion leaves nothing behind. Trade-offs: the client has to handle a 'cancelling' intermediate state, and 'cancel' is not instant, which users dislike. Failure scenario: a team implements DELETE /jobs/{id} as a database row delete, and the worker process reads the job into memory at start, so deleting the row does nothing at all; the report completes, no record of it exists anywhere, and the support ticket says 'the user cancelled and we still got the file'. Alternative: if the work is short and chunkable, make the job cancellable at a fine granularity and hold a lock on the resource, so a cancel takes a job-scoped advisory lock the worker checks â€” but the state machine and the honest polling are still needed, because the check is always racy by nature."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** Work that takes longer than a request should hold open. The pattern is to acknowledge immediately with `202`, expose the work as a resource the client can poll, and optionally deliver the terminal result out of band.

**The problem:** an HTTP request cannot be held open for ten minutes. Load balancers time out, proxies kill idle connections, mobile networks drop, and the client is left in an unknown state â€” exactly the ambiguity of 5.4.4. The answer is to acknowledge quickly and expose the work as a resource.

**The pattern**
```
POST /exports
  â†’ 202 Accepted
    Location: /jobs/job_7f3a
    Retry-After: 2
    { "id": "job_7f3a", "status": "queued" }            // or a bare Location + empty body

GET /jobs/job_7f3a
  â†’ 200 OK
    { "id": "job_7f3a", "status": "running", "progress": 0.42, "startedAt": "...", "expiresAt": "..." }
  â†’ 200 { "id": "job_7f3a", "status": "succeeded", "result": { "downloadUrl": "https://...", "expiresAt": "..." } }
  â†’ 200 { "id": "job_7f3a", "status": "failed", "error": { "code": "SOURCE_TOO_LARGE", "detail": "..." } }
  â†’ 404 (never existed or expired â€” indistinguishable on purpose)
  â†’ 410 Gone (expired, but you want to say so)
```
**Rules that make it correct**
- `202` means *accepted for processing*, **not** "maybe". If you completed the work, return `201`/`200`. Returning `202` and then doing the work synchronously is a lie that produces clients that poll for results that already exist.
- The job **is a resource**, with its own URI, so it can be fetched, referenced, and authorized.
- `Retry-After` on the `202` is a hint for the first poll interval.
- Terminal states are `succeeded` and `failed`; a client that polls forever is a bug, so give jobs a TTL and return `410` after it.
- **Expose progress** for anything over a few seconds; a progress bar changes user behaviour more than a faster job.
- **The result should be a reference, not an inline blob.** A generated CSV belongs at a presigned URL with its own expiry, not inside a polling response.
- **`GET /jobs/{id}` must be cheap and cacheable-ish**: read one row, or a cached status. Do not recompute.
- **Notifications: polling vs webhook vs WebSocket.**
  - *Polling* â€” simplest, works everywhere, no infrastructure. Back off exponentially from ~1s to ~10s, jitter it, and stop when the client sees a terminal state. Fine for a handful of long jobs.
  - *Webhook* â€” the client gives you a URL and you `POST` a signed notification when the job finishes (5.4.16). Best for many jobs, and the client does not need to be online.
  - *WebSocket / SSE* â€” best for interactive UI where the connection is already open. See **PHASE 5 Real-Time Systems**; note that a dropped connection needs a resync (fetch the current status on reconnect), so it is a *transport optimization*, not a source of truth.
  - A robust design supports polling always, and adds a webhook for efficiency.

**Cancellation**
```
POST /jobs/job_7f3a/cancel     (or DELETE /jobs/job_7f3a)
  â†’ 202 if cancellation was requested and the job is still cancelable
  â†’ 200/409 if it already finished; 409 with a clear code is honest
  â†’ 204 if it was cancelled before starting
```
Cancellation is a **request**, not a guarantee: a job already past its cancellation checkpoint will finish. So the status resource must have a `cancelling` state that eventually resolves to `cancelled` or `completed`, and the client must handle all three. This is the same "unknown outcome" problem as idempotency, and it is why the underlying work must be idempotent and checkpointed.

**Idempotency.** `POST /exports` should accept an `Idempotency-Key` so a client that times out on the `202` does not start five exports. And the job itself must be safe to run twice (write to a temp location, then atomically publish) â€” a duplicated export is cheap, a duplicated charge is not.

**When not to use this:** under ~2 seconds of work, just do it synchronously; the extra round trips and the polling code in the client are not worth it. The threshold is about p99 latency, not average.

**Questions**
1. What is the difference between `202` and "I did it but slowly"?
2. Why is the job a resource?
3. Polling, webhook, or WebSocket?
4. Why is cancellation a request rather than a command?
5. When should the work just be synchronous?

It may be mid-write, holding a lock, waiting on a third party, or past the point where side effects (a billing event, a stored file) are already visible. The only honest contract is: we will stop at the next safe checkpoint, and until then the outcome is genuinely unknown. Claiming success immediately is not a simplification, it is a false statement about work that is still running, and the resulting 'cancelled but present' artifacts are exactly the kind of bug that takes a week to reproduce. The safe-checkpoint design means the job checks a cancellation flag between chunks, and the work it has already done is written to a staging location that is only promoted atomically, so cancelling before promotion leaves nothing behind. Trade-offs: the client has to handle a 'cancelling' intermediate state, and 'cancel' is not instant, which users dislike. Failure scenario: a team implements `DELETE /jobs/{id}` as a database row delete, and the worker process reads the job into memory at start, so deleting the row does nothing at all; the report completes, no record of it exists anywhere, and the support ticket says 'the user cancelled and we still got the file'. topics.title: Bulk Operations: Batch Endpoints and Partial Failure
topics.description: A bulk endpoint performs many independent operations in one request. The hard part is not the loop â€” it is the failure semantics, and you must choose them explicitly.
keyConcepts: Shapes
Synchronous batch (up to a few hundred items, sub-second) returns per-item results.
Asynchronous batch / import (thousands of items, or anything slow) is a 202 + job (5.4.14) whose result is a report file.

207 Multi-Status is the WebDAV status for a body containing multiple independent statuses. WebDAV is a real part of HTTP, but the 207 code is obscure: many HTTP client libraries, API gateways, and monitoring tools do not treat it as a success, and some SDKs throw on any non-2xx. The safer, boring choice is 200 OK with a per-item results array, and it is what most public APIs do. If you use 207, document it prominently and test your SDKs.
Per-item results, either way
index (or the client's own key) is mandatory â€” the client must be able to correlate results back to inputs, especially if the input order is not preserved or the client retries a subset.

Atomic vs non-atomic is a product decision: a bulk import of a spreadsheet is non-atomic (partial success with a report of failures is the useful behaviour); a payment batch must be atomic or per-item idempotent. Say which you chose in the docs, and if you offer both, make it explicit (?atomic=true or a distinct endpoint).

Ordering and atomicity of the database work: for a non-atomic batch, wrap each item in its own transaction (so one failure does not roll back 999 successes) â€” or accept a single transaction and document that it is all-or-nothing. Never leave it implicit.
Limits: cap the item count (100-1000 for sync), cap the total body size, cap per-item payload size, and reject the whole request with 413/422 if the cap is exceeded rather than truncating silently.
Partial failure of the *request* vs of the *items*: a malformed outer envelope (not an array, missing the auth header) is a 400 for the whole request; a bad individual item is a per-item error.
Do not return 4xx for a batch where some items succeeded. A client retrying a 422 batch endpoint re-submits the whole batch. This is a real and common bug.

**Shapes**

```json
    { "index": 1, "status": 201, "id": "ord_2" },
    { "index": 2, "status": 422, "error": { "code": "INVALID_SKU", "pointer": "/data/items/0/sku", "detail": "unknown sku" } }
```

topics.title: Webhooks: Signatures, Retries, Ordering, and Receiver Design
topics.description: A webhook is an HTTP request your server makes to a URL the client gave you, delivering an event. It is the only way to notify a client that is not currently talking to you â€” and it is at-least-once, so the whole design hinges on that.
keyConcepts: The envelope
id is the dedupe key and must be stable across retries of the same event. delivery changes per attempt. Conflating them is a classic bug that makes receiver-side dedupe impossible.
Version the payload explicitly and add fields, never remove or repurpose them, within a version. A new major type (order.created.v2) is cleaner than a silent semantic change.
Signature verification â€” the security core

Sign the raw body, before JSON parsing. Re-serializing a parsed object changes whitespace and key order, so the HMAC will not match. This means your framework must expose the raw bytes: in Express, mount a body parser that keeps a rawBody buffer; in Fastify, add a content-type parser that stores the raw string; in NestJS, a small middleware or rawBody: true option on the factory.

Include a timestamp in the signed material. Without it, a signature captured from your own logs (or from a proxy log that includes bodies and signatures) can be replayed indefinitely. With it, an old signature expires in minutes.
Constant-time comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) â€” a naive === leaks the correct hash one byte at a time. Guard the length first, since timingSafeEqual throws on a mismatch.
Timestamp in a separate header vs in the signed payload: either works; the convention of t=...,v1=... in a single header is widely used and easy to rotate.

Secret rotation: emit a signature per active secret (e.g. v1=...,v2=... or a comma-separated list), publish both in the portal, and retire the old one after a notice period. Rotating by simply replacing the value breaks every receiver for an hour.
Never put the secret in the payload or in a URL query string (URLs end up in logs and referrers).
TLS is required; a signature over plaintext is theatre.
Retries and delivery
commonMistakes: verifying the signature after re-serializing the JSON; signing only the body with no timestamp; naive === comparison; retrying on 2xx; never retrying; no dedupe guidance in the docs; treating the delivery log as optional; following redirects; one secret with no rotation path; assuming ordering.
practiceTasks: implement a sender (HMAC over ts.rawBody, 8 attempts with jittered backoff, a delivery log, DLQ after exhaustion, replay-from-dashboard) and a receiver (raw-body capture, timestamp tolerance, constant-time compare, atomic dedupe with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, async processing, order-tolerance with a per-entity version). Then test: a tampered body, a stale timestamp, a signature replayed with a new timestamp, a 3-attempt failure then success, a permanent 400, a slow receiver, and secret rotation mid-flight.

interviewQuestions.text: Why sign the raw body and a timestamp?
What is the difference between `id` and `delivery`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our documentation tells receivers to dedupe on the payload's id, and a support ticket shows an event processed twice even though the id was the same. Decision: id is the event identity and is identical across every delivery attempt of that event; delivery (or attempt) is the identity of one HTTP request and is unique per attempt, and it is the only thing that appears in the delivery log. Reasoning: the two answer different questions. Deduplication is about the *event* â€” 'have I already processed the fact that order 42 was paid?' â€” so the key must be the same no matter how many times we retry, otherwise every retry looks like a new event and the receiver does the work again, which is exactly the double-charge we are seeing. The delivery identifier is about the *HTTP transaction*, so it must be unique per attempt, otherwise the delivery log collapses 5 attempts into 1 row and you cannot tell whether a retry succeeded. Once you conflate them you also break the other important property: because id is stable, the receiver can safely store it in a unique-constrained table and let the database decide whether it is a duplicate, atomically, which is far more reliable than a check-then-act in application code. Trade-offs: two identifiers is one more field to document, and a client who stores only delivery will never dedupe correctly, so the naming and the docs have to be unambiguous. Failure scenario: a receiver treats delivery as the dedupe key, our delivery pipeline retries after a 30-second timeout because the receiver was slow but had already committed the effect, and the receiver sees a new id, processes the event again, and ships a second physical product. The logs show one event id and no apparent duplicate, so the bug is invisible in the sender's tooling."

topics.title: OpenAPI and Swagger: Design-First vs Code-First
topics.description: OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API â€” operations, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security. It is the closest thing to a compilable contract, and it can drive documentation, client generation, mock servers, and contract tests.

The honest recommendation
Generating clients
Documentation as a contract
The reference â€” generated from the spec: every endpoint, every field, types, required-ness, status codes, examples. Generated, so it is never wrong.

The guide â€” hand-written: authentication setup, pagination semantics, idempotency, rate limits, error codes, webhook setup, and a task-oriented quickstart. This is the part humans actually read, and the part the spec cannot generate.
Runnable examples â€” curl for every operation, ideally executable in CI against a sandbox. Examples that are generated from the same DTOs stay correct.
Linting specs in CI

oasdiff breaking is the single highest-value CI check: it catches a removed field, a narrowed enum, a changed required-ness, a new required parameter, and a changed status code â€” all of which silently break clients that generated from the last version.

practiceTasks: add @nestjs/swagger (or Fastify's schema) to one module, generate openapi.json, commit it, and add a CI script with spectral lint plus oasdiff breaking. Then deliberately introduce three breaking changes (remove a field, add a required parameter, remove a response code) and confirm the CI fails for each with a useful message. Finally, generate a TypeScript client and use it in a test instead of hand-built fetch calls.

interviewQuestions.text: Design-first or code-first, and why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a 70-endpoint public API with three internal consumers and a partner integration, changed weekly by six engineers. Decision: code-first with a committed, diffed spec. Reasoning: my failure mode is not a bad design â€” it is a spec that no longer matches the server, because historically half the endpoints were documented in Confluence and half in code, and they had already diverged in eleven places. With code-first, the DTO classes are the single source of truth and the spec is generated from them, so it is structurally incapable of describing a body the server would reject. Because the generation is deterministic, I can commit the spec and run oasdiff breaking in CI, which gives me the thing design-first is actually good at: a reviewable, machine-checked diff on every PR that says 'this change breaks these clients'. Trade-offs: I lose the pre-implementation design review, so for the two or three *major* changes per year I do write a proposal document first, but I do not gate every endpoint on YAML, and I explicitly reject the idea of hand-editing the spec â€” hand-edited generated artefacts drift within a month. Failure scenario: a team chose design-first, a developer added a required field to the spec and implemented it, and the spec was never regenerated, so the docs and the server disagreed; the SDK was generated from the spec, and a field marked optional in the spec turned out to be required in the server, so the SDK let developers build requests that failed at runtime. Alternative: if I had independent client teams in other languages and a governance board, I would go design-first but with a CI step that boots the service and validates real responses against the spec, which is the only mechanism that actually prevents drift."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API â€” operations, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security. It is the closest thing to a compilable contract, and it can drive documentation, client generation, mock servers, and contract tests.

**Design-first vs code-first**
| | Design-first | Code-first |
|---|---|---|
| Source of truth | The spec (YAML/JSON) | The DTOs and decorators |
| Workflow | Write/review/approve the spec, then implement | Implement, then generate the spec |
| Strengths | Design is reviewed *before* anyone writes code; independent client teams can build in parallel; language-agnostic; enforced by linting in CI | Cannot drift from the implementation; zero duplication; FastAPI, NestJS (with `@nestjs/swagger`), tRPC-adjacent tools, and Spring all do it well; fastest to change |
| Weaknesses | **Drifts from reality** unless generated or diffed; two artefacts to maintain; developers resent the YAML | The spec reflects the *implementation*, including its mistakes; hard to use as a design-review artefact; framework-coupled |
| Middle path | Hand-written spec validated against a live server in CI (`openapi-response-validator`, or `oasdiff` between the committed spec and a generated one) | Generate the spec, commit it, and diff it in CI so drift is a failing build |

**The honest recommendation:** code-first for services you own end to end (the spec is generated from the same DTO classes that validate at runtime, so it cannot describe a body the server does not accept), plus a CI diff against the committed spec so changes are reviewable. Design-first when the API has independent consumers, a governance process, or a non-JS implementation team â€” the *design review* is the value, not the YAML.

**Generating clients.** A committed spec plus a generator (`openapi-generator`, `orval`, `swagger-typescript-api`, `Kiota`, `NSwag`) produces typed SDKs. Do it in CI and publish, rather than having people hand-write clients â€” hand-written clients are where "the API says field `totalCents`, the client says `total`" bugs live. Validate that the generated code compiles in the SDK repo, so a breaking spec change fails the build rather than a consumer's.

**Documentation as a contract.** Three tiers, and you need all three:
1. **The reference** â€” generated from the spec: every endpoint, every field, types, required-ness, status codes, examples. Generated, so it is never wrong.
2. **The guide** â€” hand-written: authentication setup, pagination semantics, idempotency, rate limits, error codes, webhook setup, and a task-oriented quickstart. This is the part humans actually read, and the part the spec cannot generate.
3. **Runnable examples** â€” curl for every operation, ideally executable in CI against a sandbox. Examples that are generated from the same DTOs stay correct.

**Linting specs in CI.** Use Spectral with a rule set: `oasdiff` for breaking changes against the last released spec (a breaking change must be a conscious, approved act), and operation-level rules (every operation has a `operationId`, a summary, tag(s), and at least one error response). A missing `operationId` means generated method names are auto-derived and unstable, which breaks every client on rename.

```bash
# in CI
spectral lint openapi.yaml                  # style + completeness
oasdiff breaking main..HEAD openapi.yaml    # fail the build on a breaking change
openapi-generator validate -i openapi.yaml
```
- **`oasdiff` breaking** is the single highest-value CI check: it catches a removed field, a narrowed enum, a changed required-ness, a new required parameter, and a changed status code â€” all of which silently break clients that generated from the last version.
- Validate the **examples** in the spec (a strict validator will catch a `null` in a non-nullable field and a missing required field in an example).
- Keep the spec in the same repo as the code and in the same PR. A spec in a wiki is already obsolete.

**Keeping docs in sync, honestly**
- Nothing keeps them in sync except automation: generate, diff, validate. Documentation discipline alone fails at 60 endpoints.
- Changelog entries for every breaking change, with the migration path, referenced from the `Deprecation` header (5.4.8).
- A deprecation registry: a table of deprecated fields with the version, the reason, the replacement, and the removal version. Publish it and check it in CI that every entry has a removal date.
- **Examples are the docs most people read.** Generate them from the same fixtures your e2e tests use, so a test proves the example works.

**Questions**
1. Design-first or code-first, and why?
2. What does linting an OpenAPI spec in CI actually catch?
3. Why does a missing `operationId` matter?
4. What are the three documentation tiers?
5. How do you keep examples honest?

topics.bodyMarkdown:
**Definition:** OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API â€” operations, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security. It is the closest thing to a compilable contract, and it can drive documentation, client generation, mock servers, and contract tests.

**Design-first vs code-first**
| | Design-first | Code-first |
|---|---|---|
| Source of truth | The spec (YAML/JSON) | The DTOs and decorators |
| Workflow | Write/review/approve the spec, then implement | Implement, then generate the spec |
| Strengths | Design is reviewed *before* anyone writes code; independent client teams can build in parallel; language-agnostic; enforced by linting in CI | Cannot drift from the implementation; zero duplication; FastAPI, NestJS (with `@nestjs/swagger`), tRPC-adjacent tools, and Spring all do it well; fastest to change |
| Weaknesses | **Drifts from reality** unless generated or diffed; two artefacts to maintain; developers resent the YAML | The spec reflects the *implementation*, including its mistakes; hard to use as a design-review artefact; framework-coupled |
| Middle path | Hand-written spec validated against a live server in CI (`openapi-response-validator`, or `oasdiff` between the committed spec and a generated one) | Generate the spec, commit it, and diff it in CI so drift is a failing build |

**The honest recommendation:** code-first for services you own end to end (the spec is generated from the same DTO classes that validate at runtime, so it cannot describe a body the server does not accept), plus a CI diff against the committed spec so changes are reviewable. Design-first when the API has independent consumers, a governance process, or a non-JS implementation team â€” the *design review* is the value, not the YAML.

**Generating clients.** A committed spec plus a generator (`openapi-generator`, `orval`, `swagger-typescript-api`, `Kiota`, `NSwag`) produces typed SDKs. Do it in CI and publish, rather than having people hand-write clients â€” hand-written clients are where "the API says field `totalCents`, the client says `total`" bugs live. Validate that the generated code compiles in the SDK repo, so a breaking spec change fails the build rather than a consumer's.

**Documentation as a contract.** Three tiers, and you need all three:
1. **The reference** â€” generated from the spec: every endpoint, every field, types, required-ness, status codes, examples. Generated, so it is never wrong.
2. **The guide** â€” hand-written: authentication setup, pagination semantics, idempotency, rate limits, error codes, webhook setup, and a task-oriented quickstart. This is the part humans actually read, and the part the spec cannot generate.
3. **Runnable examples** â€” curl for every operation, ideally executable in CI against a sandbox. Examples that are generated from the same DTOs stay correct.

**Linting specs in CI.** Use Spectral with a rule set: `oasdiff` for breaking changes against the last released spec (a breaking change must be a conscious, approved act), and operation-level rules (every operation has a `operationId`, a summary, tag(s), and at least one error response). A missing `operationId` means generated method names are auto-derived and unstable, which breaks every client on rename.

```bash
# in CI
spectral lint openapi.yaml                  # style + completeness
oasdiff breaking main..HEAD openapi.yaml    # fail the build on a breaking change
openapi-generator validate -i openapi.yaml
```
- **`oasdiff` breaking** is the single highest-value CI check: it catches a removed field, a narrowed enum, a changed required-ness, a new required parameter, and a changed status code â€” all of which silently break clients that generated from the last version.
- Validate the **examples** in the spec (a strict validator will catch a `null` in a non-nullable field and a missing required field in an example).
- Keep the spec in the same repo as the code and in the same PR. A spec in a wiki is already obsolete.

**Keeping docs in sync, honestly**
- Nothing keeps them in sync except automation: generate, diff, validate. Documentation discipline alone fails at 60 endpoints.
- Changelog entries for every breaking change, with the migration path, referenced from the `Deprecation` header (5.4.8).
- A deprecation registry: a table of deprecated fields with the version, the reason, the replacement, and the removal version. Publish it and check it in CI that every entry has a removal date.
- **Examples are the docs most people read.** Generate them from the same fixtures your e2e tests use, so a test proves the example works.

**Questions**
1. Design-first or code-first, and why?
2. What does linting an OpenAPI spec in CI actually catch?
3. Why does a missing `operationId` matter?
4. What are the three documentation tiers?
5. How do you keep examples honest?

**Model answer, Q1:** "Context: a 70-endpoint public API with three internal consumers and a partner integration, changed weekly by six engineers. Decision: code-first with a committed, diffed spec. interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a review checklist, and the team argues about which smell matters most. Decision: the most expensive to fix is 'no error contract', followed closely by 'no versioning plan'. Reasoning: error contracts are cheap to add on day one and essentially impossible to change later, because every client starts branching on whatever you shipped, and those branches live in other repositories and other languages. If I start with {'error': 'Something went wrong'} and then move to problem details, I have to ship a dual-format error response, keep both formats alive indefinitely, and instrument each client to migrate â€” and clients migrate when they happen to, which means never. The same shape applies to versioned URLs: I can add /v2 later, but I can never make the *first* version have been versioned, and I cannot retroactively give clients a deprecation plan. The others are more recoverable. An unbounded list gets a limit parameter. Inconsistent pagination gets unified in one paginator, and clients that used the old shape keep working because the parameter names are still accepted. Exposing database ids gets a translation layer that emits opaque ids while accepting both. Chatty APIs get composed server-side or behind a BFF, with the old endpoints still available. Missing ETags can be added non-breaking. So I rank by reversibility: contract-level decisions that clients will hard-code are the expensive ones, and behavioural details are cheap to evolve. topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** A repeatable pass over a proposed contract, run *before* implementation, that catches the mistakes in 5.4.1 through 5.4.17 while they are still cheap to fix. Cheap to fix is the entire argument for doing it at design time.

**The review checklist**
- [ ] Every URL is a plural noun; no verbs; consistent casing; no trailing slashes
- [ ] Nesting is at most one level, and every nested child is also addressable flat
- [ ] State transitions are action endpoints, not settable fields
- [ ] Every method is used per its semantics; `GET` never mutates
- [ ] Every operation has: a `2xx` with a documented body, and a `4xx` with a problem document
- [ ] Status codes are precise: `201`+`Location`, `202` for accepted work, `409` for conflicts, `422` for semantic validation, `429`+`Retry-After` for limits
- [ ] Every list endpoint is paginated with a hard cap, a stable sort, and a tiebreaker
- [ ] Every non-idempotent, money-touching, or webhook-receiving endpoint accepts an `Idempotency-Key`
- [ ] Error bodies are RFC 9457 with a stable `code`, field `pointer`s, and a `traceId`
- [ ] Every request body is a DTO with `whitelist`/`forbidNonWhitelisted`; no `data: req.body`
- [ ] Money is integer minor units + currency; dates are RFC 3339 UTC; large ids are strings
- [ ] Authorization is per-object, not just per-role; a `404` is returned for inaccessible private resources
- [ ] `ETag`/`Last-Modified` exist on cacheable reads; `Cache-Control` is deliberate per sensitivity
- [ ] Versioning strategy is documented, with a `Deprecation`/`Sunset` plan and usage measurement
- [ ] The OpenAPI spec exists, is linted, and has a breaking-change diff in CI
- [ ] Rate limits are documented and enforced with truthful headers
- [ ] Long operations use `202` + a status resource; cancellation is a modelled transition
- [ ] Webhooks are signed with a timestamp, retried with backoff, and have a delivery log
- [ ] A correlation id flows in the request, out in the response, and through the logs
- [ ] Pagination and filter parameters are namespaced and cannot collide with field names
- [ ] No endpoint returns an unbounded list, ever

**The smells**
| Smell | Why it is bad | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Verbs in URLs (`/getUser`, `/createOrder`) | Method already carries the verb; the URL stops being a resource | `GET /users/{id}`, `POST /orders` |
| Mixed naming (`/user` and `/users`, `/Order` and `/orders`) | Every client needs special cases; impossible to generate well | Pick one convention, apply everywhere |
| Unbounded lists (`GET /orders`) | One request can take the database down; no pagination story | Cursor pagination with a hard cap |
| No error contract | Clients parse prose; every service differs | RFC 9457 everywhere, from one package |
| Exposing database ids and internal shapes | Leaks schema, breaks refactors, invites enumeration | Opaque public ids, purpose-built response DTOs |
| No versioning plan | The first breaking change forces a fork or an outage | Versioned URLs, additive-first policy, sunset headers |
| Inconsistent pagination | Three pages of the same entity paginate differently | One paginator, one parameter naming scheme |
| Chatty APIs | N+1 over HTTP: 6 round trips for one screen | Compose server-side; embed sub-resources; a BFF |
| `200` with an error body | Every proxy, cache and tool believes it succeeded | Correct status codes |
| `POST` for a read that is too slow, with no `202` | The client is stuck and does not know it | `202` + status resource |
| Sensitive data in the URL | Enters logs, history, `Referer` | Body or headers |
| Returning full internal objects | Leaks every field added later, forever | Explicit response DTOs / serializers |
| `DELETE` that actually soft-deletes but returns `204` with no signal | Clients cannot tell a delete from a no-op | `200` with the object, or a distinct `archived` state |
| One giant "v1" module | Nothing is reusable, nothing is ownable | Feature modules with explicit boundaries |
| `updated_at` returned as a string the client is told to send back for concurrency | Client-forgeable and format-fragile | `ETag` + `If-Match` or a `version` field compared server-side |

**How to run the review.** In a real team: a written checklist, a 30-minute session per new *resource* (not per endpoint), and one rule that the API owner can block a change. The goal is not to reject designs; it is to make the trade-offs explicit once, at the boundary, instead of discovering them in ten client implementations.

**Questions**
1. Why should state transitions be action endpoints?
2. What is a "chatty API" and what are the fixes?
3. Why is exposing database ids a problem?
4. How do you run this review without becoming a blocker?
5. Which smell is most expensive to fix later?

**Model answer, Q5:** "Context: a review checklist, and the team argues about which smell matters most. If I start with `{'error': 'Something went wrong'}` and then move to problem details, I have to ship a dual-format error response, keep both formats alive indefinitely, and instrument each client to migrate â€” and clients migrate when they happen to, which means never. The same shape applies to versioned URLs: I can add `/v2` later, but I can never make the *first* version have been versioned, and I cannot retroactively give clients a deprecation plan. The others are more recoverable. An unbounded list gets a `limit` parameter. Inconsistent pagination gets unified in one paginator, and clients that used the old shape keep working because the parameter names are still accepted. Exposing database ids gets a translation layer that emits opaque ids while accepting both. Chatty APIs get composed server-side or behind a BFF, with the old endpoints still available. Missing `ETag`s can be added non-breaking. So I rank by reversibility: contract-level decisions that clients will hard-code are the expensive ones, and behavioural details are cheap to evolve. Failure scenario: a company ships v1 with a flat error shape and no version in the path, and eighteen months later the biggest client needs a real error taxonomy for a compliance audit; the only options are a year of dual-format maintenance or a v2 that most clients never adopt, so the bad contract lives on indefinitely. Alternative: pick the expensive decisions carefully at the start and revisit the cheap ones whenever it is convenient, which is the opposite of how teams allocate review attention."

topics.title: Caching Headers for APIs
topics.description: Assigning a cache policy to each response â€” how long it may be stored, by whom, and how it is revalidated â€” matched to the sensitivity of the data behind it.
keyConcepts: A workable policy
no-cache is not "do not cache" â€” it means *store it but revalidate before use*. no-store is the one that means do not store. Confusing the two is the most common caching bug.
must-revalidate stops a stale response being served after it expires even if the origin is unreachable â€” a correctness guarantee for money and permissions.

Generate ETags from a version or a content hash, not from a timestamp; a weak ETag (W/"...") means "semantically equivalent, possibly different bytes" and is what you want for a JSON representation whose key order may vary.
Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept is required whenever the body depends on those headers, or the CDN will serve a Brotli body to a client that cannot decode it, or a CSV to a client that asked for JSON.
Vary: Authorization / Cookie effectively disables shared caching â€” which is correct for per-user data. Do not instead rely on cache keys including the cookie if the CDN is not configured for it.

ETags on paginated lists are expensive to get right (they depend on the whole page's content and on the query string) and are often not worth it. Cursor-paginated, frequently-changing lists are usually no-cache or not cacheable at all.
Never cache a response that varies by an undeclared header. If your endpoint's body depends on Accept-Language, X-Tenant, or Authorization, it must either be private/no-store or declare Vary.
Set-Cookie and caching: a Set-Cookie response is not cacheable by shared caches unless explicitly allowed; a login response must be no-store.

CDN keys: include the query string, and normalize it (sorted parameters) or the same resource has N cache entries. Do not cache anything with a cursor if the same page content could serve different users.
Interaction with the rest of the design

Idempotency and caching are opposites: a replayed response from the idempotency store is the *same* bytes, so it can be stored with the same ETag and served with 304; but never put an idempotent response in a *shared* cache.
commonMistakes: no-cache meaning "do not cache" in a team's understanding; missing Vary: Accept-Encoding; Vary on a per-request value (cache fragmentation); caching a 429; caching anything per-user in a shared cache; strong ETags for a body whose key order varies; missing must-revalidate on balances and permissions.
practiceTasks: add caching headers to ten endpoints across your sensitivity levels, then verify with curl -I and a local proxy: a second GET with If-None-Match returns 304 with no body; a no-store response is never revalidated; Vary: Accept-Encoding is present and a client sending Accept-Encoding: identity gets a decodable body; and a 429 is not cached.

interviewQuestions.text: `no-cache` vs `no-store`?
Why does a wrong `Vary` cause a real bug?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our API returns Brotli-compressed JSON, and a handful of clients started reporting corrupt or truncated bodies. Decision: Vary: Accept-Encoding on every response whose encoding depends on the request, and an explicit test that asserts it. Reasoning: a shared cache â€” a CDN, a reverse proxy, or the browser's own HTTP cache â€” stores one entry per cache key, and by default the key is the URL. If I return Brotli to a client that sent Accept-Encoding: gzip and the cache is unaware that the representation varies, a *different* client that cannot decode Brotli gets the Brotli bytes and fails to parse them. The cache is doing exactly what it was told; the bug is that I did not tell it the response depends on a request header. The same applies to Accept (CSV versus JSON), Accept-Language, and any header that changes the body. topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** Assigning a cache policy to each response â€” how long it may be stored, by whom, and how it is revalidated â€” matched to the sensitivity of the data behind it.

The semantics of `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and `Vary` are covered in **3.5.6**; the algorithms and CDN layer are in **PHASE 6 Caching Layers**. What belongs here is applying them to an API.

**A workable policy**
| Response | Headers | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Public, unchanging reference data (countries, plans) | `public, max-age=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400` + `ETag` | Tolerable staleness, big win at the edge |
| Authenticated, per-user reads | `private, max-age=0, must-revalidate` + `ETag` | Browser may cache briefly; never a shared cache |
| Anything sensitive (PII, tokens, financial) | `no-store` | Do not persist at all |
| Anything a client must not see stale (balances, permissions) | `no-cache` + `ETag` | Always revalidate; `304` keeps it cheap |
| Writes | `no-store` (default) | Never cache a mutation result |

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate
ETag: "v7-9f2c1ab"
Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept
Last-Modified: Fri, 01 May 2026 10:00:00 GMT

# client revalidation
GET /v1/orders/42
If-None-Match: "v7-9f2c1ab"
    â†’ 304 Not Modified   (no body, no content-length)
```
- **`no-cache` is not "do not cache"** â€” it means *store it but revalidate before use*. `no-store` is the one that means do not store. Confusing the two is the most common caching bug.
- **`must-revalidate`** stops a stale response being served after it expires even if the origin is unreachable â€” a correctness guarantee for money and permissions.
- **Generate ETags from a version or a content hash**, not from a timestamp; a weak ETag (`W/"..."`) means "semantically equivalent, possibly different bytes" and is what you want for a JSON representation whose key order may vary.
- **`Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept`** is required whenever the body depends on those headers, or the CDN will serve a Brotli body to a client that cannot decode it, or a CSV to a client that asked for JSON.
- **`Vary: Authorization` / `Cookie`** effectively disables shared caching â€” which is correct for per-user data. Do not instead rely on cache keys including the cookie if the CDN is not configured for it.
- **ETags on paginated lists** are expensive to get right (they depend on the whole page's content and on the query string) and are often not worth it. Cursor-paginated, frequently-changing lists are usually `no-cache` or not cacheable at all.
- **Never cache a response that varies by an undeclared header.** If your endpoint's body depends on `Accept-Language`, `X-Tenant`, or `Authorization`, it must either be `private`/`no-store` or declare `Vary`.
- **`Set-Cookie` and caching:** a `Set-Cookie` response is not cacheable by shared caches unless explicitly allowed; a login response must be `no-store`.
- **CDN keys:** include the query string, and normalize it (sorted parameters) or the same resource has N cache entries. Do not cache anything with a cursor if the same page content could serve different users.

**Interaction with the rest of the design**
- **Idempotency and caching are opposites**: a replayed response from the idempotency store is the *same* bytes, so it can be stored with the same `ETag` and served with `304`; but never put an idempotent response in a *shared* cache.
- **`ETag` + `If-Match`** is the concurrency primitive (5.4.5); **`If-None-Match`** on `GET` is the caching primitive. Same header family, different purpose.
- **Rate limits and caching interact**: a `429` must never be cached (`no-store`), or a client will be throttled after a single refusal.
- **A `304` response must not carry a body**, and should repeat the caching headers so the freshness lifetime is refreshed.

1. `no-cache` vs `no-store`?
2. Why does a wrong `Vary` cause a real bug?
3. When are ETags on list endpoints not worth it?
4. How does caching interact with `ETag`-based concurrency?
5. What must never be cached?

**Model answer, Q2:** "Context: our API returns Brotli-compressed JSON, and a handful of clients started reporting corrupt or truncated bodies. If I return Brotli to a client that sent `Accept-Encoding: gzip` and the cache is unaware that the representation varies, a *different* client that cannot decode Brotli gets the Brotli bytes and fails to parse them. The cache is doing exactly what it was told; the bug is that I did not tell it the response depends on a request header. The same applies to `Accept` (CSV versus JSON), `Accept-Language`, and any header that changes the body. The related failure is the reverse: a `Vary` that is too broad, listing a header that varies per request (a timestamp, a correlation id, a session nonce), which fragments the cache so every request is a miss and the hit rate collapses to zero. So `Vary` needs to be the minimal correct set, and `Authorization`/`Cookie` in `Vary` is the honest way to say 'this is per-user, do not share'. Trade-offs: every variant multiplies storage and reduces the hit rate, and `Vary: Accept-Encoding` with a poorly configured CDN still misses because the CDN normalises encodings. Failure scenario: the CDN is configured to cache only `200` responses, and our endpoint returns `Vary: Accept-Encoding`; a client that sends `Accept-Encoding: identity` gets the Brotli body, and since Brotli content has no magic number in a JSON media type, the failure surfaces as a JSON parse error on the client with no server-side clue. Alternative: always negotiate encoding at the edge rather than the origin â€” terminate TLS and compression at the CDN, disable origin-side compression for cacheable responses, and let `Vary: Accept-Encoding` be handled by the edge's own normalisation. That removes the failure mode from the application entirely, at the cost of moving a decision into infrastructure that you then have to configure correctly once."

**Mistakes:** `no-cache` meaning "do not cache" in a team's understanding; missing `Vary: Accept-Encoding`; `Vary` on a per-request value (cache fragmentation); caching a `429`; caching anything per-user in a shared cache; strong ETags for a body whose key order varies; missing `must-revalidate` on balances and permissions.

**Mini task:** add caching headers to ten endpoints across your sensitivity levels, then verify with `curl -I` and a local proxy: a second `GET` with `If-None-Match` returns `304` with no body; a `no-store` response is never revalidated; `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is present and a client sending `Accept-Encoding: identity` gets a decodable body; and a `429` is not cached.

topics.title: Why GraphQL Exists, and What It Does Not Solve
topics.description: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for an API described by a single type schema, where the client sends a document describing exactly the fields it wants, and the server returns a response shaped like that document.
keyConcepts: The problem it solves: over-fetching and under-fetching
Over-fetching: the server returns fields nobody asked for. Costs bandwidth, JSON parse time, and serialization work on the server.

Under-fetching: the client needs data that does not exist at any single REST endpoint, so it makes a second request, and if the second request is slow the screen arrives in two pieces. Costs round-trip latency and creates waterfall rendering.
Multiple round trips are the real cost, not payload size, on a high-latency network. This is the actual argument for GraphQL, and it is strongest on mobile.
What GraphQL does NOT solve

Authorization. Every field is a separate authorization decision. A field you forgot to guard is a data leak. A guard applied per row is an N+1 (5.5.5, 5.5.11). GraphQL has no opinion on authN/authZ; see PHASE 7.
Caching at the CDN. A POST is not cached by default. Every CDN in the world caches GET by URL. See 5.5.10.
N+1 queries. Field resolvers run per parent object, so 100 posts Ã— 1 author query = 101 queries. It is *easier* to write N+1 in GraphQL than in REST, and DataLoader is mandatory, not optional.
Query cost. A client can ask for a query that is exponentially more expensive than any REST endpoint you would have designed. Depth, complexity and cost limits are required.
Operational simplicity. It is a new protocol with a schema registry, code generation, a resolvers layer, query analysis, and a client cache that has its own invalidation model.

Partial failure semantics. GraphQL returns 200 with data containing nulls and an errors array. That is a new contract for clients, proxies, and monitoring â€” and 200 means your alerting will not fire unless you parse the body.
Stable, cacheable URLs. A REST resource is a URL. A GraphQL query is a document; making it cacheable requires persisted queries and GET (5.5.10).
commonMistakes: adopting GraphQL for over-fetching alone (bandwidth is cheap; latency is the real issue); believing DataLoader is optional; thinking a 200 with errors is the same as a REST 4xx; expecting CDN caching to keep working; assuming one GraphQL endpoint is one database query; treating the schema as an implementation detail rather than a published contract.
practiceTasks: take one screen in an app that makes three REST calls. Write the equivalent GraphQL query and a BFF route that does the server-side composition. Then instrument both: count queries, bytes, and p95 latency. Then try the same thing *without* DataLoader and record how the query count scales with the page size.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does GraphQL actually solve?
Why is multiple round trips worse than large payloads?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a mobile app on a 200ms round-trip network needs the user's profile plus their recent activity. With REST that is three endpoints, so the screen renders in about 600ms of pure latency plus payload, and the waterfall is visible in the network tab. Decision: this is the strongest case for GraphQL, and I would consolidate those reads into one query. Reasoning: the cost structure of a mobile network is dominated by round-trip latency, not by bytes. A response of 4 KB and a response of 40 KB both arrive in roughly the same time on a high-latency link, because the transfer is one or a few packets; what costs 200ms is the request/response handshake plus the server's own time. Three sequential requests therefore cost roughly three times one request, no matter how small each one is. The other half is client complexity: with three endpoints the client has to join the results, handle partial failure where the profile loaded but the activity did not, and implement a waterfall that a single request removes by construction. GraphQL fixes both â€” one round trip, and the server returns all three shapes in one atomic response, so there is no partial state. Trade-offs: I have traded a fixed, cacheable, cheap contract for a flexible, non-cacheable, potentially expensive one. The server now has to solve the join efficiently (batching, DataLoader), guard every field, and enforce query cost limits, and the CDN stops helping because the request is a POST. Failure scenario: a team moves a mobile screen to GraphQL for one round trip, then discovers that the resolver for the activity list is N+1 with a per-row permission check, so the single query is now 200ms *slower* than the three REST calls, and they have lost CDN caching and gained a schema to govern. Alternative: keep REST for the reads and add a BFF endpoint â€” one server-side endpoint that composes the three REST calls and returns one response. That gets the round-trip win with none of the schema, cache, or cost-analysis problems, which is why a BFF is the answer far more often than a full GraphQL adoption."

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** GraphQL is a query language and runtime for an API described by a single type schema, where the client sends a document describing exactly the fields it wants, and the server returns a response shaped like that document.

**The problem it solves: over-fetching and under-fetching.**
```
REST, a profile screen needs name, avatar, and the last 5 posts' titles
  GET /users/42                     â†’ 4 KB, 3 of 40 fields used
  GET /users/42/posts?limit=5       â†’ 5 KB, 20 fields per post, 2 used
  = 2 round trips, 9 KB transferred, 89% wasted

GraphQL, one request
  query { user(id: 42) { name avatar posts(first: 5) { title } } }
  = 1 round trip, ~1 KB, 100% used
```
- **Over-fetching**: the server returns fields nobody asked for. Costs bandwidth, JSON parse time, and serialization work on the server.
- **Under-fetching**: the client needs data that does not exist at any single REST endpoint, so it makes a second request, and if the second request is slow the screen arrives in two pieces. Costs round-trip latency and creates waterfall rendering.
- **Multiple round trips are the real cost**, not payload size, on a high-latency network. This is the actual argument for GraphQL, and it is strongest on mobile.

**What GraphQL does NOT solve**
- **Authorization.** Every field is a separate authorization decision. A field you forgot to guard is a data leak. A guard applied per row is an N+1 (5.5.5, 5.5.11). GraphQL has no opinion on authN/authZ; see **PHASE 7**.
- **Caching at the CDN.** A `POST` is not cached by default. Every CDN in the world caches `GET` by URL. See 5.5.10.
- **N+1 queries.** Field resolvers run per parent object, so 100 posts Ã— 1 author query = 101 queries. It is *easier* to write N+1 in GraphQL than in REST, and DataLoader is mandatory, not optional.
- **Query cost.** A client can ask for a query that is exponentially more expensive than any REST endpoint you would have designed. Depth, complexity and cost limits are required.
- **Operational simplicity.** It is a new protocol with a schema registry, code generation, a resolvers layer, query analysis, and a client cache that has its own invalidation model.
- **Partial failure semantics.** GraphQL returns `200` with `data` containing `null`s and an `errors` array. That is a new contract for clients, proxies, and monitoring â€” and `200` means your alerting will not fire unless you parse the body.
- **Stable, cacheable URLs.** A REST resource is a URL. A GraphQL query is a document; making it cacheable requires persisted queries and GET (5.5.10).
- **It is not automatically faster.** A GraphQL response can easily be *slower* than the equivalent REST endpoint (debugging scenario #2), because of resolver overhead, N+1, and a bigger server-side surface.

**The honest summary:** GraphQL moves complexity from the client to the server. The client gets flexibility and one round trip; the server gets a query-planning problem, a caching problem, an authorization problem, and a schema-governance problem. It is a good trade when you have many clients with different needs, a team that can own a schema, and mobile latency to save. It is a bad trade for a simple, well-understood CRUD API with one web client.

A response of 4 KB and a response of 40 KB both arrive in roughly the same time on a high-latency link, because the transfer is one or a few packets; what costs 200ms is the request/response handshake plus the server's own time. interviewQuestions.text: Why is nullability a design decision and not a detail?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a schema where every field is non-null, and one flaky third-party enrichment call now nulls the entire product page for a few percent of requests. Decision: non-null only for values the system guarantees, nullable at every boundary, and treat nullability as part of the API contract that clients code against. Reasoning: non-null is a promise with a large blast radius. When a non-null field's resolver throws â€” an unexpected null from a database, a serialization failure, a downstream timeout â€” GraphQL cannot return a partial value, so it propagates the error upward: the field becomes null, and if its parent is also non-null the parent becomes null, all the way up. Making the field nullable gives the error somewhere to land: the field is null, the error appears in errors with its path, the parent stays intact, and the client renders the rest of the page. That is the difference between a degraded page and a broken page. Nullability also has a design dimension: User.displayName should be nullable because a user genuinely may not have set one, and making it non-null would force the API to invent an empty string, which is a lie the client cannot distinguish from a real name. Trade-offs: nullable means every client has to handle null, which is annoying in TypeScript, and it is easy to under-apply and end up with everything optional and no guarantees. Failure scenario: a team makes Order.customer non-null because in the database it is a required foreign key, and then an order created through a legacy import path has a dangling customer reference, so one order's customer field errors and, because Order is non-null in a list, the entire orders connection becomes null â€” the customer's whole order history disappears because of one bad row. Alternative: make the field nullable *and* fix the data integrity, so the schema tells the truth about the possibility of absence. And enforce it in tests: a resolver for a non-null field should never return null, which is exactly what a schema-level test that resolves every field against fixtures will tell you."
